sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: e-National Agriculture Market (e-NAM) http://www.enam.gov.in National Agriculture Market (NAM) is a pan -India electronic trading portal which networks the existing APMC mandis to create a unified national market for agricultural commodities. The NAM Portal provides a single window service for all APMC related information and services. This includes commodity arrivals & prices, buy & sell trade offers, provision to respond t o trade offers, among other services. While material flow (agriculture produce) continue to happen through mandis, an online market reduces transaction costs and information asymmetry. Agriculture marketing is administered by the States as per their agri -marketing regulations, under which, the State is divided into several market areas, each of which is administered by a separate Agricultural Produce Marketing Committee (APMC) which imposes its own marketing regulation (including fees). This fragmentation of markets, even within the State, hinders free flow of agri commodities from one market area to another and multiple handling of agri-produce and multiple levels of mandi charges ends up escalating the prices for the consumers without commensurate benefit to the farmer. NAM addresses these challenges by creating a unified market through online trading platform, both, at State and National level and promotes uniformity, streamlining of procedures across the integrated markets, remo ves information asymmetry between buyers and sellers and promotes real time price discovery, based on actual demand and supply, promotes transparency in auction process, and access to a nationwide market for the farmer, with prices commensurate with qualit y of his produce and online payment and availability of better quality produce and at more reasonable prices to the consumer.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Expert System in Agriculture An Expert System (ES), also called a Knowledge Based System (KBS), is a computer program designed to simulate the problem -solving behavior of an expert in a narrow domain or discipline. The expert system could be developed for decision-making and location specific technology dissemination process. An expert system is software that attempts to reproduce the performance of one or more human experts, most commonly in a specific problem domain, and is a traditional application and/or subfield of artificial intelligence. Expert system helps in selection of crop or variety, diagnosis or identification of pests, diseases and disorders and taking valuable decisions on its management. The expert systems developed earlier were more of text based and could be utilized only by the extension officials and scienti sts. Expert system for agriculture (Paddy, Sugarcane, Banana, Ragi and Coconut) and animal husbandry for the three states in their respective languages i.e., Tamil Nadu (Tamil), Karnataka (Kannada) and Kerala (Malayalam) was developed.

Decision Support System (DSS) Decision support systems are a class of computer -based information systems including knowledge -based systems that support decision -making activities. DSS is a computerized system for making decisions. A decision is a choice between alternatives based on es timates of the values of those alternatives. Supporting a decision means helping farmers working alone or in a group gathers intelligence, generate alternatives and make choices. Accordingly, the DSS has been contemplated and designed to get best possible options and decision by farmer themselves for the day today agriculture operation. Drop down formula or multiple combo boxes have been created using simple dot net programme. Each box in the DSS is correlated with each one for retrieving the best possible decision support for crop cultivation.

sections.heading: rop Doctor
sections.text: Crop doctor is a vital component in the expert system, which act as artificial intelligence. It is picture and image based ‘if and then rule’ based programme which has written using dot net programme. It deals with diagnosing the pest, disease and nutritio nal disorders affecting the selected crops. The first obvious sign is given as thumbnail images in the Key Visual Symptoms (Primary Symptom) with multiple stages (Secondary Symptoms). Primary and secondary symptoms have been documented in stage -by-stage an d loaded in the expert system shell by using if and then rule based programme. The concerned experts have validated all the symptoms, which loaded in the expert system shell. Call center services are available from 6.00 am to 10.00 pm on all seven days of the week at each KCC location. Kisan Call Centre agents known as Farm Tele Advisor(FTAs), are graduates or above (i.e. PG or Doctorate) in Agriculture or allied (Horticulture, Animal Husbandry, Fisheries, Poultry, Bee -keeping, Sericulture, Aquaculture, Agricultural Engineering, Agricultural Marketing, Bio -technology, Home Science etc. and possess excellent communication skills in respective local language. A Kisan Knowledge Management System (KKMS) to facilitate correct, consistent and quick replies to the queries of farmers and capture all the details of their calls, has been developed. sections.heading: Levels of KCC
sections.text: The Kisan Call Center, consists of three levels namely Level -I (the basic Call Center interface, with high quality bandwidth and local language proficient Agriculture Graduate), Level-II (Subject Matter Specialists on concerned important crops and enterpri ses, connected through good bandwidth telecom and computer connectivity) and Level -III (the Management Group to ensure ultimate answering and resolution of all the farmers queries which are not resolved at Level-II, connected on off line mode). Level - I: The call coming to the call center is picked up by an operator (level I functionary) who after a short welcome message takes down the basic information and the query of the caller. These details are fed into a computer located next to the operator by the o perator himself. And the first level receiver of the call would also feeds into the computer the question being asked by the farmer. The first level operators preferably would be an agricultural graduate with rural background knowing local language. They s hould also possess good communication skills. They would be in a position to answer a majority of the questions likely to be asked by the farmers. Level - II: The level -II consists of Subject Matter Specialists (SMS) who are located at their respective place (Research Stations, ATICs, KVKs, Agricultural colleges), of work. In case the first level operator is not able to answer the question, the operator forwards (in call sharing mode) the call to the concerned Subject Matter Specialist. The data relating t o the caller including the question asked is also be transferred to the Level -II functionary on his computer along with the call. Hence, when the specialist takes the forwarded call, his computer also shows the data and question asked so that there is no r epetition. It is envisaged that in normal cases, the entire spill over questions from the first level get answered at this level. In case, it is not possible to answer, there is a system to revert back to the caller by post / fax / email or by telephone in 72 hours. Level - III: The level - III consists of a dedicated cell located at the Nodal Office. This would receive the questions that have not been answered at the first and the second levels. Appropriate replies to these questions would be then framed in consultation with the concerned specialists available within or outside the State, by the nodal cell. The replies would be sent to the farmers promptly by post/e -mail/fax/ telephone etc. within 72 hours of receipt of the question 52

topics.title: Farm Crop Management System (FCMS)
topics.definition: Collection of Individual Farmer data regarding personal, Contact, Bank, land and other various resources available at farm holding is the first process of Farm Crop Management System (FCMS). The villages are categorized into micro climate zones and farm level plans will be developed by considering the factors like soil, irrigation and rainfall.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: Collection of Individual Farmer data regarding personal, Contact, Bank, land and other various resources available at farm holding is the first process of Farm Crop Management System (FCMS). The villages are categorized into micro climate zones and farm level plans will be developed by considering the factors like soil, irrigation and rainfall. A basket of options will be provided to the farmers to choose the farm plan. Accordingly the technologies and inputs will be assessed besides credit, machineries and credit requirement. Further the stake holders like input dealers, fertilizer manufacturers, plant protection chemical companies, service providers like PWD, Electricity, credit institutions, insurance companies etc., will be informed about the farmer requirement for advanced planning and support. A Crop Monitoring System has been conceptualized which facilitate field monitoring during critical crop stages. Corrective measures if any needed it will be sent to the farmers through SMS/voice alerts. The yield will be assessed and informed to the market providers to initiate procurement process. Market Intelligence will also be provided to the farmers then and there to select profitable market for higher return.

sections.heading: Scheme Benefits Tracking Module
sections.text: The benefits provided under State, Central and centrally sponsored programmes will be maintained in the AGRISNET portal. The information will be integrated to the individual farmer ID and will contain the detailed list of benefits and photographs showing disbursement of said benefits. For capital assets provision is being created for periodical monitoring and uploading photograph depicting the status of the asset. For technology oriented benefits the various stages of implementation along with its performance will be captured as image and uploaded. The list of beneficiaries under each scheme will be available to public view so as to maintain transparency in implementing the scheme. This system is being implemented in all the districts. To envisage timely inf ormation dissemination and farmer’s data updation an interactive voice response system through mobile has been developed on a collaborative mode with IITM -RTBI, Chennai. sections.heading: Optimal Climate Conditions for Maize Growth

sections.heading: Climate Limitations for Maize Growth
sections.text: Temperature more than 35°C reduces the pollen germination. Temperature < 15°C delays silking and tasseling.

sections.heading: Soil Requirements for Maize Growth
sections.text: Maize is best adapted to well-drained sandy loam to silty loam soil. Water stagnation is extremely harmful to the crop, therefore proper drainage is must.

sections.text: The grain cob is harvested, when cob sheath turns brownish and grains become hard. sections.heading: Shelling
sections.text: Hand shelling is a common practice, but efficiency is very poor. Now, corn sheller of greater efficiency, which is manually driven, tractor drawn, electricity operated is available.

sections.text: Sorghum stubbles/roots have high C: N ratio (50:1), causing temporary immobilization of soil ‘N’ and affecting succeeding crops.

sections.heading: Curing
sections.text: Harvested heads are cured by heaping in shade for one day without drying to make greener ear heads mature. Then drying, threshing, and cleaning are done.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Moong Varieties
sections.text: Moong varieties have different maturity periods, yield potentials, and resistance to diseases.

items: Samrat: matures in 60-65 days, suitable for summer and Kharif season with a yield potential of 12-15 q ha.

Pant moong 4: matures in 65-70 days, resistant to yellow mosaic virus, and yield potential is 10-12 q ha.

sections.heading: Field Preparation
sections.text: A thorough land levelling is must for quick drainage. The crop requires fine seedbed preparation.

sections.heading: Time of Sowing
items: Kharif: Second fortnight of June to first fortnight of July
Rabi: October to November
Summer: Middle of March to middle of April

sections.heading: Seed Rate and Spacing
sections.text: During Kharif season 12-15 kg seed per hectare should be sown in 45 cm apart, while during Rabi and summer seasons 20 kg seed per hectare should be sown in rows 30 cm apart.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment
sections.text: Before sowing seed should be treated with Thiram or Carbendazim (Bavistin) at the rate of 2.5 g/kg of seed.

sections.heading: Rhizobium Culture
sections.text: Rhizobium culture is a must to get a bumper crop, as it helps in the development of nodules on the roots which are beneficial for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil.

sections.heading: Manures and Fertilizers
sections.text: Greengram is generally raised on the residual fertility of soil. In case of light soils of poor fertility, it needs addition of organic manures like FYM or compost @ 8-10 tonnes/ha.

topics.title: Zinc Sulphate and Elemental Sulphur for Higher Yields
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Application of 20 kg/ha each of zinc sulphate and elemental sulphur is essential for higher yields.

sections.heading: Water Management
sections.text: For rainy season crop, irrigation is not needed but drainage is very important. For Rabi and summer five to six irrigations may be given. The first irrigation should be given about 20-25 days after sowing. The subsequent irrigations should be given at an interval of 12-15 days and irrigation should be stopped after 40-45 days of sowing.

sections.heading: Weed Control
sections.text: Two weedings at 20 days interval from 25 days after sowing keep the field free from harmful weeds. Chemicals like Fluchloralin (Basalin) 1kg a.i. per hectare in 800- 1000 litres of water may be applied as pre-planting spray.

sections.heading: Diseases
sections.text: Important diseases are yellow mosaic, mosaic mottle, leaf crinkle, leaf curl, seed and seedling rot, cercospora leaf spot, anthracnose and charcoal rot. The symptoms and control measures are given below-

topics.title: Yellow Mosaic Virus
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Symptoms of Yellow mosaic virus appear with a month of sowing, causing leaf lamina to become yellow and scattered round spots.

sections.heading: Control Measures
items: Grow resistant varieties like Asha, Pant moong-4, Narendra moong-1 etc.
Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

topics.title: Mosaic Mottle
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Leaf margin shows upward rolling, become deformed, irregular light green areas appeared alternating with normal green in leaf surface.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Leaf margin shows upward rolling, become deformed, irregular light green areas appeared alternating with normal green in leaf surface. Control measures: Grow resistant/tolerant varieties, Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

sections.heading: Leaf Crinkle
sections.text: Symptoms appear first in third leaf after 3-4 weeks of sowing. Leaves become enlarge followed by crinkling Control measures: Rogue out disease plant as soon as they appear.

topics.title: Leaf Curl
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A viral disease characterized by curling of leaf margins downwards, reddish-brown discoloration on the under surface of leaves, and chlorosis around lateral veins.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: It is a viral disease; chlorosis appear around the lateral vein near the leaf margin of young plants. The affected leaves show curling of margins downwards while the veins on the under surface of the leaf show reddish-brown discoloration.

sections.heading: Control Measures
items: Spraying of Oxydemeton methyl (Metasystox) (0.1%) + Melathion (0.1%) at 10 days interval is very effective.

topics.title: Cercospora Leaf Spot
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Caused by two species of cercospora fungus, small round spots with violet red in colour may be observed.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.text: Spraying of Mabcozeb 75 WP at the rate of 2 kg in 1000 litre of water per hectare at 10 days interval is very effective.

topics.title: Anthracnose
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Diseased by fungus Colletorichum capsici, characterized by dark brown circular spot that increases in size with concentric ridges and ash color.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Diseased is caused by fungus Colletorichum capsici, dark brown circular spot appears initially, later the spots increase in size by developing concentric ridges and the colour turns into ash colour.

sections.heading: Control measures
items: Spraying of Mabcozeb 75 WP at the rate of 2 kg in 1000 litre of water per hectare at 10 days interval

topics.title: Charcoal Rot

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text: Affected parts of the plant turn into reddish-brown to black in colour.

sections.heading: Control measures
items: 1. Diseases can be controlled by treating the seed with Brassicol (0.25%) before sowing.

sections.heading: Control
sections.text: Dusting by 2% Methyl parathion dust at the rate of 25-30 kg ha can be effective to control this disease. Spraying of Endosulfan 1.5 litres in 1000 litres of water can also be efficient.

Spraying of monocrotophos 36EC at the rate of ml/Litre of water can also be done.

topics.title: Black Gram (Vigna mungo L.)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Blackgram is a pulse crop rich in protein and phosphoric acid, used for various culinary preparations and as a green manuring crop.

sections.heading: Uses of Black Gram
sections.text: It is used for preparation of 'bari' (spiced ball) which makes a delicious curry. It is the chief constituent of 'Papad.' Its husked dal is ground into a fine paste and allowed to ferment and then the fermented dal is mixed with equal quantity of rice flour to make 'dosa' and 'idli'. The dal of black gram is also used in the preparation of ‘halwa' and 'imarti'.

sections.heading: Health Benefits
sections.text: Excessive use of black gram causes flatulence which can, however be prevented by adding little as a foetida, pepper and ginger in the culinary preparations. It should not be taken by those who are easily predisposed to rheumatic diseases and urinary calculi as it contains oxalic acid in high concentration.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Uses
items: It fits well as 'catch crop’.
It is also an important crop for cultivating as ‘paira crop’ in paddy.
The green plant (i.e., used as fodder) is very nutritive and it is very useful to milch cow specially.

sections.heading: Environmental Benefits
rows: Black gram has deep root system which binds the soil particles very tightly
acts as cover crop and protects the soil from erosion.

sections.heading: History
sections.text: Black gram is a native of India as is seen from Vedic literature. There is mention of urd seed in Vedic texts such as Kautilya’s “Arthasastra” and “Charak Samhita”. According to Zokovskij (1962) urd originated in India from Phaseolus sublobatus (wild progenitor).

sections.text: The area under blackgram is highest in UP (539 ha) followed by Maharashtra (480 ha). The production under this crop is highest in Andhra Pradesh (251 tonnes) followed by UP (239 tonnes).

sections.text: Vigna mungo var. niger includes varieties with early maturity and black, bold seeds. Vigna mungo var. viridis includes varieties with longer maturity period, small size seeds, and green colour.

sections.heading: General Guidelines
sections.text: In kharif, the crop is sown in rows 30-45 cm apart due to vigorous plant growth, while in other seasons, a narrow row of 20-30 cm is recommended. The plants are thinned to a spacing of 5-10 cm after germination and establishment.

sections.heading: Chemical Seed Treatments

sections.text: Plant identified: Short and erect. Pod: Hairy and black at maturity: Seed: Medium in size and brown in colour. Maturity: 80-85 days. It is resistant to powdery mildew and yellow mosaic disease. Yield: 12-15 q/ha.

sections.heading: Pusa-I
sections.text: Plants are medium tall and semi spreading with average yield of 12-15 q/ha. Pods are medium long and hairy containing 5-6 seeds. It is resistant to yellow mosaic disease.

sections.heading: T-9
sections.text: Plants are dwarf and semi-erect with dark green leaves and hairy pods. Average yield is 10-12.5 q/ha. This variety is susceptible to yellow mosaic disease. It is suitable for cultivation for summer and spring season. This variety is recommended for general cultivation in Haryana. It is a short duration (75-90 days) variety.

Application of S @ 20 kg/ha and Mo 0.5 kg/ha is beneficial.

topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness

sections.heading: Requirements for Irrigation

Under irrigated conditions of rabi, spring and summer seasons

sections.heading: Importance of Weed Control
sections.text: The short stature of crop in sole stands provides scope for intense weed competition. Initial 30-40 days after sowing is critical period of crop-weed competition.

sections.heading: Recommended Weed Control Methods

Pre-plant incorporation of fluchloralin or pre-emergence application of pendimethalin or alachlor @ 1 kg/ha

sections.heading: Cercospora Leaf Scope

sections.heading: Treatment for Cercospora Leaf Scope
items: Spray the crop with Blitox -50 or Indofil M -45 @ 1.5 to 2.0 Kg/ha in 500 l of water.

sections.heading: Bacterial Leaf Scope
sections.text: Symptoms appear as water soaked dots on the under surface of the leaf which remain small in size and the surrounding tissues becomes necrotic.

sections.heading: Treatment for Bacterial Leaf Scope
items: Spray the crop with copper oxychloride @ 1.52 to 2.0 Kg in 500 l of water.

sections.heading: Control Measures

topics.title: Pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan L.)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Pigeonpea is the second most important pulse crop in the country.

sections.heading: Uses of Pigeonpea
sections.text: It is consumed extensively as dal, as it is rich in protein (21%), iron and iodine. It is also rich in essential amino acids like lycine, tyrocene, cystine and arginine.

sections.heading: Other Uses of Pigeonpea
items: The pod husk and seed husk are used as feed for cattle.
The dry sticks are used for thatching and fuel purpose.

sections.heading: Environmental Benefits of Pigeonpea
sections.text: Pigeonpea being a legume possesses valuable property as restorer of nitrogen in soil. The plants shed large number of leaves, which add organic matter to soil.

topics.title: Origin of Pigeonpea
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: India is believed to be the center of origin and diversity of pigeonpea.

sections.heading: Geographical Distribution
sections.text: The closest wild relative of pigeonpea (Atylosia canifolia) was found in India and Australia. The centre of origin is the eastern part of peninsular India, including the state of Orissa, where the closest wild relatives (Cajanus cajanifolia) occur in tropical deciduous woodlands.

sections.heading: Domestication
sections.text: From India it was domesticated to East Africa and West Africa. There was first encountered by Europeans, so it obtained the name Congo Pea. By means of the slave trade, it came to the American continent, probably in the 17th century.

topics.title: Pigeonpea Area and Distribution
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Pigeonpea is grown in over 50 tropical countries, mainly in Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

sections.heading: Main Producing Countries
items: India
Myanmar
Malawi
Uganda
Kenya
Tanzania
Nepal
Congo
Haiti

sections.heading: Major Regions of Cultivation
sections.text: Pigeonpea is mainly grown in Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

sections.heading: Early-Maturing Varieties
sections.text: In Punjab and Haryana, early-maturing varieties are grown, which escape frost.

topics.title: Cajanus indicus
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A type of legume that comprises two varieties: Cajanus indicus var. bicolor (arhar) and Cajanus indicus var. flavus (tur).

sections.heading: Characteristics of Cajanus indicus var. bicolor (Arhar)
sections.text: Late-maturing, tall and bushy perennial types with dark coloured pods containing 4 to 5 seeds.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Cajanus indicus var. flavus (Tur)
sections.text: Early maturing, relatively short stature varieties with yellow flowers and plain pods containing 2-3 seeds.

topics.title: Climatic Requirement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Pigeonpea can be grown in a wide range of climatic conditions, including tropical and subtropical areas with temperatures between 20°-40°C.

sections.heading: Optimum Conditions
sections.text: Moist and humid conditions during the vegetative phase and dry conditions during the reproductive phase are suitable for successful raising of pigeonpea.

sections.heading: Limitations
items: Cannot withstand water logging
Cannot withstand frost

sections.heading: Photoperiod and Light Intensity
sections.text: Pigeonpea is a short-day plant with a critical photoperiod of 13 hours. Low light intensity at pod formation is harmful.

topics.title: Soil Requirement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Pigeonpea can be grown on a wide range of soils, but sandy loam to clay loams are ideal.

sections.heading: Ideal Soil Conditions
sections.text: The soil should be deep, well drained and free from soluble salts.

sections.heading: Soil pH Range
items: pH range of 5.5-8.0 successfully

sections.heading: Limitations Due to Soil Acidity
sections.text: It cannot tolerate soil acidity owing to aluminium toxicity.

topics.title: Cropping System
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Pigeonpea can be intercropped or sown mixed with a number of other crops, such as sorghum, maize, rice, groundnut, sesame, urdbean, greengram, cowpea, ragi and soybean, and an additional yield may be obtained.

sections.heading: Cropping System Details
sections.text: There is a possibility of raising early maturing pigeonpea as a summer crop with intercrop of greengram or cowpea. In this cropping system, pigeonpea may be sown in mid-April keeping a row-to-row distance of 75-90 cm, intercropped with 2-3 rows of greengram.

sections.heading: Harvest Timing
sections.text: Greengram becomes ready for harvest by the end of June (65-70 DAS).

topics.title: Field Preparation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: A clod and weed-free seed-bed for proper germination and establishment of seedlings is achieved by opening the soil through soil-turning plough or disc harrow followed by the cross-harrowing or ploughing with desi plough on or before the onset of monsoon.

sections.heading: Importance of Field Preparation
sections.text: Thorough levelling is essential for quick drainage and also to avoid water logging. Sowing pigeonpea on a ridge and furrow planting is preferred to overcome water logging.

sections.heading: Methods of Field Preparation
items: soil-turning plough or disc harrow
cross-harrowing
ploughing with desi plough

topics.title: Sowing Method
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Seed should be sown behind the plough or with the help of seed drill in rows.

sections.heading: Row Spacing
sections.text: The row spacing in kharif varies from 40-60 cm in short and medium duration varieties to 60-90 cm in long duration varieties. In rabi season, the crop is grown in 30 cm rows.

sections.heading: Thinning
sections.text: After germination, the seedlings are thinned to maintain an intra-row spacing of 15-20 cm.

sections.heading: Optimum Population
items: 1.5-3.0 lakh/ha in rabi

topics.title: Seed Treatment
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Seed should be treated with thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed, Rhizobium culture, or Trichoderma harzianum before sowing.

sections.heading: Inoculation Methods
sections.text: Seed inoculation with Trichoderma harzianum alone or serial inoculation of T. harzianum, followed by Rhizobium may significantly reduce wilt incidence, enhance nodulation and root/shoot growth.

sections.heading: Effectiveness of Inoculations
items: Trichoderma harzianum + Rhizobium was ineffective

topics.title: Sowing Pigeonpea
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The sowing time for pigeonpea should be adjusted to avoid rains and frost at flowering and reproductive stages.

sections.heading: Regional Sowing Times
sections.text: For early rabi planting in Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, September sowing is ideal. The rabi cultivation of pigeonpea in rice fallows is increasingly popular, and is sown immediately after rice harvest in southern India.

sections.heading: Specific Sowing Times by Region
items: Haryana: mid-March to mid-June (T-21)
Uttar Pradesh and northern Rajasthan: mid of June to July end, second fortnight of June
Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal: September
Southern India: immediately after rice harvest
Ist week of July (UPAS-120)
First fortnight of April for double cropping (medium-early varieties)

sections.heading: Late Pigeonpea Sowing
sections.text: The late pigeonpea is sown with the onset of monsoon, preferably by first week of July.

sections.heading: Importance of Irrigation
sections.text: The critical stages for irrigation are branching, flowering and pod filling.

sections.heading: Irrigation at Critical Stages
sections.text: At times of prolonged drought, irrigation at flowering and pod filling stages is highly rewarding in Kharif.

topics.title: Disease Management
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Disease management
topics.definition: Control measures for various plant diseases include treating seeds with thiram, using resistant varieties, crop rotation, removing excess water, and ensuring proper aeration.

sections.heading: Causes of Diseases
sections.text: Various plant diseases are caused by viruses, mites, and fungi.

sections.heading: Types of Diseases
items: Wilt: The plant remains green and show wilting. Removal of roots shows browning of the xylum which curtail the uptake of nutrients.
Sterility mosaic: This is caused by virus. The virus is transmitted by mites which results in malformation of flowers and no pods will be formed.
Phytophthora stem blight: Brown colour spots will appear on the stem and the rotting will start at these spots and plant becomes week and fall down.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.text: Before sowing, seed should be treated with thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed. Use of resistant varieties is best in disease-prone areas. Use crop rotation. Remove the excess rain or irrigation water. There should be proper aeration in the field.

topics.title: Insect Management: Pod Borer
topics.definition: Pod borer is the major insect in North India.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.text: For its control, spray monocrotophos 36 SL@750 ml/ha or 187.5 ml cypermethrin 25 EC or 300 ml fenvalerate 20 EC or 537.5 ml deltamethrin 2.8 EC in 750 liters of water per hactare at 50 % pod formation stage.

topics.title: Threshing and Drying Seeds
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The process of separating seeds from their pods, typically involving threshing, winnowing, and drying to achieve a suitable moisture content.

sections.heading: Threshing
sections.text: Ground and bundled. These are taken to threshing floor and staked upright, dried for a few days and shaken vigorously to separate pods.

sections.heading: Winnowing
sections.text: The resultant material, i.e. pods and dry leaves, is beaten with sticks or is trampled by bullocks. The seeds and husk are separated by winnowing.

sections.heading: Drying
sections.text: Threshed and cleaned produce should be further sun dried to reduce the moisture content to 10-11%.

topics.title: Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea L.)
topics.definition: The groundnut is a legume crop that belongs to the family Leguminosae/Fabaceae, resistant to soil erosion and useful as a rotational crop.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Groundnuts
sections.text: Groundnut cake is chief oil cake feed to animals (7-8% N, 1.5% P2O5 and 1.2% K2O) and also used as manure.

sections.heading: Nutritional Value of Groundnuts
items: rich in nutrients, providing over 30 essential nutrients and phytonutrients
good source of niacin, folate, fiber, magnesium, vitamin E, manganese and phosphorus

topics.title: Origin and History of Groundnut
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Groundnut is a native of Brazil, South America.

sections.heading: History of Spread
sections.text: The crop has spread from Brazil to Peru, Argentina and Ghana, from where it was introduced by the Portuguese into Africa from where it was introduced into Jamaica, Cuba, West Indies islands and North America.

sections.heading: Global Expansion
items: from Mexico across the Pacific to Philippines
then spread to China, India, Malaysia and Indonesia

topics.title: Area and Distribution
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Groundnut is grown in almost all tropical and subtropical countries of the world.

sections.heading: Important Groundnut Growing Countries
items: China
India
USA
Nigeria
Indonesia
Myanmar
Sudan

sections.heading: Productivity by State
sections.text: Tamil Nadu has the highest productivity (1630 kg ha), followed by Gujarat (1360 kg ha).

topics.title: Groundnuts
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Groundnuts have been divided into two groups: the erect or bunch type and the trailing or spreading type.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Groundnut Types
sections.text: Morphologically groundnuts have been divided into two groups. The erect or bunch type-include Arachis hypogaea subspecies fastigiata. Pods in erect type are borne in bunch close to the base of plant. Erect types are normally short duration. Seeds have no dormancy and sometimes the first form pod may sprout before harvest if conditions are suitable. This is due to presence of water-soluble auxins.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Groundnut Types
items: The trailing or spreading type-include Arachis hypogaea subspecies procumbens.
Pods are spreading so harvesting is difficult. Comparatively it is longer duration crop than bunch type.

topics.title: Climatic Requirement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Groundnut is grown in the tropics and subtropical countries, lying between 45ºN and 35ºS, and up to an altitude of 1000 m.

sections.heading: Ideal Climate Conditions
sections.text: The arid and semi-arid regions with 500-700 mm rainfall during crop growth period are ideal for ground production. The crop can be grown successfully in places receiving a maximum rainfall of 1250 mm.

sections.heading: Climate Limitations
sections.text: The groundnut, however, cannot withstand frost, long and severe drought or water stagnation.

sections.heading: Soil Temperature Requirements
sections.text: It seems that plant will grow best when the mean temperature is from 24-33ºC. During ripening period, it requires about a month of warm and dry weather.

topics.title: Soil Requirement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Groundnut thrives best in well-drained sandy and sandy loam soils, with pH between 6.0-6.5.

sections.heading: Optimal Soil Conditions
sections.text: Groundnut is grown on a wide variety of soil types but, thrives best in well-drained sandy and sandy loam soils, as light soil helps in easy penetration of pegs. Heavy and stiff clays are not desirable for groundnut cultivation as pod development is hampered in those soils.

sections.heading: Soil pH
sections.text: Groundnut gives good yields in the soils with pH between 6.0-6.5.

topics.title: Cropping Systems
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Groundnut is grown in rotation with various crops, including wheat, lentil, chickpea, pea, barley, pearl millet, maize, sorghum, castor, cotton, and safflower.

sections.heading: Common Cropping Systems
sections.text: The most common cropping systems are: Groundnut-wheat/barley/ chickpea/field pea / lentil.

sections.heading: Regional Variations
items: Sorghum is grown after harvest of groundnut in Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.

topics.title: Field Preparation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Deep ploughing should be avoided for groundnut due to difficulties in harvesting, but a combination of soil turning plough followed by two harrowings can achieve good surface tilth up to 12-18 cm depth.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.text: Deep ploughing should be avoided for groundnut due to difficulties in harvesting, but a combination of soil turning plough followed by two harrowings can achieve good surface tilth up to 12-18 cm depth.

topics.title: Seed Treatment
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Seeds should be shelled by hand one week before sowing to prevent damage, and treated with a fungicide to check for diseases.

sections.heading: Preparation of Seeds
sections.text: Pods should be shelled by hand one week before sowing. Hand shelling ensures little damage to seeds. Pods shelled long before sowing time are liable to suffer from loss of viability and storage damages.

sections.heading: Seed Treatment with Fungicides
sections.text: Treat the selected kernels with 5 g of Thiram or Captan or Ceresan per kg of kernels so as to check various seed and soil borne diseases.

sections.heading: Inoculation with Rhizobium Culture
sections.text: Seed should be inoculated with proper strain of Rhizobium culture particularly in those places where groundnut is to be grown for the first time.

topics.title: Seed Rate, Spacing and Sowing Method
topics.definition: Seed rate depends upon the growth habit of variety and seed weight for obtaining good yields.

sections.heading: General Guidelines
sections.text: Seed rate can vary according to the region also. In bunch types, the row-to-row distance is kept 30-40 cm and in spreading types 45-60 cm.

sections.heading: Seeding Requirements
items: 80-100 kg of seeds per hectare for bunch types
60-80 kg for spreading types

sections.heading: Plant-to-Plant Distance
sections.text: Plant to plant distance would be 15 and 20-22.5 cm for bunch and spreading types respectively.

sections.heading: Sowing Methods
items: Seed drill
Behind the country plough
Hand dibbling
Tractor-mounted groundnut planter

sections.heading: Sowing Depth
sections.text: The depth of sowing should be 5 cm.

topics.title: Fertilizer Requirement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Groundnut needs more phosphorous, sulphur, calcium, and nitrogen for its growth.

sections.heading: Nutrient Requirements
sections.text: Groundnut needs more phosphorous, sulphur, calcium, and nitrogen for its growth.

items: can be partially met by seed inoculation with efficient strains of rhizobium

topics.title: Maintaining Organic Carbon in Soil for Good Yields
topics.definition: A desirable level of organic carbon in the soil (0.3-0.7%) must be maintained to ensure overall health of soil and continued good yields.

sections.heading: Fertilizer Application
sections.text: Apply 15 kg N, 50 kg P2O5 and 25 kg ZnSO4/ha at the time of sowing. Phosphorus should be applied preferably through single super phosphate; it provides sulphur in addition to phosphorous.

sections.heading: Fertilizer Placement
sections.text: The fertilizers should be placed at the time of sowing about 4-5 cm in the side of the seed and 4-5 cm below the seed level.

sections.heading: Calcium and Yield
sections.text: Calcium too has pronounced effect on proper development of pods and kernels. Use of gypsum @ 100-150 kg/ha at the time of field preparation can add to the yield.

topics.title: Water Management for Groundnuts
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Groundnut does not require irrigation as a rainy season crop, but care should be taken to ensure the soil is friable and has sufficient moisture content.

sections.heading: Importance of Irrigation in Groundnut Cultivation
sections.text: Irrigations are necessary in southern part of country where groundnut grown in Rabi season too, three to four irrigations are necessary.

sections.heading: Critical Stages for Irrigation
items: Flowering
Pegging

sections.heading: Last Irrigation Before Harvesting
sections.text: The last irrigation before harvesting will facilitate the full recovery of pods from the soil.

topics.title: Scheduling of Irrigation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Irrigation at 25% depletion of available soil moisture throughout the growth period results in high pod yield.

sections.heading: Optimal Irrigation Schedules
sections.text: Irrigation at 25% depletion of available soil moisture from pegging to early pod development and at 50% DASM at other stages appears to be ideal for high water use efficiency.

sections.heading: IW/CPE Ratio for High Water Use Efficiency
sections.text: An IW/CPE ratio of 1.0 at moisture sensitive stages and 0.6 during other stages leads to high water use efficiency.

topics.title: Weed Management
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A reduction of 20-45% in yield due to weeds has been recorded.

sections.heading: Recommended Weed Control Measures
sections.text: Two weedings 20 and 45 (days after sowing) DAS are recommended. No weeding or intercultural operation should be done after pegging has commenced; pegs have started moving undergrounds.

sections.heading: Earthing Up
sections.text: Earthing up can be done in bunch and semi spreading types to facilitate maximum penetration of pegs.

sections.heading: Pre-Emergence Application
items: Pre- emergence application of Pendimethalin @ 1 kg a.i./ha along with 2 inter-cultures at 30 and 45 DAS have been recommended in irrigated conditions.
Fluchloralin (Basalin) at the rate of 1 kg a.i. per hectare dissolved in 800-1000 litres of water can also be used as pre-planting incorporation.

topics.title: Disease Management
topics.definition: The management of diseases in groundnut crops.

sections.heading: Tikka Disease or Leaf Spot
sections.text: Cercospora arachidicola and Cercospora personatum cause Tikka disease, appearing 3-4 weeks after sowing. Spots on leaves are circular to irregular, surrounded by a yellow halo, and can be reddish brown to black on the upper surface and smooth and light brown on the lower surface.

sections.heading: Collar Rot and Seed Rot
sections.text: Aspergillus niger causes collar rot and seed rot. Symptoms include rotting of seeds, soft rot of hypocotyls, and post emergence collar rot of seedlings. Treatment involves using Thiram or Captan on healthy seeds.

sections.heading: Sclerotium Rot
sections.text: Sclerotium rolfsii causes sclerotium rot, characterized by white thread-like fungal growth and yellow to brown leaves. Soil application of Brassicol before sowing is beneficial.

sections.heading: Charcoal Rot
sections.text: Microphomina phaseoli causes charcoal rot, marked by a red-brown water-soaked lesion on the stem of infected plants. Spraying Brassicol before sowing is effective.

sections.heading: Rust
sections.text: Puccinia arachidis causes rust, characterized by red pustules on leaves that turn dark brown. Treatment involves spraying Zineb as soon as symptoms appear.

topics.title: Insect Management: White Grub
topics.definition: White-grub, a menace in the light soils of Rajasthan, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana can be controlled effectively by treating seed with Chlorpyriphos 20 EC or Quinalphos 25 EC@ 15 ml/kg of seeds.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.text: White grubs live in soil and remain active from July

topics.title: Pest Control in Agriculture
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Controlling pests such as aphids, jassids, thrips, moths, and leaf minor using various methods including spraying pesticides.

sections.heading: Pest Control Methods
sections.text: Using light traps to destroy moths may control leaf minor. Carbaryl 50 WP 0.02% spray is most economical.

sections.heading: Spraying Pesticides
items: Spray 500 ml malathion 50EC in 500 lt. of water per hectare

topics.title: Aflatoxin
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: A carcinogenic substance produced by mould such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus in kernels during post harvest processing and storage.

sections.heading: Prevention and Control Measures
sections.text: It is desirable to store groundnuts in gunny bags as pods rather than kernels. The gunny bags are stacked in a store-room over planks in tiers comprising not more than ten in each in such a way that air keeps circulating.

topics.title: Soybean (Glycine max L. Merril)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Soybean is an important pulse crop rich in food value.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Uses of Soybean
sections.text: It is a cheapest, richest and easiest source of best quality protein and fat. It is more considered as oilseed crop owing to its multiplicity of uses as food and industrial products, it is called a ‘wonder crop or miracle crop’. It is the number one oilseed crop of the world which contains 40% protein and 20% oil.

sections.heading: Nutritional Value of Soybean
sections.text: Soybean protein is rich in the valuable amino acid lysines (5%) in which most of the cereals are deficient. The seeds contain good quality protein rich in lysine and oil is having considerable amount of essential fatty acids (Omega-6 and Omega-3). It also contains phytochemicals known as isoflvines which protect human body against chronic diseases such as cancer, diabetes, osteoporosis and blood pressure.

sections.heading: Benefits of Soybean for Soil Fertility
sections.text: Soybean, being leguminous crop, improves the soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen and also through leaf fall at maturity.

topics.title: Climatic Requirement for Soybean
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Soybean grows well in warm and moist climates from sea level to an elevation of 3,000 m.

sections.heading: Optimum Temperature Range
sections.text: The optimum temperature range for germination is 15-32C, while the optimal temperature range for growth and development is 26.5-30C.

sections.heading: Temperature Effects on Oil Content
items: Low temperatures reduce oil content.
Higher temperatures during seed formation increase oil content in seed.

sections.heading: Temperature and Nodulation
sections.text: Temperatures above 42C severely hamper nodulation, while temperatures below 18C prevent pod setting.

sections.heading: Optimum Relative Humidity for Pod Formation
sections.text: A relative humidity of 70-75% is optimum for pod formation.

sections.heading: Tolerance to Frost and Water Logging
sections.text: Soybean cannot tolerate frost and water logging.

sections.heading: Growth Requirements
items: Annual rainfall of 400-750 mm.
A photoperiod of 13-14 hours, provided that temperatures are favourable.

topics.title: Varieties
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A variety is a distinct cultivar of a plant species, often with specific characteristics such as growth habit, leaf shape, or seed color.

sections.heading: Characteristics
sections.text: Varieties have different characteristics such as growth habit, leaf shape, and seed color.

sections.heading: Variety Descriptions
items: Bragg: Medium tall (90-100 cm.), erect, branched with six or seven upright branches. Leaves and pods are covered with brown hairs. Maturity period is 110-115 days. The seeds are bold, yellow with black hilum .The oil content in the seed varies from 23-25 percent whereas protein content varies from 42-45 percent. The average yield is 1625-1875 kg/ha.

Lee: Dwarf (40 cm.), erect and branched. Pods and leaves are covered with brownish hair. Maturity period is 110-115 days. Seeds are light yellow in colour with black hilum. Oil content in seed varies from 23-25 percent. Average yield is 1500- 2000 kg/ha.

Clark- 63: Dwarf (70 cm.), leaves and pods are covered with light yellow to brown coloured hairs. Maturity period is 90-95 days. Seeds are yellow with dull luster and black hilum. Oil content in seeds varies from 18- 20 percent The average yield is 2500-3000 kg/ha.

PK 416: Medium sized and ovule is yellow in colour. This variety is tolerant to yellow vein mosaic virus, rhizoctonia blight & bacterial leaf spot. This variety gives average yield of 25-30 q/ha in 120 to 125 days.

sections.heading: Regions with good scope for intercropping
sections.text: In north India, it has tremendous scope as an intercrop in pigeonpea, maize, cotton and upland rice. In southern part of the country, soybean has a good scope as intercrop in cotton, sorghum, pigeonpea, groundnut and sugarcane. In central India, it has been found very remunerative on the fallow lands in Kharif.

sections.heading: Common rotations followed in north India

topics.title: Sowing Time
topics.definition: The last week of June to first fortnight of July is the optimum sowing time for soybean cultivation.

sections.heading: Optimum Sowing Time
sections.text: In northern and central India, the last week of June is the optimum time of sowing under irrigated conditions.

sections.heading: Sowing Seasons
items: October and November (rabi crop)
Middle of February or middle of March (summer crop)

topics.title: Field Preparation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: The seed bed should be well pulverized, free from clods and perennial weeds, and well leveled.

sections.heading: Steps for Field Preparation
sections.text: The land should be prepared by ploughing 4-5 times followed by planking after each ploughing. Generally one deep ploughing with mould board plough followed by 3-4 light ploughings by desi plough will ensure the proper tilth.

topics.title: Seed Rate
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The amount of seed required per hectare for a specific crop or crop combination.

sections.heading: General Seed Rates
sections.text: Soybean crop needs about 70-80 kg/ha seed during kharif season (timely sown) and 100-120 kg/ha seed during spring and summer seasons (late sown). Intercropping with other crops either in alternate rows or 2 rows of soybean between two rows of main crop would require 60% of the seed rate.

sections.heading: Seed Rate Variations Based on Crop Variety
items: Small seeded varieties require 55-60 kg/ha seed.
Medium and bold seeded varieties require 70-75 kg/ha and 80-90 Kg/ha, respectively.

topics.title: Sowing Method
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The seeds are sown by different methods, including seed drill or behind the plough.

sections.heading: General Guidelines for Sowing Soybean
sections.text: Soybean can be planted at spacing of 45 cm row to row and 4-5 cm plant to plant. A seeding depth of 5 cm is optimum.

sections.heading: Effects of Rainfall on Sowing
sections.text: Rainfall immediately after sowing results in crust formation inhibiting seedling emergence.

sections.heading: Soybean as an Inter Crop
items: pigeonpea, cotton and upland paddy in northern India
sorghum, cotton, sugarcane, pigeonpea and groundnut in southern India

sections.heading: Paired Row Method
sections.text: The paired row method utilizes the resources more efficiently with higher yield.

topics.title: Seed Treatment
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Seeds must be treated with Thiram or Captan @ 2g/kg seed or Trichoderma viridi @ 5 gm. per kg of seed to get rid of seed borne diseases.

sections.heading: Importance of Seed Treatment
sections.text: The inoculation of seed with Rhizobium culture is most important when the crop is cultivated first time in any land.

sections.heading: Rhizobium Culture for Soybean
sections.text: Seeds should be inoculated with Rhizobium japonicum strains of soybean culture to overcome the problem of poor nodulation.

sections.heading: Storage and Sowing of Inoculated Seeds
sections.text: Inoculated seeds are stored under shade till the time of sowing. Sowing should be finished within two hours of inoculation.

topics.title: Fertilizer Requirement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A fertilizer requirement refers to the amount of nutrients needed by a crop for growth.

sections.heading: Nitrogen Requirements
sections.text: An application of 25 kg N/ha as a starter dose will be sufficient to meet the nitrogen requirement of the crop in initial stage. A response of higher nitrogen application has been observed in fields deficient in nitrogen.

sections.heading: Phosphorus and Potassium Requirements
sections.text: Apply 80 kg PO/ha to meet the phosphorous demand of the crop at the time of sowing. In K deficient soils, basal application of 40 kg KO/ha is recommended.

sections.heading: Sulfur Requirements
sections.text: In areas with low S availability, 20 kg S/ha is necessary.

sections.heading: Zinc Requirements
sections.text: Application of 20 kg ZnSO /ha recommendation is made for all soybean growing zones.

topics.title: Water Management
topics.definition: Irrigation at active growth stage is required; however there should not be any moisture stress at the end of flowering to pod initiation stages.

sections.heading: Requirements for Irrigation
sections.text: The crop requires about 600-650 mm rainfall. Soil deficient in moisture requires pre-sowing irrigation for the good germination. Irrigation at active growth stage is required; however there should not be any moisture stress at the end of flowering to pod initiation stages. In rainfed crop prolonged dry spells, requires protective irrigation .The spring or summer crop of soybean requires assured irrigation facilities.

sections.heading: Importance of Timing
sections.text: Irrigation at active growth stage is required; however there should not be any moisture stress at the end of flowering to pod initiation stages.

sections.heading: Weeding Methods

topics.title: Disease Management - Bacterial Blight
topics.definition: Bacterial blight is characterized by small reddish-brown spots surrounded by water-soaked margins with yellow holes on pods, often appearing in cool and moist conditions.

sections.heading: Causes and Conditions
sections.text: Cool and moist conditions are favourable for bacterial blight.

sections.heading: Symptoms
items: Small reddish-brown spot surrounded by water-soaked margin with yellow holes on pods
Yellow pustules appear on leaves which later changes to reddish brown with marginal yellowing

topics.title: Bacterial Pustules
topics.definition: Conditions favourable for bacterial pustules can be controlled by using disease-free seed, practicing crop rotation, and growing resistant variety.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.text: The seed should be treated with Cerasan or Captan @ 3.0 g per kg of seed or Trichoderma viridi @ 5 gm per kg of seed before sowing. The crop should be sprayed twice with Copper Oxychloride 50 % WP (Blitox) or Streptocycline (500 ppm) at an interval of 10 days depending on the severity of the disease.

sections.heading: Downy Mildew (Pernospora Sp)
sections.text: Small chlorotic spots appear on the upper surface of the leaves which later turn greyish to dark brown with downy growth on the lower surface of the leaves. For control, the seed should be treated with Captan @ 3.0 gm per kg of seed before sowing.

sections.heading: Dry Root Rot (Macrophomina phaseoli (Tassi) Goid)
sections.text: Small, round or irregular black sclerotia appears below the epidermis on the affected stem and root. The plant wilts within a week. On examination of the stem, dark sunken lesions are seen on the stem and dry rot symptoms appear on basal stem and main root.

sections.heading: Yellow Mosaic (Virus)
sections.text: The affected leaves become yellow with a slight crinkling and reduction in size. The plants are stunted in growth and set a few pod only. Regular spraying of the crop with a mixture of Methyl demiton 25 EC (Metasystox 25 EC) @ 1.5 ml per litre of water starting from third week or onwards at an interval of 10-15 days keep the white fly population under control and the crop becomes free from the incidence of yellow mosaic virus.

topics.title: Insect Management: Stem Borer Beetle
topics.definition: The stem borer beetle is a small, pale brown longicorn beetle that bores into plant stems, causing drying of leaves and withering of plants.

sections.heading: Control Methods
sections.text: Spraying the crop with specific insecticides can control the stem borer beetle.

sections.heading: Control Measures
sections.text: Insecticides such as Dimethoate 30 EC, Monocrotophos 36 SL, and Methyl demiton 25 EC can be used to control the caterpillar.

topics.title: Sesame (Sesamum indicum L.)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Sesame is a member of the family Pedaliaceae, comprising sixteen genera and about sixty species, several of which can be crossed with S. indicum.

sections.heading: Origin
sections.text: The origin of cultivated sesame (Sesamum indicum L.) is generally accepted as the Ethiopian area in Africa, with considerable argument in favour of Afghan-Persian region or even a polytopic origin.

sections.heading: Genome Grouping
sections.text: The genus sesame can be grouped into three on the basis of chromosome number: Group I (2n=26), Group II (2n=32), and Group III (2n=64).

sections.heading: Climatic Requirement
sections.text: Sesame is considered a crop of the tropics and subtropics, but its cultivation can be extended to the temperate zone by breeding suitable varieties.

topics.title: Sesame Cultivation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Sesame is a crop that requires hot conditions for high yield, with optimal temperatures between 25-27 C.

sections.heading: Optimal Temperature and Germination
sections.text: A temperature of 25-27 C encourages rapid germination, initial growth and flower formation.

sections.heading: Light Periods and Flowering
items: Sesame is a short day plant with 10-hour day length in 42-45 days for flowering.
Many varieties have become adapted to various light periods with wide yield variations.

sections.heading: Soil Requirements and Resistance
sections.text: Sesame can be grown in a variety of soil types, but sandy-loam, fertile, well-drained soils are ideal for its good growth and high yield. It is extremely susceptible to salinity and salt concentrations.

sections.heading: Rainfall Requirements and Distribution
sections.text: For high yield, rainfall should be distributed over the period of its growth approximately in the following proportions- 35% germination to first bud, 45% first bud to flowering and not more than 20% from flowering to maturity.

sections.heading: Soil pH and Topography
sections.text: Sesame prefers soils with neutral in reaction (pH 6.5-7.5), but can produce good yield on slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soils (pH 5.5-8.0). The sesame field should be at higher level as compare to the surroundings for quickly disposal excessive rainwater after or during heavy rainfall.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Season
sections.text: Sesame is cultivated both as a pure crop and a mixed crop with groundnut, cotton, tobacco, pigeon pea, jower, mung etc in kharif season. It is also grown as pure crop during both kharif and pre-kharif season.

topics.title: Crop Varieties (State Wise)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Most crop varieties take 80-95 days to mature during all the seasons, with productivity varying from 350-400 kg/ha in kharif, 600-800 kg/ha in rabi, and 800-1000 kg/ha in pre-kharif.

sections.heading: Land Preparation
sections.text: Soil should be pulverized well. About 2-3 crosswise ploughing is required for sowing the crop in sandy loam type of loose soils and 3-4 ploughing are needed to make fine tilth of the silty loam field.

sections.heading: Season and Sowing
sections.text: Sesame is mainly a kharif season crop. This crop is usually sown early in the season as compare to other kharif crops. Time of sowing depends on the onset of monsoon in kharif season.

topics.title: Sowing Time of Sesame in Different Regions in India
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: The sowing time of sesame varies across different regions in India, depending on the kharif season.

sections.heading: Sesame Sowing Time by Region
sections.text: Sesame is sown at different times in various regions of India. In southern India, it is sown during the kharif season, starting from 2nd half of May. In eastern and central India, it is sown as a rainfed crop during the same period. In northern India, it is sown towards the end of July.

sections.heading: Pre-Kharif Crop
sections.text: Sesame can also be grown as a pre-kharif crop in different regions of India. This type of crop is generally sown from the end of February to 1st half of March in central and eastern India.

topics.title: Sowing Methods for Sesame Seeds
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Sesame seeds are sown at temperatures above 20 C, with alternative crops grown in south India where temperature fluctuations are minimal.

sections.heading: Method of Sowing
sections.text: In mixed cropping, the seed is sown either in parallel rows alternating with the main crop or broadcast in the entire field. In pure cropping, it is generally broad cast.

sections.heading: Seed Rate
items: 1.0 - 1.5 kg seeds/ha (Mixed cropping)
4-5 kg seeds/ha (Pure cropping)

sections.heading: Seed Treatment
sections.text: Sesame seeds must be treated with fungicides like Agrosan G N, Tafason, Aratan 6, Mancozeb 75% WP, Carbendazin 50% WP, Dithane M-45 or Indofil-4-45 to protect them from infection.

sections.heading: Spacing
sections.text: During kharif, 35-40 cm row to row and 15-20 cm plant to plant spacing is recommended. During pre-kharif season, 30 cm row to row X 10 cm plant to plant spacing is followed.

sections.heading: Depth of Sowing
sections.text: 2.0-2.5 cm depth of sowing was the best for sesame seeds. Both shallow and deep sowing should be avoided for better emergence and uniform crop stand.

sections.heading: Manuring
sections.text: FYM 5-7 t/ha should be applied 10-15 days before sowing, mixed thoroughly with soil during ploughing. Additional fertilizers may be applied for irrigated kharif crop.

topics.title: Intercultural Operation
topics.definition: Thinning and weeding are the most important cultural operations done in sesame cultivation.

sections.heading: Thinning
sections.text: Thinning and weeding are the most important cultural operations done in sesame cultivation. If the seeds germinate properly about 80-100 plants/m appear in the field. These excess plants must be removed from the field to facilitate good growth necessary for obtaining high crop yield. Huge number of plants has to be thinned out to maintain optimum plant density.

sections.heading: First Thinning
sections.text: The first thinning is generally done at 10-15 DAS when the weak and abnormal plants are uprooted leaving the healthy plants in the field. At this stage, 10-15% more plants are kept so that if some plants die the extra plants cover up the gap.

sections.heading: Final Thinning
sections.text: The final thinning is done 10 days after the first thinning when the extra plants if present at close distance are removed to maintain optimum plant density. During this stage, weeding has also been done.

sections.heading: Weeding
sections.text: To get good harvest, the crop should be kept free of weeds at early stages of growth. Several weeds are infested the sesame field particularly during kharif season and causes considerably yield loss.

sections.heading: Control of Weeds
sections.text: Normally the weeds are controlled by hand weeding. One hand weeding at 10-15 DAS and another at 25-30 DAS can control the weeds very effectively and keep the sesame field clean and produce good yield of kharif crop.

sections.heading: Application of Alachlor
sections.text: The application of alachlor 1.5 kg/ha at 1 DAS in 500 liters of water effectively controlled weeds in sesame field and recorded quite high yield comparable to that of weed free check.

sections.heading: Irrigation
sections.text: Kharif sesame is generally grown under rainfed condition in India. However, if dry spell occurs coinciding with flowering or capsule setting, one irrigation under such condition can provide 10-15% more yield.

sections.heading: Water Requirement for Irrigation
sections.text: Pre-kharif crop requires irrigation due to scarcity of rain water. Here, irrigation must be given at critical growth stages like seedling (10-15 DAS), branching (25-30 DAS), peak flowering (45-50 DAS) and capsule development (65- 70 DAS) stages.

topics.title: Sesame Field Management
topics.definition: Controlled by spraying Chlorpyriphos 2.5 ml/l, Dimecron 40 EC 1.5 ml/l at initial stage of infestation to prevent diseases such as leaf spot, stem rot, charcoal rot, root rot, and blight.

sections.heading: Diseases
sections.text: Leaf spot (Cercospora sesami), stem rot (Macrophoma sesami), charcoal rot (Macrophomina phaseolina), root rot (Thielaviopsis basicola) and blight (Phytophthora nicotiana var sesami) are important diseases that should be prevented by following suitable crop rotation, seed treatment, using disease-free good quality seeds.

sections.heading: Disease Prevention
items: Suitable crop rotation
Seed treatment
Using disease-free good quality seeds

sections.heading: Phyllody and Leaf-Hoppers
sections.text: Phyllody is the most destructive disease of sesame caused by mycoplasma like organism transmitted through leaf-hoppers. The attack of leaf-hoppers should be controlled by spraying insecticide.

sections.heading: Harvesting
sections.text: Sesame is normally takes 80-95 days to mature. Harvesting should be done early morning hours of the day at a relatively low temperature and high humidity to avoid shattering of seeds.

sections.heading: Harvesting Procedure
sections.text: The plants should be cut before all capsules are mature to avoid loss of seed yield due to shattering. Immediately after harvesting, the crop should be brought to the threshing floor and stacked in the floor for 2 days then spread over the floor in sun for drying and threshing.

sections.heading: Threshing
sections.text: Threshing is done by beating the upper parts of plants with sticks or by run over of animals. Immediately after threshing the seeds should be cleaned and dried again to reduce moisture content to around 7% for storing or marketing.

sections.heading: Yield
sections.text: 8-10 q of seeds per ha

topics.title: Use of Sesame Seed
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: 77.7% of sesame seeds are used for oil extraction, while 20% are used for domestic purposes, and 2.3% are used for seed purpose.

sections.heading: Domestic Use
sections.text: Sesame seeds are used either normal or fried for the preparation of various types of foodstuffs, sweets, cakes, pastry etc. It is also used in most of the family functions. Parched seeds are sprinkled on a variety of dishes and served on ceremonial occasions.

sections.heading: Use of Oil
sections.text: Sesame oil is used as edible vegetative fat, fixative in perfumery, and scented hair oil. Low quality oil is used for lubrication, lightning purpose, and preparation of soap, resin, and paints.

topics.title: Forage Crop Introduction
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: The crop-livestock interaction is very strong, with only 5.1% of the total cropped area under forage cultivation in India.

sections.heading: Importance of Forage Crops
sections.text: The fodder production in the country is not sufficient to meet the requirements of the growing livestock population and also the forage offered to animals are mostly of poor quality.

sections.heading: Livestock Population and Productivity
items: India has a huge population of livestock, with over 548 million animals in 2012.
The productivity of milk and other livestock products per animal is very low compared to other countries.

topics.title: Role and Importance of Fodder
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Fodder plays an important role in economizing the cost of production of livestock products especially of milk.

sections.heading: Importance of Fodder in Livestock Production
sections.text: Cultivated fodder has an important role in meeting requirement of various nutrients & roughage to produce milk most economically.

sections.heading: Role of Fodder in Rumen Satisfaction
items: Feeds given to animals not only meet nutrient requirement but fills the rumen to satisfy the animal.

topics.title: Fodder Crops in Agriculture
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Feeds must meet the requirements of cattle production and microbes to promote digestion.

sections.heading: Importance of Fodder Crops
sections.text: Fodder crops provide all the critical elements like highly digestible protein, carbohydrates, fats and minerals.

sections.heading: Nutritional Value of Green Fodders
sections.text: Green fodders are a very good source of B-carotene (precursor of vitamin A).

sections.heading: Traditional Fodder Cultivation
items: Fodder cultivation has been traditional in most parts of the country.
Farmers cultivate certain varieties and crops for fodder production and area allocation depending upon availability of land, water and requirement for own livestock.

topics.title: Conservation of Forage Crops
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Silage-making is a technology that empowers farmers to provide quality roughage throughout the year using forages, crop residues, agro-industrial by-products.

sections.heading: Benefits of Silage-Making
sections.text: Cost optimization and increased farm productivity & profitability

sections.heading: Comparison with Hay-Making
items: Less dependent on specific weather conditions
Can be extended to a great variety of forage and fodder crops

topics.title: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Sorghum is most important fodder crop for livestock because of its wide adaptation, rapid growth, high green and dry fodder, ratoon ability and drought tolerance.

sections.heading: Uses of Sorghum
sections.text: Besides being an important food crop, sorghum is also valued for its fodder and stover. Sorghum fodder is suitable silage and hay making and thus can supplement the fodder supply during lean season.

sections.heading: Advantages of Sorghum
items: Suitable for cultivation in areas that are too dry for maize.
Dry stover forms important feeding stock for animals especially in dry areas.
Livestock relishes its fodder due to sucrose content in its straw.

topics.title: Origin and History of Sorghum
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Cultivated sorghum probably originated in East Central Africa, in or near Ethiopia or sudan because of the great diversity of types growing in that region.

sections.heading: Types of Sorghum
sections.text: It is known under a great many names: milo, guinea corn in West Africa, kafir corn in South Africa, durra in Sudan, mtama in eastern Africa, jowar in India and kaoliang in China.

topics.title: Soil and its preparation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Well drained sandy loam to loam soils with a pH range of 6.5 to 7.5 are ideally suited for its cultivation.

sections.heading: Preparation of Soil
sections.text: The field should be thoroughly prepared and levelled to make weeds free sowing. Better crop stand is obtained on well-prepared soils.

sections.heading: Soil Preparation Steps
items: One ploughing with soil turning plough followed by two harrowing (crosswise) and planking is sufficient to get a good seed bed.

sections.heading: Importance of Drainage
sections.text: The crop can’t tolerate longer water stagnation hence, provision of good drainage is essential.

topics.title: Sowing Time
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The time at which crops are sown, depending on the type of variety and region.

sections.heading: Variety Types
sections.text: Single or double cut varieties are sown with the onset of monsoon in June-July. Multi cut types are sown during March-April in areas with irrigation facility which provides four cuts till September-October in northern India.

sections.heading: Regional Sowing Times
sections.text: However, in southern India, where minimum information is available, the exact sowing time is not specified.

topics.title: Agrimoon Temperature Sowing
topics.definition: Temperatures do not fall below 15C, it is grown during Rabi season also in the month of October-November.

sections.heading: Best Period for Sowing
sections.text: For summer sowing of multi cut types, mid-March to mid-April is the best period, while for monsoon season crop, sowing should be done preferably between 25 June and 10 July.

topics.title: Seed Rate and Sowing Method
topics.definition: The amount of seeds to be sown per unit area, as well as the method of sowing, is crucial for optimal crop growth.

sections.heading: Sowing Methods
sections.text: There are two main types of sowing methods: single cut and double cut.
