topics.title: Multicut Varieties/Hybrids
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Varieties or hybrids that can be cut multiple times, with some providing up to four cuts.

sections.heading: Characteristics
sections.text: Multicut varieties/hybrids have profuse tillering and quick regeneration capacity.

sections.heading: Yields
items: Up to 65 t/ha of green fodder (PCH 106)
55-60 t/ha of fodder in 4 cuts (Meethi Sudan)

topics.title: Dual Purpose Varieties/Hybrids
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Varieties or hybrids that can be used for multiple purposes, such as taking single cut of fodder.

sections.heading: Characteristics
sections.text: Dual purpose varieties/hybrids are resistant to leaf diseases and drought. They yield about 45-50 t/ha of green fodder.

sections.heading: Varieties
items: CSV 15
CSH 13

topics.title: Fertilizer Requirement
topics.definition: The amount of fertilizer required to meet the needs of crops for secondary and micro nutrients.

sections.heading: General Guidelines
sections.text: In single cut varieties, basal application of 60:30:30 Kg N: P2O5: K2O per hectare should be given at sowing time followed by top dressing with 30 Kg N/ha, one month after sowing.

sections.heading: Adjustments for Climate and Soil Conditions
items: In low rainfall and rainfed areas, 60 Kg N/ha is applied at sowing time.
For two cuts and multicut, dose of 60:60:60 Kg& 70:30:30 kg N: P2O5; K2O/ha, respectively, as basal should be applied.

sections.heading: Top Dressing
sections.text: Top dressing of 50 kg N/ha should be done after each cut.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If crop suffers due to dry spell, spraying of 2 % urea solution should be done. In sulphur deficient soils (below 10 ppm available S), the application of 40-60 Kg S/ha is advantageous not only for improving biomass production but quality f the fodder also.

topics.title: Weed Management
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Weeds compete with crops for water and nutrients, leading to yield losses.

sections.heading: Timing of Weeding
sections.text: One hand weeding is necessary at 15-20 DAS. Weeding should be done later depending on crop requirements.

sections.heading: Challenges During Rainy Season
sections.text: Inter culturing becomes difficult during rainy season.

sections.heading: Chemical Weed Control
items: Apply atrazine @ 500g/ha between 7-15 days after sowing using 625 L of water

topics.title: Disease and Insect-Pest Management
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Sorghum is infected by a number of insects and disease pathogens, and various management strategies are recommended.

sections.heading: Management Strategies
sections.text: Field sanitation, use of healthy seed, and seed treatment with Thiram @ 3 g/Kg seed are recommended. Resistant varieties should be grown to avoid diseases and pests.

sections.heading: Control of Specific Pests
items: Carbofuran 3G @ 3-4 Kg/ha applied in trench at sowing time for shoot fly control.
Sowing during July to avoid stem borer attack.

topics.title: Harvesting
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Single cut varieties are harvested at 50-100% flowering stage.

sections.heading: Timing of Harvest
sections.text: Single cut varieties are harvested at 50-100% flowering stage. In multi cut varieties, the first cut is taken 55 days after sowing and the subsequent at 40 days interval.

sections.heading: Cutting Height for Multi Cut Varieties
sections.text: In multi cut varieties, first cut should be taken 8-10 cm above ground level so as to facilitate profuse tillering.

topics.title: Hydrocyanic Acid (HCN) or Dhurin
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Young sorghum plants contain hydrocyanic acid (HCN) or Dhurin, a poisonous chemical that is toxic to animals in excess of 200 ppm concentration.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects of HCN
sections.text: Heavy nitrogen fertilization and water stress increases HCN content. Silage or hay making removes the toxin.

sections.heading: Harvesting and Handling
items: Irrigation before harvest may be effective in reducing HCN.
For hay making, pre-flowering is ideal stage for harvest.

sections.heading: Maturity and Risk of Poisoning
sections.text: Danger of HCN poisoning is greatest at immature stages of sorghum growth and decreases with maturity.

topics.title: Napier Grass (Pennisetum purpureum)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The hybrid Napier for fodder is highly valued for its abundant herbage yield, palatability and good herbage quality.

sections.heading: Characteristics
sections.text: It contains 8.5-10.2% CP, 28-34.5% crude fibre and 10-11.5% ash on dry matter basis.

sections.heading: Growth and Production
sections.text: It grows faster and produces more herbage and the stems are hard.

sections.heading: Harvesting and Utilization
items: The oxalate contain of some of the varieties may be high (> 3%). It can be mitigated if harvested at longer intervals (45-60 days).
It is ideal for green fodder, silage and hay.
Legumes fodder may be mixed with grass in the ratio of 1:2 to produce balanced silage.

sections.heading: Combination with Other Crops
sections.text: A combination of Napier grass with berseem, Lucerne or cowpea provides good quality palatable fodder for cattle. It is considered as a soil restoring crop also as grass leaves the soil richer in organic matter.

topics.title: Origin and History
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Napier grass is native of Rhodesia in South Africa, where it is found growing extensively.

sections.heading: Early Introduction
sections.text: It was introduced in India in 1912 from South Africa.

sections.heading: Honouring Col. Napier
sections.text: The name napier grass is given in the honour of Col. Napier, who first drew the attention of the Rhodesian Department of Agriculture in 1909 to the fodder value of this grass.

topics.title: Climatic Requirements
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: It grows well at high temperatures, can withstand to drought conditions for fairly long spell.

sections.heading: Optimum Temperature
sections.text: The optimum temperature is 31 C but it performs well in areas having temperatures above 15 C.

sections.heading: Rainfall Requirements
sections.text: It grows in areas with rainfall of over 1000 mm but it cannot tolerate the flooding /water logging.

sections.heading: Weather Conditions
sections.text: Light showered alternated with bright sunshine are very congenial to the crop.

topics.title: Cowpea
topics.definition: Cowpea belongs to family Leguminoceae and is also known as Lobia, black eye pea, kaffir pea, marble pea, China pea and southern pea.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Uses
sections.text: Cowpea is recommended for irrigated areas. It is generally grown in mixture with pearlmillet, sorghum etc. to enhance the green fodder yield and supplement the nutritive value of non- leguminous fodders.

topics.title: Climate Requirement
topics.definition: Cowpea is best suited for moderately humid tropic and sub-tropics up to an elevation of 1500m.

sections.heading: Optimum Temperature
sections.text: The optimum temperature for its growth is 27C, and the minimum is 15C.

sections.heading: Soil Temperature Requirement
sections.text: It requires average soil temperature >19C for 3 days from sowing to emergence, that limits its cultivation in north during winter.

topics.title: Soil and its Preparation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Cowpea can be grown on various soils, with light soils being preferred for good crop growth.

sections.heading: Preparation of Soil
sections.text: Field should be prepared by two cross harrowing and planking so as to get a levelled and weed free sees bed for a quick germination and faster initial growth.

topics.definition: Management of diseases and insect pests in agriculture.

sections.heading: Mosaic Virus Disease
sections.text: It is a serious seed-borne disease of cowpea. The symptoms appear as chlorotic patches on cotyledons, that later cover entire foliage. The secondary infection spreads through aphids. Selection resistant varieties, use of healthy seeds, control of aphids and rouging of infected plants are useful in its management.

sections.heading: Jassids (Empoascakerri)
sections.text: Both nymphs and adults suck sap from leaves in dry weather. Affected leaves turn yellow and fall off. Spray 0.03% Monocrotofos or Phosphamidon is effective.

sections.heading: Flea/Galerucid Beetle (Madurasia obscurella)
sections.text: The beetle feeds on leaves, buds and flowers. Severe attack can cause defoliation. Apply phorate 10 G kg/ha at sowing along with early sowing to avoid pest attack.

sections.heading: Hairy Caterpillar (Amsactamoorei)
sections.text: The young larvae feed on lower surface of leaves and skeletonize them leading to severe yield losses. Collection and destroying eggs and larvae in early stages. Dusting 0.05% dichlorovos spray is recommended.

sections.heading: Cowpea Stem Fly (Melangromyza phaseoli)
sections.text: The maggots bore into younger stems and tunnels towards the base causing damage to stem. The affected plants wither and die. Clean culture, use of resistant varieties and 0.05% monocrotophos spray control stem fly.

sections.heading: Yield Levels by Irrigation Condition

topics.title: Cluster Bean or Guar (Cyamopsis tetragonaloba L)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Clusterbean is a multipurpose legume of papilionaceae family valued for its gum, seed, and fodder production besides green manuring.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Uses
sections.text: The fodder of clusterbean as well as its grain is quite nutritive, rich in protein, fat and minerals. The crude protein and crude fibre content varies from 15-18% and 25-30%, respectively.

sections.heading: Cultivation and Production
sections.text: It can be grown alone or mixed with sorghum, Bajra, etc. Its gum is highly mucilaginous, which is being used in various industries such as textiles, cosmetics, explosives, paper, food processing etc.

sections.heading: Economic Importance
sections.text: Today clusterbean is one of the significant foreign exchange earner of the country. Clusterbean is grown on about 2 lakh ha in India mainly in the states of Rajasthan, Haryana, Gujarat, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra.

topics.title: Bacterial Blight Management
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Disease and Insect management
topics.definition: Bacterial blight is a seed borne disease that appears as small water soaked lesions on leaves, which later become necrotic, and may also appear on flowers and pods.

sections.heading: Management of Bacterial Blight
sections.text: Seed treatment with hot water at 50C for 10 minutes controls the disease. At the appearance of disease or at 8 weeks after sowing, spray the crop with 75 g streptocyclin and 500 g copperoxicloride in 500 litre of water to save the crop from this disease.

sections.heading: Alternaria Leaf Spot Management

sections.heading: Characteristics of Cotton
sections.text: Fibre is used for making cloth, thread and other synthetic fibres. The fibre is almost pure cellulose.

topics.definition: Cotton has been used as a fabric in India from time immemorial.

sections.heading: Early History of Cotton
sections.text: The excavations of Mohen-jo-daro indicates a high degree of art in spinning and weaving with cotton at that time. It finds mention in the Rig-Veda, the oldest scripture of the Hindus.

items: Egypt

topics.definition: The important cotton growing countries are India, USA, former USSR, China, Brazil, Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey, Mexico and Sudan.

sections.heading: Leading Cotton-Producing States in India
sections.text: In India, the states of Maharashtra (26.63%), Gujarat (17.96%) and Andhra Pradesh (13.75%) are the leading cotton producing states, these states have a predominantly tropical wet and dry climate.

sections.heading: Global Cotton Production
items: The five leading exporters of cotton in 2011 are the United States, India, Brazil, Australia, and Uzbekistan.
Current estimates for world production are about 25 million tonnes annually, accounting for 2.5% of the world's arable land.

sections.heading: Global Cotton Trade
rows: China is the world's largest producer of cotton, but most of this is used domestically.
The United States has been the largest exporter for many years.

title: Farming System and Sustainable Agriculture
description: 64 topics covering Sustainable Agriculture, Sustainability in Agriculture, Sustainable Agriculture vs Modern Agriculture and more.

topics.title: Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Agriculture that meets present needs without endangering the resource base of future generations.

sections.heading: Core features
items: Prevents land degradation and soil erosion.
Replenishes nutrients in the soil.
Controls weeds, pests and diseases through biological and cultural methods.
Minimizes dependence on synthetic fertilizers, pesticides and antibiotics.
Uses manures, crop rotation and minimal tillage.

sections.heading: Also known as
items: Alternative farming
Regenerative agriculture
Natural or organic farming
Eco-farming
Permeaculture

topics.title: Sustainability in Agriculture
topics.definition: The capacity of agriculture to remain productive while maintaining its resource base.

sections.heading: Five characteristics
items: Ecologically sound: soil, crop, animal and human health are maintained.
Economically viable: farmers can produce enough for self-sufficiency.
Socially just: basic needs and productive resources are fairly accessed.
Humane: plant, animal and human life are respected.
Adaptable: rural communities can adjust to changing farming conditions.

sections.heading: WCED 1987 concept
items: Today's economic development should not be at the expense of tomorrow's development prospects.

topics.title: Sustainable Agriculture vs Modern Agriculture
topics.definition: The source contrasts resource-conserving sustainable agriculture with chemical-input-based modern agriculture.

sections.heading: Plant nutrients
items: Sustainable: farmyard manure, compost, green manure, biofertilizers and crop rotations.
Modern: chemical fertilizers.

topics.title: Problems of Modern Agriculture
topics.definition: Environmental problems associated in the source with modern agricultural development and faulty practices.

sections.heading: Major problems
items: Ozone layer damage from atmospheric pollutants such as CFC, nitrogen oxide and methane.
Increasing CO2 contributes to global warming, sea-level rise and rainfall-pattern changes.
Water and wind erosion cause loss of productive soil.
Deforestation increases erosion, floods, reservoir siltation and runoff.
Improper irrigation may cause soil salinization and alkalization.
Excessive groundwater extraction depletes groundwater.
Pesticide and fertilizer residues pollute surface and groundwater.
Biological diversity is reduced.

topics.title: Major Components of Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Resource and crop-management practices used to sustain productivity while reducing environmental damage.

sections.heading: Components
items: Soil and water conservation prevents degradation and can extend the crop-growing season.
Efficient irrigation-water use reduces salinity, alkalinity and high water-table problems.
Crop rotations reduce insect-pests, diseases and weeds.
Crop rotations improve soil productivity and reduce erosion.
Integrated nutrient management combines organic, inorganic and biological nutrient sources.
Integrated pest management reduces dependence on agrochemicals.
Good weed management uses preventive measures, tillage, timely intercultivation and crop rotation.

topics.title: Goals of Sustainable Agriculture
topics.definition: Long-term production goals based on resource conservation and efficient use.

sections.heading: Goals
items: Use nutrient cycling and nitrogen fixation.
Reduce external and non-renewable inputs.
Improve equitable access to productive resources and opportunities.
Use the biological and genetic potential of plants and animals.
Maintain current production levels over the long term.
Integrate farm management with conservation of soil, water, energy and biological resources.

topics.title: Factors Affecting Ecological Balance
topics.definition: Major land, water and input-management factors that disturb ecological balance.

sections.heading: Major factors
items: Deforestation and overgrazing reduce vegetation, alter climate and biodiversity, and cause resource loss.
Loss of vegetative cover accelerates soil erosion.
Poor-quality irrigation water and poor drainage cause salinity and sodicity.
Over-extraction of groundwater lowers the water table.
Over-irrigation can accumulate harmful salts.
Excess fertilizer use reduces soil biological activity and contributes to nitrate pollution.
Pesticides can cause resistance and environmental contamination.

topics.title: Soil Management for Sustainable Agriculture

sections.heading: Soil degradation
items: Water and wind erosion are major causes.
Chemical degradation includes salinization and loss of nutrients and organic matter.
Short- and long-term measures are required.

sections.heading: Conservation practices
items: Contour farming.
Agronomic and cultural measures.
Contour bunding and graded bunding.
Contour ditches and bench terracing.
Runoff cycling.
Alternative land use such as pasture and fuel-fodder-timber systems on non-agricultural land.

sections.heading: Watershed approach
items: Stores drainage water for recycling.
Stored water can support crops during drought.
Can improve rainfed-crop productivity.

topics.title: Integrated Nutrient Management (INM)

sections.heading: Main components
items: Recycle crop residues and animal wastes.
Use composting and vermicomposting for materials unsuitable for direct application.
Use biological nitrogen fixation through BGA, Azolla, Rhizobium, Azotobacter and Azospirillum.
Use phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms.
Use green manuring to improve fertility and supply nutrients.
Include legumes in rotations and intercropping.
Biogas plants and suitable sewage/sludge use can contribute to nutrient recycling.

sections.heading: Green manure examples
items: Sesbania aculeata (Dhaincha).
Crotalaria juncea (Sannhemp).
Sesbania rostrata.

sections.heading: Sesbania rostrata

topics.title: Management of Water Resources
topics.definition: Efficient use, conservation and recharge of irrigation and other water resources.

sections.heading: Recommendations
items: Use proper land shaping and leveling.
Use efficient irrigation-system design.
Use pipe channels to reduce seepage losses.
Use furrow, alternate-furrow or skip-furrow irrigation for row crops.
Use sprinkler and drip systems in water-scarce areas.
Use surface and groundwater conjunctively.
Provide drainage in canal command areas.
Use suitable cropping systems instead of continuous lowland rice.
Use recommended crop-production technology.
Develop integrated watersheds.
Recharge groundwater using basins, recharge wells, check dams and percolation ponds.

topics.title: Management of Rainwater
topics.definition: Planned use and conservation of rainfall for sustainable crop production.

sections.heading: Source facts
items: Rainfall varies widely across space and time.
The source states about 70% of India's cultivated area depends entirely on rainfall.

sections.heading: Options
items: Use agro-climatic analysis to assess rainfall probability.
Select cropping systems based on agro-climatic conditions.
Prepare contingency crop plans for abnormal weather.
Use improved soil and water management.
Conserve soil moisture in situ.
Harvest and recycle runoff.
Use improved management packages for cropping systems.

topics.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
topics.definition: A combination of agronomic, biological, chemical, physical and other methods that keeps harmful organisms at economically insignificant levels with minimum interference to beneficial organisms.

sections.heading: Core principle
items: Bio-agents are an integral part of IPM.
Priority is given to methods that reduce unnecessary pesticide dependence.

sections.heading: Examples
items: Predator: Coccinella spp.
Parasitoid: Trichogramma species.

sections.heading: Agronomic components
items: Land preparation can create unfavorable conditions for pests, diseases and weeds.
Select resistant or tolerant cultivars.
Adjust sowing time to escape peak pest pressure.
Avoid excessively dense plant populations.
Use mechanical or manual intercultivation.
Apply balanced NPK; excessive nitrogen may increase crop succulence.
Manage irrigation and drainage to avoid pest and disease build-up.
Use intercropping.
Use crop rotation.

Soil acidity.

Human and livestock pressure.

topics.title: Soil Erosion
topics.definition: Detachment of soil particles from the parent soil body.

sections.heading: Types
items: Wind erosion.
Water erosion.
Wave erosion.

sections.heading: Wave erosion
items: Caused by combined action of wind and water.
Occurs mainly along canal and river banks.
Can be controlled by lining canals.

sections.heading: Basic relationship
items: Erosion = f(erosivity) × (erodibility).
Erosivity is the potential ability of rain to cause erosion.
Erodibility is soil vulnerability to erosion based on inherent properties.

topics.title: Factors and Losses Due to Soil Erosion
topics.definition: Rainfall, vegetation and soil properties control erosion and its effects.

sections.heading: Factors
items: Rainfall amount, intensity, duration and distribution affect runoff and erosion.
Vegetative cover intercepts rainfall and reduces erosion.
Topography affects runoff and particle transport.
Increasing slope generally increases erosion.

sections.heading: Major losses
items: Loss of rainwater from fields.
Loss of fertile topsoil.
Loss of plant nutrients.
Siltation of reservoirs and reduced storage capacity.

sections.heading: Source figures
items: Soil loss is stated as 16.35 t/ha annually.
Permissible limit is stated as 11 t/ha.

topics.title: Water Erosion and USLE
topics.definition: Water erosion is described through sheet, rill and gully stages; USLE is used to predict soil loss.

sections.heading: Stages
items: Sheet erosion: uniform removal of a thin topsoil layer.
Rill erosion: small channels formed by runoff.
Gully erosion: advanced rill stage with deep and wide channels.

sections.heading: USLE
items: A = R K L S C P.
A = predicted soil loss.
R = rainfall and runoff factor.
K = soil erodibility.
L = slope length.
S = slope gradient.
C = soil cover and management.
P = erosion-control practice.

topics.title: Wind Erosion
topics.definition: Wind-driven movement of soil particles through saltation, suspension and surface creep.

sections.heading: Particle movement
items: Saltation: bouncing of fine particles around 0.1–0.5 mm.
Suspension: movement of very fine particles or dust below 0.1 mm.
Surface creep: movement of particles above 0.5 mm and below 1.0 mm along the surface.

sections.heading: Factors
items: Wind velocity is a major factor.
The source states wind velocity above 5–6 m/s is undesirable.
Soil texture, structure, cohesiveness, bulk density, organic matter, moisture and surface roughness affect erosion.
Vegetative cover reduces erosion.

sections.heading: Wind erosion equation
items: E = I R K F C W D B.
E = soil loss by wind erosion.
I = soil cloudiness factor.
R = surface cover factor.
K = surface roughness factor.
F = soil textural class factor.
C = local wind factor.
W = field width factor.
D = wind direction factor.
B = wind barrier factor.

topics.title: Natural Resource Management
topics.definition: A sustainable-agriculture approach focused on efficient use and conservation of limited natural resources.

sections.heading: Need
items: Green Revolution increased food production, but sustainability is now a major concern.
Limited land and water resources require continuous productivity improvement.
Poor resource management and excessive agrochemicals threaten sustainability.
Impacts include biodiversity loss, land and water degradation, pollution and climatic changes.

sections.heading: Water-resource pressures
items: Limited expansion of irrigation potential.
Non-judicious use of water.
Poor irrigation-project efficiency, stated as only 30–40%.
Conveyance losses.
Diversion of agricultural water to non-agricultural uses.
Increasing groundwater pollution.

topics.title: Strategies for Natural Resource Management
topics.definition: Resource-conservation strategies for maintaining agricultural productivity and ecological balance.

sections.heading: Biological diversity

Preserve genetic diversity.
Ensure sustainable use of species and ecosystems.

sections.heading: Diversification
items: Use crop diversification.
Integrate dairy, fisheries, poultry, horticulture and forestry.
Reduce monoculture effects.
Improve soil health and resource use.
Support nutrient recycling.
Reduce risk and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Improved systems
items: Integrated intensive farming system uses farm-grown biological inputs and nutrient recycling.
Precision farming improves input-use efficiency.
Use soil-test-based fertilizer application.
Use land leveling and micro-irrigation.
Include legumes in crop rotations.

sections.heading: Other measures
items: Use organic farming.
Reclaim degraded land.
Use integrated water management.
Use bio-intensive integrated pest management.

topics.title: High External Input Agriculture (HEIA)
topics.definition: An agricultural system dependent on substantial external inputs such as hybrid seed, fertilizers, pesticides, machinery and irrigation.

sections.heading: Development
items: Developed in response to rising food demand.
Green Revolution emphasized higher harvest per unit area and increased cropping seasons.
High-yielding hybrid varieties required new production practices.

sections.heading: Input dependence
items: Chemical fertilizers were used heavily because hybrid varieties were nutrient sensitive.
Pesticides were needed because new crops were susceptible to pests and diseases.
Weedicides or manual weeding were needed because dwarf hybrids competed poorly with weeds.
Mechanization became an integral component.
New crops required more water and improved irrigation.

sections.heading: Sustainability issue
items: Many external resources were not recycled.
The system depended on regular external inputs for high yields.
Stopping inputs could make the system unproductive.

topics.title: Advantages of HEIA
topics.definition: Benefits attributed in the source to high external input agriculture.

sections.heading: Advantages
items: Rapid increase in agricultural production.
Improved food availability.
Reduction of some nutrition-related problems.
Improved varieties can give yields in a short period.
Mechanization helps address labour shortages.
Higher income and profit margins.
Higher land productivity.
Improved market facilities.

topics.title: Disadvantages of HEIA
topics.definition: Environmental, economic and social problems associated in the source with high external input agriculture.

sections.heading: Major disadvantages
items: Reduced biodiversity can disturb environmental balance.
Machinery may increase soil erosion through constant furrowing.
Dependence on imported machinery, fertilizers, pesticides and hybrid seed.
Pesticides can kill natural enemies as well as target pests.
Agrochemicals can affect soil pH, CEC, structure, texture and soil organisms.
High capital requirements can disadvantage capital-poor farmers.
Traditional varieties and indigenous knowledge may decline.
Farmers may face environmental, social and economic problems.

topics.title: Limitations of Green Revolution Practices
topics.definition: Shortcomings identified by the source in planning and long-term effects of Green Revolution practices.

sections.heading: Economic and ecological issues
items: Surplus production could contribute to lower commodity prices.
Long-term dependence on pesticides and chemical fertilizers was not fully anticipated.
Quick crop response encouraged artificial-manure use without awareness of long-term effects.
The source states that 40–50% of applied nitrogen may be wasted in tropical countries.
Nitrogen losses increase with high rainfall, drought, erosion and low organic matter.
Continuous NPK use may create micronutrient deficiencies.
Nitrous oxide contributes to atmospheric and ozone-related concerns.

sections.heading: Pesticide issues
items: Pesticide poisoning can affect people.
Repeated use can lead to pest resistance.
Pesticides can kill natural enemies.
Pesticides can contaminate water, air, soil and food.
Pesticides can enter food chains and food webs.

topics.title: Low External Input and Sustainable Agriculture (LEISA)
topics.definition: An integrated agricultural system designed to maintain optimum production using fewer external inputs in an eco-friendly manner.

sections.heading: Need
items: Developed in response to high capital needs and environmental impacts of HEIA.
Combines selected traditional principles with newer technology.
The source describes LEISA as integrating bio-dynamic, environmental, natural, organic and regenerative subsystems.

sections.heading: Ecological principles
items: Maintain favorable soil conditions and stimulate soil microorganisms.
Maintain nutrient balance through fixation, deep nutrient use, recycling and needed supplementation.
Control microclimate-related resource losses.
Use biological and mechanical erosion control.
Prioritize natural biological pest control.
Promote biodiversity and plant–plant and plant–animal interactions.

sections.heading: Core practices
items: Maintain a living soil.
Create biodiversity.
Recycle resources.
Use natural pest management.

topics.title: Living Soil and Soil Organisms

sections.heading: Requirements
items: Adequate water, air and nutrients.
Favorable soil structure for water, nutrients and root growth.
Suitable soil temperature.
Absence of poisonous substances.
Active soil microorganisms.

sections.heading: Soil organisms
items: Microflora: bacteria, fungi and algae.
Microfauna: protozoa.
Mesofauna: nematodes.
Macro animals: weevils, centipedes, termites, rats, worms and snakes.

sections.heading: Microorganism functions
items: Decompose organic matter into humus.
Mineralize humus and release nutrients.
Assist nitrogen fixation.
Convert insoluble phosphate to soluble forms.
Help plants absorb nutrients.
Maintain soil sanitation.
Help suppress harmful microorganisms.

topics.title: Resource Cycling and Recycling

sections.heading: Nutrient balance

sections.heading: Methods

Mechanical control.
Natural pesticides.
Artificial pesticides when included within the listed integrated methods.

Big onion.

topics.title: Major Irrigation Problems

items: Soil salinity.

topics.title: Saline and Alkali Soils
topics.definition: Salt-affected soils distinguished in the source using EC, ESP, pH, salt composition and physical condition.

sections.heading: USDA classification
items: Saline: EC >4 mmhos/cm; ESP <15; pH <8.5.
Saline-alkali: EC >4; ESP >15; pH >8.5.
Alkali: EC <4; ESP >15; pH 8.5–10.0.

sections.heading: Saline soil
items: Common in arid and semi-arid areas.
Favored by high water table, high salt concentration, high temperature and low rainfall.
Main soluble salts include chlorides and sulphates.
ESP is below 15%; pH is below 8.5.
EC is above 4 mmho/cm.
Generally flocculated with relatively normal aeration and permeability.
Can be reclaimed mainly through leaching and ponding.

sections.heading: Alkali soil
items: Common in Indo-Gangetic plains and poorly drained low-lying areas.
Carbonates mainly involve sodium.
ESP is above 15%; pH is above 8.5.
EC is below 4 mmho/cm.
Soil is dispersed and compact with poor aeration and permeability.
Amendments such as gypsum or iron pyrite are important.

sections.heading: Formulas
items: ESP = exchangeable sodium / total cation exchange capacity × 100.
SAR = Na+ / √(Ca2+ + Mg2+) .

topics.title: Wasteland: Meaning and Classification
topics.definition: Land that is unproductive or underutilized because of neglect, degradation or constraints, though some wastelands can be reclaimed.

sections.heading: Definitions
items: Wasteland Survey and Reclamation Committee (1961): lands unavailable for cultivation or left as fallows and cultivable wastes.
National Wasteland Development Board: lands currently unutilized due to different constraints.
Wastelands include culturable and unculturable categories.
They are also termed degraded lands.

sections.heading: Classification
items: Culturable wastelands have potential for vegetative cover but face constraints such as erosion, waterlogging and salinization.
Many culturable wastelands can be made productive through treatment and reclamation.
Unculturable wastelands cannot be developed for vegetative cover, such as barren rocky or snow-covered areas.

sections.heading: Source figure
items: About 158 mha of India's 329 mha geographical area is stated as being under different kinds of land degradation.

topics.title: Management of Wastelands

sections.heading: Ravine land
items: River erosion and deposition create ravine lands.
Known locally as khadar, diara, char, rao and cho in different regions.
Use soil-conservation measures.
Live hedges help control erosion and sediment deposition.

sections.heading: Coastal sandy areas
items: Afforestation is recommended.
Wide forest belts can moderate cyclone effects.
Casuarina tolerates salinity and moisture stress.

sections.heading: High-altitude and steep slopes
items: Excess runoff during monsoon can cause erosion and floods.

items: Avoids or largely excludes synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, hormones and feed additives.

Maintain long-term soil productivity.
Avoid agrochemical pollution.
Minimize fossil-energy use.

sections.heading: Core principles
items: Crops should obtain nutrients through soil biological activity under suitable conditions.

Biomass management should support a self-supporting nutrient system.

sections.heading: IFOAM-style principles presented in source
items: Principle of health.
Principle of ecology.
Principle of fairness.
Principle of care.

sections.heading: Biofertilizers
items: Contain selected microorganisms.

sections.heading: Major groups
items: Free-living nitrogen fixers.
Symbiotic nitrogen fixers.
Associative symbiotic organisms such as Azospirillum.
Phosphorus-solubilizing bacteria and fungi.
Arbuscular and ectomycorrhiza.

sections.heading: Other biological inputs
items: Azolla.
Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR).
Mycorrhizal fungi.

topics.title: Important Biofertilizers and Microbial Inputs

sections.heading: Nitrogen-fixing groups
items: Azotobacter: free-living nitrogen fixer.

sections.heading: Phosphorus-related inputs

sections.heading: PGPR

Benefit crops through growth-promoting effects.

topics.title: Organic Manures

sections.heading: Sources
items: Cattle shed wastes.
Human habitation wastes.

Slaughterhouse wastes.
Agro-industry by-products.
Crop residues.
Water hyacinth, weeds and tank silt.
Green manure and green-leaf material.

sections.heading: Groups
items: Bulky organic manures.
Concentrated organic manures.

sections.heading: Benefits of bulky manures

topics.title: Farmyard Manure (FYM)
topics.definition: Decomposed mixture of dung and urine of farm animals with associated litter and refuse.

sections.heading: Preparation
items: Trenches are described as about 6 m long, 2 m wide and 1 m deep.
Dung and urine-soaked material is collected daily.
Litter and refuse are mixed with soil to absorb urine.
Collected material is placed in the trench in sections.

sections.heading: Use
items: Partially rotten FYM should be applied about 3–4 weeks before sowing.
Manure left exposed in the field for long periods may lose nutrients.
Immediate incorporation after spreading reduces losses.
Responsive crops listed include potato, tomato, sweet potato, carrot, radish, onion, sugarcane, rice, Napier grass and several orchard crops.

topics.title: Composting Methods
topics.definition: Controlled decomposition of organic wastes into a stable manure-like material.

sections.heading: Aerobic method
items: Organic material is decomposed in the presence of air.
Turning is used to facilitate decomposition.
The source states decomposition ordinarily completes in about 4–5 months.
In heavy rainfall or high-water-table areas, heaps may be prepared above ground.

sections.heading: Anaerobic method
items: Uses a pit with compacted layers of farm residues.
Fresh cow dung, ash and water are added.
The pit is filled and decomposition proceeds without regular aeration.

topics.title: Vermicompost
topics.definition: Compost produced through the feeding and activity of earthworms on organic waste.

sections.heading: Process
items: Earthworms feed on waste organic material.
Organic matter is converted into vermicompost.
The source describes a harvesting and separation process after about four months.
The compost is dried in shade and sieved.
Earthworms are collected for the next preparation cycle.

sections.heading: Handling
items: Water is supplied as required during preparation.
Finished compost is packed in suitable polythene or laminated bags.

topics.title: Green Manuring

Can improve crop yield.
Improves soil fertility.
Improves soil structure.
Helps prevent soil erosion.

sections.heading: Green-leaf manuring

sections.heading: In situ practice
items: Green-manure crops are incorporated into the soil at a suitable stage.
Legumes and nitrogen-fixing plants are especially useful.

Optimize utilization and conservation of resources.

items: Soil and climate.

Current resource utilization.

Farmer's managerial skill.

sections.heading: Enterprise-selection factors
items: Local soil and climate.
Farmer resources.

System economics.
Managerial skill.
Local social customs.

topics.definition: A participatory research approach based on interdependence among farming-system components and the natural environment.

sections.heading: Core idea
items: Farmers participate in identifying research problems.
Farmers participate in testing possible solutions.
Technology should be evaluated beyond technical performance.
Research should be grounded in small-farmer conditions.

topics.title: Characteristics of Farming System
topics.definition: Features that make farming-system research and development farmer-oriented, location-specific and sustainability-focused.

sections.heading: Characteristics
items: Farmer-oriented and holistic.
Effective farmer participation.
Problem-solving approach.
Dynamic system.
Gender sensitive.
Responsible to society.
Environmental sustainability.
Location-specific technology.
Diversified enterprises to reduce environmental risk.

sections.heading: Additional characteristics
items: Bottom-up approach.

Extensive on-farm activities.
Collaboration between farmers and scientists.

topics.title: Objectives of Farming System

sections.heading: Objectives
items: Increase productivity per unit area and time.
Improve profitability through complementary enterprises.
Promote balanced food production.
Improve environmental safety.

Reduce production risk through enterprise diversification.

sections.heading: Factors
items: Physical and biological conditions set limits on suitable enterprises.
Quantity and quality of land, water and other resources influence choices.
Farmer goals and attitudes affect the system.
Resource availability and resource-use level shape enterprise combinations.

topics.title: Cropping System
topics.definition: Principles and practices of cropping and their interaction with farm resources, technology and environmental conditions.

sections.heading: Multiple cropping
items: Sequential cropping: two or more crops grown in sequence on the same field in a year.
Intercropping: two or more dissimilar crops grown simultaneously.

sections.heading: Types of intercropping
items: Mixed intercropping: simultaneous crops without distinct rows.
Row intercropping: crops arranged in different rows.
Strip intercropping: crops grown in strips wide enough for independent management.
Relay intercropping: crops introduced in sequence so growth cycles overlap.

sections.heading: Other terms
items: Monoculture: repetitive growing of a sole crop.
Diversification and multiple cropping can help distribute production risk.

topics.title: Dairy Integration in Farming System

sections.heading: Benefits
items: Livestock diversification helps reduce risk.
Forage crops transfer nutrients within the farm.
Dung can be used as crop manure.
Crop residues provide livestock feed.

sections.heading: Cattle groups
items: Draft breeds.
Dairy breeds.
Dual-purpose breeds.
Exotic breeds.
Buffaloes.

sections.heading: Feed groups
items: Roughages: legumes, non-legume hays, straw and silage.
Concentrates: grains and grain/oilseed by-products.
Vitamin and mineral mixtures may supplement rations.

topics.title: Biogas / Gobar Gas Plant

sections.heading: Types

Fixed-dome type.

Multiple kids and relatively fast growth support production.
Provides employment through the year.

sections.heading: Feed

Crop residues can be used with suitable treatment or supplementation.
Concentrates include grains, bran, oilseed products and other feed materials.

topics.title: Poultry Farming

Poultry houses need ventilation, water and power.
The site should be well drained and protected from floodwater.
Shed width is stated as not exceeding about 25–33 feet.

sections.heading: Feed and cost

topics.title: Fisheries in Farming System

items: Fish ponds can receive nutrient-rich wastes from poultry or livestock.

topics.title: Bee Keeping / Apiculture

sections.heading: Bee species
items: Apis cerana is better acclimatized to higher Himalayan areas.
Apis mellifera and Apis dorsata are described as more profitable in plains.

sections.heading: Management
items: Beekeepers should know local nectar and pollen sources.

Pollen sources include maize, sorghum, millets, sunflower and palm.

sections.heading: Timing
items: The source identifies arrival of suitable nectar/pollen sources as important for starting beekeeping.

items: Moriculture = cultivation of mulberry.

Sericulture includes mulberry cultivation, silkworm rearing and silk reeling.

Silk production contributes to rural socio-economic development in some areas.
Silk goods are exported to multiple international markets.

topics.title: Agroforestry in Farming System
topics.definition: Integrated land management combining trees with crops, animals or other agricultural enterprises.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Supports integrated and self-sustained land management.
Can supply fuel, fodder, fruit and timber.
Can support soil conservation and nutrient cycling.

sections.heading: Agri-horticultural system
items: Fruit trees are combined with short-duration arable crops.
Also called food-cum-fruit system.
Fruit-tree examples: guava, pomegranate, custard apple, sapota and mango.
Pulses are important arable crops for this system.

sections.heading: Alley cropping
items: Food crops are grown in alleys formed by tree or shrub hedgerows.

sections.heading: Tree farming
items: Useful where arable crops are less profitable.
Dryland farmers may prefer trees because of labour scarcity and drought-related crop failure.

title: Fundamentals of Plant Breeding
description: 67 topics covering History and milestones of plant breeding, Development of plant breeding in India, Important scientists and contributions and more.

topics.title: History and milestones of plant breeding
topics.definition: Plant breeding developed from deliberate selection and artificial crossing into a science based on genetics.

sections.heading: Early milestones
items: Babylonians and Assyrians artificially pollinated date palm as early as 700 BC.
Thomas Fairchild produced the first artificial hybrid in 1717.
Joseph Kolreuter studied extensive tobacco and Solanum crosses during 1760–1766.
Thomas Andrew Knight produced new fruit varieties through artificial hybridization.
Le Coutier reported wheat selection results in 1843.
Patrick Shireff practiced individual plant selection in wheat and oats.
Vilmorin proposed individual plant selection with progeny testing in 1857.
Nilsson and associates refined single-plant selection at Svalöf around 1890.
Johannsen proposed the pure-line theory in 1903.
G.H. Shull's maize work became a foundation for modern hybrid maize breeding.

sections.heading: Major achievements
items: Norman Borlaug developed Mexican semi-dwarf wheat varieties in the 1960s.
Norin 10 supplied the dwarfing gene used in Mexican semi-dwarf wheat.
M.S. Swaminathan introduced Mexican dwarf wheats into India.
IRRI used Dee-geo-woo-gen (DGWG) in development of IR 8 rice.
C.A. Barber and T.S. Venkatraman contributed to sugarcane noblisation.

topics.title: Development of plant breeding in India
topics.definition: Indian plant breeding developed through agricultural departments, research institutes, coordinated projects and agricultural universities.

sections.heading: Institutional milestones
items: Department of Agriculture was created by Government of India in 1871.
Imperial Agricultural Research Institute was established at Pusa in 1905.
The institute shifted to New Delhi in 1936 after earthquake damage in 1934.
Its name changed to Indian Agricultural Research Institute in 1946.
Imperial Council of Agricultural Research was established in 1929.
It became Indian Council of Agricultural Research in 1946.
Indian Central Cotton Committee was established in 1921.
PIRRCOM began in 1956 for cotton, oilseeds and millets.
All India Coordinated Maize Improvement Project started in 1957.
First hybrid maize varieties were released by the project in 1961.
First Agricultural University was established at Pantnagar in 1960.

topics.title: Important scientists and contributions
topics.definition: Several classical breeding methods and concepts are associated with named scientists.

sections.heading: Named contributions
items: Allard and Bradshaw — G × E interaction.
Hull — recurrent selection for SCA.
Jenkins — recurrent selection for GCA.
Davenport — dominance hypothesis.
Flor — gene-for-gene hypothesis.
Johannsen — pure-line concept.
Harlan and Pope — backcross method.
Jones — double-cross scheme.
Jones and Davis — cytoplasmic genetic male sterility.
Hopkins — ear-to-row method.
Lonnquist — modified ear-to-row method.
Blakeslee and Nebel — colchicine.
Goulden — single-seed descent.
Lewis — self-incompatibility classification.
Vavilov — centres of diversity and law of homologous series.
Vilmorin — progeny testing.
Fairchild — first artificial hybrid.
Rimpau — triticale.
Hugo de Vries — mutation.
Shull — heterosis.
Yuan Long Ping — father of hybrid rice.

topics.title: Activities in plant breeding
topics.definition: Plant breeding proceeds through creation or discovery of variation followed by selection, evaluation, multiplication and distribution.

sections.heading: Sources of variation
items: Naturally existing variability includes domestication, germplasm collection and introduction.
New variability can be created by hybridization.
Hybridization includes intervarietal, distant and somatic forms.
Mutation, polyploidy and somaclonal variation create new variability.
Genetic engineering is another source of new variation.

sections.heading: Breeding sequence
items: Selection identifies desirable plants or lines.
Evaluation tests performance and target traits.
Multiplication increases seed or planting material.
Distribution makes the improved material available for cultivation.

topics.title: Concept, nature and role of plant breeding
topics.definition: Plant breeding is the art, science and technology of improving plant genetic makeup for economic use and human benefit.

sections.heading: Core concept
items: Plant breeding is also described as the science of crop improvement.
It changes and improves plant heredity.
N.W. Simmonds described plant breeding as the current phase of crop evolution in 1979.

sections.heading: Role
items: Breeding converts genetic variation into agronomically useful varieties.
The programme is directed by the crop, environment and economic objective.

topics.title: Objectives of plant breeding
topics.definition: Objectives are crop-specific improvements in yield, quality, resistance, adaptation, maturity and other useful traits.

sections.heading: Yield and quality
items: Higher economic yield may mean grain, fodder, fibre, tuber, cane or oil yield.
Yield improvement may use high-yielding varieties or hybrids.
Quality targets include grain size, colour, milling and baking quality in wheat.
Rice breeding may target cooking quality.
Barley breeding may target malting quality.
Vegetable breeding may target nutritive and keeping quality.
Pulse breeding may target protein content.
Oilseed breeding may target oil content.
Cotton breeding may target fibre length, strength and fineness.

sections.heading: Stress and protection
items: Abiotic targets include drought, salinity, heat, cold, frost and wind resistance.
Biotic resistance targets diseases and insects.
Genetic resistance is described as an economical way to reduce losses.
Resistant donor parents can be used from the gene pool.

sections.heading: Plant type and maturity
items: Earliness reduces crop management period and may reduce insecticide use.
Early varieties can permit new crop rotations.
Cotton maturity was reduced from 270 to 170 days in the source example.
Pigeonpea maturity was reduced from 270 to 120 days.
Sugarcane maturity was reduced from 360 to 270 days.
Determinate growth is desirable in mung, pigeonpea and cotton.
Dormancy can prevent pre-harvest germination in greengram, blackgram, barley and pea.
Desirable agronomic traits include plant height, branching, tillering and growth habit.
Dwarf cereals are associated in the source with lodging resistance and fertilizer response.

sections.heading: Special objectives
items: Breeding may eliminate toxic compounds such as neurotoxin in khesari, erucic acid in Brassica and gossypol in cotton seed.
Non-shattering is important in green gram.
Synchronous maturity is desirable in crops requiring repeated pickings.
Photo- and thermo-insensitive varieties expand cultivation into new regions.
Wider adaptability helps stabilize production across environments.
Breeding can create varieties for new seasons; maize can be grown in kharif, rabi and zaid situations.

topics.title: Scope, future prospects and undesirable effects
topics.definition: Future breeding combines classical genetics with molecular biology and biotechnology, while maintaining attention to genetic diversity.

sections.heading: Future prospects
items: Population growth creates continuing demand for crop improvement.
Molecular biology provides sharper tools for breeders.
Biotechnology has enabled field testing of genetically modified crops.
Genes from diverse organisms may improve biotic and abiotic stress resistance.
Plants may be engineered to produce valuable compounds such as pharmaceuticals.
The source cites transgenic Brassica napus producing hirudin as an example.

sections.heading: Undesirable effects
items: Modern improved varieties may be more uniform than landraces.
Reduced diversity can increase vulnerability to new pathogen races.
Uniform varieties may have a narrow genetic base and poorer adaptability.
Shared pedigree parents can create danger of genetic uniformity.
Plant breeding can sometimes create undesirable combinations such as Raphanobrassica and Pomato.
Strong selection for major pests and diseases may increase susceptibility to minor pests or diseases.
The source cites chickpea grey mold epidemics, Karnal bunt in wheat and mealy bugs in Bt cotton as examples.

topics.title: Genetics and cytogenetics in plant breeding
topics.definition: Genetic and cytogenetic principles provide the basis for planned crop improvement.

sections.heading: Important concepts
items: Mitosis and meiosis.
Chromosomes and chromosomal structural changes.
Numerical chromosome changes.
Mendel's laws of inheritance.
Gene interaction, linkage and crossing over.
Pleiotropy, penetrance and expressivity.
Cytoplasmic inheritance.
Polygenic and oligogenic characters.
Mutations and population genetics.
Plant biotechnology.

sections.heading: Mode of reproduction
items: Mode of reproduction determines whether crop populations are mainly homozygous or heterozygous.
Self-pollinated crops such as wheat are generally homozygous.
A homozygous line is therefore a common breeding target in self-pollinators.

topics.title: Vegetative reproduction
topics.definition: Asexual vegetative reproduction produces new plants from vegetative plant parts without gamete fusion.

sections.heading: Natural vegetative structures
items: Tuber — potato.
Bulb — onion and garlic.
Rhizome — ginger and turmeric.
Corm — bunda and arvi.
Sub-aerial stems include runners, stolons and suckers.
Mint and date palm are examples of crops using sub-aerial stems.

sections.heading: Artificial vegetative reproduction
items: Stem cuttings are used in sugarcane, grapes and roses.
Layering, budding, grafting and gootee are used for fruit trees and ornamentals.
Tissue culture permits vegetative multiplication in many plant species.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
items: A desirable plant can be used directly as a variety even when heterozygous.
Desirable mutant buds, branches or seedlings can be multiplied directly.
Vegetative propagation can preserve a selected genotype unchanged.

topics.title: Apomixis
topics.definition: Apomixis is seed formation in which the embryo develops without fertilization.

sections.heading: Types
items: Apomictic progeny is generally genetically identical to the parent.
Facultative apomixis occurs when sexual reproduction can also occur.
Obligate apomixis occurs when sexual reproduction is absent.
Adventive embryony develops embryos directly from nucellus, integument or chalaza.
Apospory produces unreduced embryo sacs from ovular somatic cells.
Diplospory develops the embryo sac from the megaspore, often with modified meiosis.
Parthenogenesis develops the embryo from an embryo-sac cell without pollination.
Gonial parthenogenesis uses the egg cell.
Somatic parthenogenesis uses another embryo-sac cell.
Apogamy develops an embryo from synergids or antipodals.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
items: Apomixis is undesirable when sexual progeny, selfs or hybrids are required.
It is useful for maintaining a desirable genotype unchanged.
Apomictic reproduction can preserve selected varieties without segregation.
Asexually reproducing crops are often highly heterozygous and may show severe inbreeding depression.
Breeding programmes for such crops should avoid unnecessary inbreeding.

topics.title: Sexual reproduction and gametogenesis
topics.definition: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote and creates recombination.

sections.heading: Flower and sporogenesis
items: Perfect or hermaphrodite flowers contain stamens and pistil.
Staminate flowers contain stamens but not pistils.
Pistillate flowers contain pistils but not stamens.
Monoecious species have male and female flowers on the same plant.
Dioecious species have male and female flowers on different plants.
Sporogenesis is production of microspores and megaspores.
Microsporogenesis occurs in anthers.
Each pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid microspores.
Megasporogenesis occurs in ovules.
A megaspore mother cell produces four haploid megaspores; usually three degenerate.

sections.heading: Gametogenesis
items: Microgametogenesis produces male gametes.
The pollen nucleus forms a generative nucleus and vegetative or tube nucleus.
The generative nucleus divides to form two sperm cells.
The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle.
Megagametogenesis forms the embryo sac from the functional megaspore.
In most crops, three mitotic divisions produce eight nuclei.
The mature embryo sac generally has one egg, two synergids, three antipodals and two polar nuclei forming the diploid secondary nucleus.

sections.heading: Significance
items: Sexual reproduction combines genes from two parents.
Recombination generates many genotypes.
Hybridization uses this variation for crop improvement.

topics.title: Modes of pollination and genetic consequences
topics.definition: Pollination is transfer of pollen from anthers to stigmas; its pattern determines genetic structure and breeding strategy.

sections.heading: Types
items: Self-pollination or autogamy uses pollen from the same flower.
Cross-pollination or allogamy transfers pollen between different plants.
Geitonogamy transfers pollen between flowers of the same plant.
Genetic consequences of geitonogamy are similar to autogamy.

sections.heading: Self-pollination mechanisms
items: Cleistogamy prevents flower opening and promotes complete self-pollination.
Some cereals open only after pollination.
In tomato and brinjal, anthers closely surround the stigma.
In legumes, floral organs enclose anthers and stigma within the keel.
These mechanisms make self-pollination efficient.

sections.heading: Genetic consequence
items: Self-pollination rapidly increases homozygosity.
Self-pollinated populations are highly homozygous.
The source states that self-pollinated species generally do not show inbreeding depression.
Breeding usually aims at developing homozygous varieties.

sections.heading: Cross-pollination mechanisms
items: Dicliny produces separate staminate and pistillate flowers.
Monoecy has male and female flowers on the same plant.
Dioecy has male and female flowers on different plants.
Protogyny means pistils mature before stamens; bajra is an example.
Protandry means stamens mature before pistils; maize and sugarbeet are examples.
Honey bees break the waxy film over alfalfa stigmas and facilitate pollination.
Self-incompatibility prevents successful self-fertilization.
Male sterility produces nonfunctional pollen.

sections.heading: Genetic consequence
items: Cross-pollination preserves and promotes heterozygosity.
Cross-pollinated species may show inbreeding depression.
They often show considerable heterosis.
Breeding may aim at hybrid or synthetic varieties.

sections.heading: Often cross-pollinated crops
items: Jowar, cotton, arhar and safflower are cited as often cross-pollinated.
Cross-pollination can exceed 5% and may reach about 30% in such crops.
Their genetic architecture is intermediate between self- and cross-pollinated crops.

topics.title: Self-incompatibility
topics.definition: Self-incompatibility is failure of pollen from a flower or plant to fertilize compatible female tissue on the same plant.

sections.heading: Classification
items: More than 300 species in about 20 angiosperm families show self-incompatibility in the source.
Heteromorphic and homomorphic systems are recognized.
Homomorphic systems include gametophytic and sporophytic control.

sections.heading: Heteromorphic system
items: Flower morphology differs between incompatibility groups.
Primula has pin and thrum forms; this is distyly.
Lythrum shows tristyly.
In distyly, compatible mating occurs between pin and thrum flowers.
The source gives Ss for thrum and ss for pin.
Pin × thrum produces Ss and ss progeny in equal frequencies.

sections.heading: Gametophytic system
items: Pollen incompatibility is determined by its own genotype.
A single S locus with multiple alleles commonly controls the system.
Pollen carrying an S allele is rejected by stylar tissue carrying the same allele.
Examples include Trifolium, Nicotiana, Lycopersicon, Solanum and Petunia.
S1S2 × S1S2 is fully incompatible.
S1S2 × S3S4 is fully compatible.
S1S2 × S2S3 is partially compatible; about 50% pollen is compatible.

sections.heading: Sporophytic system
items: Pollen reaction is determined by the genotype of the plant producing the pollen.
More than 30 S alleles are reported in Brassica oleracea in the source.
Dominance, codominance or competition can occur among S alleles.
Radish, diploid Brassica and Sinapis are examples.
Reciprocal differences may occur.
Homozygotes can occur as normal members of the system.

sections.heading: Mechanism and breeding use
items: Pollen-stigma, pollen tube-style and pollen tube-ovule interactions can block fertilization.
Gametophytic incompatibility often blocks pollen-tube growth in the stigma or style.
Sporophytic incompatibility commonly acts at the stigma.
Self-incompatibility can be exploited for hybrid seed production.
Two self-incompatible but cross-compatible lines can be interplanted to produce hybrid seed.
Environmental conditions such as high temperature and humidity can reduce incompatibility and increase selfed seed.

sections.heading: Temporary suppression
items: Bud pollination uses mature pollen on immature stigma about 1–2 days before anthesis.
Surgical removal of stigma or style can permit incompatible crosses in some species.
End-of-season pollination may exploit reduced incompatibility late in flowering.
The source reports temperatures up to 60°C inducing pseudofertility in some crops.
X-rays or gamma-rays can temporarily suppress incompatibility in some systems.
Grafting and double pollination have also been reported.

topics.title: Male sterility
topics.definition: Male sterility is production of nonfunctional pollen while female fertility remains functional.

sections.heading: Types
items: Genetic male sterility is usually controlled by a recessive ms gene.
Dominant male-sterility genes are also known, including in safflower.
Cytoplasmic male sterility is controlled by cytoplasm.
Cytoplasmic-genetic male sterility combines sterile cytoplasm with nuclear fertility-restorer genes.

sections.heading: Genetic male sterility
items: ms ms × Ms ms gives about 1:1 male-sterile and male-fertile progeny.
Male-sterile and maintainer lines can be isogenic except at the ms locus.
Male-fertile plants must be identified and removed from the female line before pollen shedding.
This rouging requirement increases hybrid-seed production cost.
The source notes commercial use in castor in the USA and arhar in India.

sections.heading: Cytoplasmic male sterility
items: Cytoplasm is inherited mainly through the egg, so progeny of a male-sterile female remain male sterile.
A recurrent pollinator can maintain the male-sterile A line.
The fertile maintainer is called the B line.
The source associates CMS genes particularly with mitochondria in maize.

sections.heading: Cytoplasmic-genetic system
items: A dominant nuclear restorer gene R restores fertility in sterile cytoplasm.
rr plants remain male sterile with male-sterile cytoplasm.
Rr or RR plants are male fertile.
The system is known in maize, jowar, bajra, sunflower, rice and wheat.
Restorer genes can be transferred through backcrossing.

sections.heading: Hybrid seed production
items: Removal of anthers before fertilization is essential when manual emasculation is required.
Male sterility reduces the need for repeated emasculation.
A, B and R lines are central to CMS-based hybrid systems.

topics.title: Domestication
topics.definition: Domestication is the evolutionary and human-directed transformation of wild plants into cultivated forms.

sections.heading: Key features
items: Domestication begins with selection and cultivation of useful plants.
Selection under cultivation changes plant form, reproduction and adaptation.
Domestication is a major source of cultivated crop diversity.

sections.heading: Breeding relevance
items: Domesticated material provides variation for selection.
Traits associated with cultivation can differ markedly from wild relatives.
Domestication history helps breeders understand available variation.

topics.title: Plant introduction
topics.definition: Plant introduction is bringing crop germplasm from one geographical region into another for cultivation, breeding or evaluation.

sections.heading: Types and purpose
items: Introductions may be primary or secondary.
Primary introduction can be directly cultivated after testing and selection.
Secondary introduction is used as breeding material and may produce improved varieties after crossing or selection.
The source cites popularization of grape cultivation in Haryana and introduction of wheat as examples.

sections.heading: History and institutions
items: Crop plants have been moved into new regions throughout agricultural history.
The source describes an organized Indian plant-introduction programme supported by ICAR from 1956.
NBPGR is identified with national management of agricultural and horticultural germplasm.
The Botanical Survey of India is associated with botanical and medicinal plant resources.

topics.title: Procedure and purposes of plant introduction
topics.definition: Introduction requires procurement, quarantine, evaluation and multiplication before safe use.

sections.heading: Procedure
items: Procurement of planting material is the first step.
Imported material is subjected to quarantine.
Introductions are evaluated for adaptation and useful traits.
Selected material is multiplied after successful evaluation.
Promising introductions can be released as varieties after required trials.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Introduce useful variation into breeding programmes.
Obtain traits not available in local material.
Provide material for direct cultivation after adaptation.
Support diversification of crops and growing regions.

topics.title: Germplasm collection and conservation
topics.definition: Germplasm collection assembles genetic resources needed for present and future crop improvement.

sections.heading: Collection
items: Germplasm may be collected from cultivated and wild material.
Collections preserve genetic diversity for breeding.
Characterization and evaluation identify useful accessions.

sections.heading: Breeding value
items: Germplasm supplies donors for disease, insect, quality and stress traits.
Exotic and indigenous material can broaden the genetic base.
Conserved accessions support future breeding when new traits are required.

topics.title: Centres of origin and diversity
topics.definition: Centres of origin and diversity identify regions where crops or their diversity are concentrated.

sections.heading: Vavilov concept
items: Vavilov developed the concept of centres of diversity.
Centres of diversity are important sources of genetic variability.
The law of homologous series is also associated with Vavilov.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
items: Regions rich in diversity can provide germplasm for crop improvement.
Wild and cultivated forms in diversity centres can supply useful alleles.
Knowledge of origin helps guide exploration and germplasm collection.

topics.title: Components of genetic variation
topics.definition: Observed phenotypic variation is partitioned into genetic and environmental components for selection decisions.

sections.heading: Variance components
items: Phenotypic variation contains genetic and environmental components.
Genetic variation includes additive and non-additive effects.
Environmental variation can mask genetic differences.
Genotype × environment interaction contributes to observed performance across environments.

sections.heading: Breeding significance
items: Selection is effective when useful variation is heritable.
Partitioning variation helps predict response to selection.
Heritability and genetic advance are used together as selection parameters.

topics.title: Heritability
topics.definition: Heritability measures the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to genetic variance in a specified population and environment.

sections.heading: Broad-sense heritability
items: Broad-sense heritability is the proportion of total phenotypic variance due to total genetic variance.
H² = Vg / Vp.
The source also expresses estimation using variance components from generations such as VF2 and VF1.

sections.heading: Narrow-sense heritability
items: Narrow-sense heritability focuses on additive genetic variance.
It is especially relevant to response from selection because additive effects are transmitted predictably.

sections.heading: Interpretation
items: Heritability is population- and environment-dependent.
High heritability does not by itself guarantee large genetic gain.
Genetic advance should be considered with heritability.

topics.title: Genetic advance
topics.definition: Genetic advance is the expected improvement in mean genotypic value from selection.

sections.heading: Measures
items: Genetic advance is the difference between mean genotypic value of selected lines and the original population.
Genetic advance as percent of mean = Genetic advance / population mean × 100.
The source classifies GA% mean as low below 10%, moderate at 10–20% and high above 20%.

sections.heading: Joint interpretation
items: High heritability + high genetic advance suggests additive gene effects and effective selection.
High heritability + low genetic advance suggests greater non-additive effects and less rewarding direct selection.
Low heritability + high genetic advance can occur when additive effects exist but environmental effects are large.
Low heritability + low genetic advance suggests strong environmental influence and ineffective selection.

topics.title: Pure-line theory and selection
topics.definition: A pure line is the progeny of a single self-fertilized homozygous plant.

sections.heading: Johannsen's findings
items: Johannsen studied Phaseolus vulgaris, variety Princess.
A market seed lot contained mixtures of larger and smaller seeds.
Selection produced genetically distinct pure lines.
Variation within a pure line was attributed to environment.
Selection within a pure line was ineffective because individuals were genetically homozygous.

sections.heading: Requirements and value
items: Successful selection requires variation.
The variation must be heritable.
Progeny testing helps distinguish genetic from environmental performance.
Pure-line selection is particularly useful in self-pollinated crops.

topics.title: Pure-line selection method: merits and limitations
topics.definition: Pure-line selection identifies superior individual plants from a variable self-pollinated population and evaluates their progenies.

sections.heading: Method
items: Select superior individual plants from a heterogeneous population.
Grow progenies separately.
Compare progenies for uniformity and target traits.
Discard inferior lines.
Test promising pure lines in yield and adaptation trials.
Multiply and release the superior line after confirmation.

sections.heading: Merits
items: Produces highly uniform varieties.
Useful for self-pollinated crops.
Uses existing variability without requiring a planned cross.

sections.heading: Limitations
items: Selection cannot create new genetic variation within an already pure line.
The method depends on available variability.
Narrow genetic base can result if the source population is limited.

topics.title: Hybridization in self-pollinated crops
topics.definition: Hybridization combines desirable genes from different parents to create new segregating variation.

sections.heading: Objectives
items: Combine complementary characters from parents.
Transfer specific resistance or quality traits.
Create transgressive segregants.
Generate variation not present in a single parent.

sections.heading: Types
items: Intervarietal hybridization crosses varieties of the same species.
Distant hybridization uses more remote parents.
Somatic hybridization can combine cells or genomes through tissue-culture approaches.

sections.heading: Basic procedure
items: Select suitable parents.
Synchronize flowering.
Emasculate the female parent where needed.
Bag and protect the female flower.
Apply pollen from the selected male parent.
Tag and record the cross.
Harvest and store F1 seed separately.
Grow F1 plants to confirm hybridity.

topics.title: Emasculation and controlled crossing
topics.definition: Emasculation removes or disables anthers of the female parent before pollen shedding to prevent unwanted selfing.

sections.heading: Methods
items: Hand emasculation removes anthers manually.
Hot-water treatment can kill pollen without removing floral parts.
Alcohol treatment can sterilize or kill pollen in suitable crops.
Suction methods can remove pollen from some flowers.
Male-sterility systems can replace manual emasculation.

sections.heading: Crossing steps
items: Emasculate at the appropriate floral stage.
Bag the emasculated flower.
Collect mature pollen from the male parent.
Pollinate the receptive stigma.
Rebag to prevent contamination.
Label the cross with parent identities and date.
Harvest crossed heads or pods after seed maturation.
Store F1 seed with original tags.

topics.title: Segregating populations and transgressive segregation
topics.definition: F2 and later generations after selfing an F1 segregate for parental genes; some individuals may exceed both parents.

sections.heading: Concept
items: F2 and onward generations are called segregating generations.
Transgressive segregation produces individuals exceeding either parent for one or more characters.
Transgressive breeding exploits these superior segregants.

sections.heading: Main methods
items: Pedigree breeding.
Bulk breeding.
Single-seed descent.
Backcross breeding.
Multiple-cross breeding.

topics.title: Pedigree method
topics.definition: Pedigree breeding selects individual plants and records their ancestry generation by generation until desirable lines become sufficiently homozygous.

sections.heading: Procedure
items: F1 plants are space planted to obtain F2 seed.
About 2,000–10,000 F2 plants may be grown in the source procedure.
About 200–500 desirable F2 plants are selected.
Selected plants are grown as separate progenies in F3.
About 3–5 best plants may be selected from each superior row.
The process continues through F4 and F5; about 20–50 families may be retained at F5.
By F6 many lines become homozygous and uniform.
F7 preliminary yield trials are conducted.
F8–F10 confirm superior lines across trials.
F10–F11 seed is multiplied and distributed.

sections.heading: Merits and limitations
items: Provides information on inheritance.
Allows breeder judgement during selection.
Can recover useful transgressive segregants.
Accurate pedigree records require substantial time.
Large selected material becomes difficult to handle.
Success depends on breeder skill.

sections.heading: Modified form
items: Mass pedigree method combines bulk handling when selection conditions are unfavorable with pedigree selection when conditions are favorable.

topics.title: Bulk method
topics.definition: Bulk breeding advances segregating generations in bulk and postpones intensive individual-plant selection until later generations.

sections.heading: Procedure
items: F1 plants are grown and F2 seed is harvested in bulk.
F2 to about F5 generations are grown as bulk populations with little or no deliberate selection.
F6 is space planted for single-plant selection.
Selected plants are grown as separate progenies in F7.
Preliminary yield testing begins around F8–F9.
Multi-location trials are conducted in later generations.
The source gives F9–F12 as a typical testing and multiplication period.

sections.heading: Merits
items: Simple and convenient.
Inexpensive and less labour-intensive.
No detailed pedigree records are required.
Natural selection operates during early generations.
Useful for studying survival of genes and genotypes.

sections.heading: Limitations
items: May take longer to develop a variety.
Breeder has less opportunity for early selection.
Inheritance information is limited.
Natural selection may favor survival rather than highest economic yield.

topics.title: Single-seed descent
topics.definition: Single-seed descent rapidly advances segregating generations by taking one seed from each plant for the next generation.

sections.heading: Core method
items: The method was suggested by Goulden in 1939.
One seed from each plant is carried forward generation after generation.
Rapid generation advance increases homozygosity without early intensive selection.
Individual plants or lines are evaluated after sufficient homozygosity.

sections.heading: Use
items: Useful when large segregating populations must be advanced quickly.
Reduces space and record requirements during early generations.
Selection is concentrated after advanced generations are obtained.

topics.title: Backcross breeding
topics.definition: Backcross breeding repeatedly crosses a hybrid to one recurrent parent to transfer a specific desirable trait.

sections.heading: Concept
items: The recurrent parent supplies most of the final genetic background.
The donor parent supplies the target gene or trait.
Repeated backcrossing recovers the recurrent-parent genotype.
Selection is made for the desired donor trait during the process.

sections.heading: Use
items: Useful for transferring disease or insect resistance.
Useful for transferring a specific quality or stress trait.
Particularly effective when the donor character is readily identifiable.

topics.title: Multiline concept
topics.definition: A multiline variety is a mixture of genetically similar lines that differ mainly in resistance genes or another specific feature.

sections.heading: Concept
items: Lines in a multiline have a common or similar genetic background.
They differ for specific resistance genes.
A multiline reduces uniform vulnerability to a pathogen population.
The approach was associated in the source with Jenson.

sections.heading: Procedure
items: Develop or identify lines differing for the desired resistance genes.
Select lines that are similar for agronomic background.
Combine the component lines in an appropriate proportion.
Evaluate the mixture for agronomic performance and disease response.

sections.heading: Applications
items: Main application is management of diseases with variable pathogen populations.
Useful where uniform single-gene resistance is vulnerable to pathogen change.

topics.title: Hardy-Weinberg law
topics.definition: Under specified assumptions, allele and genotype frequencies remain constant across generations in a random-mating population.

sections.heading: Law
items: For two alleles A and a, p + q = 1.
Expected genotype frequencies are p² AA, 2pq Aa and q² aa.
Equilibrium means genotype frequencies remain stable from generation to generation.
The law was independently developed by Hardy in 1908 and Weinberg in 1909.

sections.heading: Assumptions
items: Random mating.
No selection.
No mutation.
No migration.
No random genetic drift.
A sufficiently large Mendelian population is implied by the equilibrium model.

topics.title: Forces changing population equilibrium
topics.definition: Evolutionary forces alter allele frequencies and therefore disturb Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

sections.heading: Forces
