items: Selection changes reproductive contribution of genotypes.
Mutation introduces new alleles or changes existing alleles.
Migration moves genes between populations.
Genetic drift changes frequencies through random sampling.
Non-random mating changes genotype frequencies.
These forces are treated as evolutionary forces because they change population genetic structure.

topics.title: Population improvement schemes
topics.definition: Population improvement increases the frequency of desirable alleles in cross-pollinated populations while retaining useful heterozygosity.

sections.heading: Basis
items: Cross-pollinated crops are highly heterozygous and heterogeneous.
Inbreeding should be avoided or minimized because of inbreeding depression.
Individual genotypes are less important than allele frequencies in population improvement.
Selection can be with or without progeny testing.

sections.heading: Classes
items: Selection without progeny testing includes mass selection.
Selection with progeny testing includes progeny selection, line breeding and recurrent selection.

topics.title: Mass selection
topics.definition: Mass selection chooses many superior plants phenotypically and mixes their seed to form the next generation.

sections.heading: Procedure
items: Select plants based on phenotype.
Allow selected plants to intermate or open-pollinate according to the scheme.
Harvest seed from selected plants as required by the method.
Use the selected bulk as the next breeding population.
Repeat cycles when further improvement is required.

sections.heading: Use
items: Simple method for increasing frequency of favorable phenotypes.
Useful when target traits have adequate heritability.
Does not require detailed progeny testing.

topics.title: Recurrent selection
topics.definition: Recurrent selection repeatedly selects superior plants or progenies, intermates selected material and recombines favorable alleles.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Increase frequency of favorable alleles.
Maintain sufficient genetic variability for continued selection.
Improve a population over repeated cycles.

sections.heading: Forms
items: Recurrent selection for general combining ability targets performance with a tester or reference population.
Recurrent selection for specific combining ability targets performance in a particular cross combination.
The source associates GCA recurrent selection with Jenkins and SCA recurrent selection with Hull.

sections.heading: Cycle
items: Select superior plants or families.
Evaluate progenies as specified by the scheme.
Select the best materials.
Intermate selected plants or families.
Advance the recombined population into another selection cycle.

topics.title: Heterosis and its estimation
topics.definition: Heterosis is superiority of an F1 hybrid over a defined parental or standard reference for a target trait.

sections.heading: Types
items: The term heterosis was first used by Shull in 1914.
Average or mid-parent heterosis compares F1 with the average of two parents.
Heterobeltiosis compares F1 with the superior parent.
Economic, standard or useful heterosis compares F1 with the best commercial or standard variety.
The source describes economic heterosis as the commercially useful estimate.

sections.heading: Formula
items: Mid-parent heterosis (%) = (F1 − MP) / MP × 100.
Superior-parent heterosis (%) = (F1 − BP) / BP × 100.
Standard heterosis (%) = (F1 − standard check) / standard check × 100.

topics.title: Inbreeding depression
topics.definition: Inbreeding depression is reduction in vigor, fertility, yield or related performance caused by increased homozygosity in cross-pollinated populations.

sections.heading: Concept
items: Inbreeding increases homozygosity.
Recessive deleterious alleles become more frequently expressed.
Cross-pollinated crops can show mild to severe inbreeding depression.
Self-pollinated crops generally show much less inbreeding depression.

sections.heading: Relation to heterosis
items: Inbred lines often lose vigor during inbreeding.
Crossing suitable inbred lines can restore vigor in the hybrid.
The magnitude depends on crop, population and genetic constitution.

topics.title: Genetic bases of heterosis and inbreeding depression
topics.definition: The source discusses dominance, overdominance and epistatic explanations for heterosis and inbreeding depression.

sections.heading: Hypotheses
items: Dominance hypothesis explains heterosis through masking deleterious recessive alleles.
Overdominance attributes superior performance to heterozygous advantage at loci.
Epistatic explanations involve interactions among genes at different loci.
No single mechanism necessarily explains all cases of heterosis.

sections.heading: Breeding implication
items: Understanding genetic basis helps guide parent choice and hybrid development.
Genetic divergence and combining ability influence hybrid performance.

topics.title: Physiological basis of heterosis
topics.definition: Heterosis can be expressed through physiological differences in growth, metabolism and resource use.

sections.heading: Manifestations
items: Hybrid vigor may increase growth rate, size and yield.
Differences can occur in photosynthesis, respiration and assimilate production.
Improved physiological efficiency can contribute to superior hybrid performance.

sections.heading: Practical view
items: Physiological expression is a result of underlying genetic differences.
The breeder evaluates the final phenotype and economic performance of hybrids.

topics.title: Commercial utilization of heterosis
topics.definition: Commercial hybrid breeding exploits heterosis by producing seed from selected parental lines.

sections.heading: Requirements
items: Parents must be sufficiently uniform and stable.
Crossing must be reliable and economical.
Hybrid seed production requires effective control of self-pollination.
The hybrid must outperform relevant commercial standards for the target trait.

sections.heading: Systems
items: Male sterility can facilitate hybrid seed production.
Self-incompatibility can also be used in some crops.
Manual emasculation is possible where economical.

topics.title: Development and evaluation of inbred lines
topics.definition: Inbred lines are highly homozygous lines developed through repeated selfing or related inbreeding and used as hybrid parents.

sections.heading: Development
items: Select suitable source populations.
Self-pollinate selected plants repeatedly.
Select uniform and fertile lines during inbreeding.
Evaluate lines for agronomic performance and combining ability.
Maintain superior lines through controlled selfing or appropriate seed-production procedures.

sections.heading: Evaluation
items: Evaluate general combining ability where relevant.
Test specific combining ability through crosses.
Assess yield, quality, resistance, maturity and other target traits.
Discard weak or unstable lines.

topics.title: Composite and synthetic varieties
topics.definition: Composite and synthetic varieties are population varieties formed from selected parents or lines while retaining genetic diversity.

sections.heading: Definitions
items: A synthetic variety is produced by intercrossing selected lines with good combining ability.
A composite variety is formed by combining selected genotypes or varieties and allowing them to intermate.
Both maintain more genetic diversity than a single pure line.

sections.heading: Synthetic production
items: Evaluate candidate lines for combining ability.
Select lines with desirable performance and compatibility.
Intermate selected lines in a controlled scheme.
Bulk and maintain the resulting population.
Evaluate performance across environments.

sections.heading: Merits and limitations
items: Synthetics can maintain useful heterozygosity and broad adaptation.
They may be easier to maintain than commercial single-cross hybrids in some crops.
Performance can decline across generations due to recombination and segregation.
The number and combining ability of component lines influence performance.

topics.title: Breeding of vegetatively propagated crops
topics.definition: Clonal breeding improves crops propagated through vegetative organs and preserves selected genotypes as clones.

sections.heading: Characteristics
items: A clone is a group of plants produced from one plant by asexual reproduction.
Asexually propagated crops may lack seed, have short seed viability or produce seed rarely.
Many are perennials; annual examples include potato, cassava and sweet potato.
Many show reduced flowering or seed set.
They are commonly cross-pollinated, highly heterozygous and may show severe inbreeding depression.
Many are polyploids, such as sugarcane and potato.
Some are interspecific hybrids, including banana and sugarcane.

sections.heading: Clone properties
items: Members of a clone are genetically identical in principle.
Within-clone phenotypic variation is mainly environmental.
Phenotype reflects genotype, environment and G × E interaction.
Clones can be maintained for generations.
Clones may deteriorate through pathogens and mutation.

topics.title: Clonal selection and breeding problems
topics.definition: Clonal selection identifies superior plants and multiplies them vegetatively without fixing the genotype through sexual reproduction.

sections.heading: Selection
items: Select superior individual plants from a variable clonal population.
Multiply selected plants vegetatively.
Test clonal progenies in replicated and multi-environment trials.
Discard unstable or inferior clones.
Maintain elite clones through disease-free propagation.

sections.heading: Advantages
items: Heterozygous genotypes can be preserved.
A desirable plant can be released without homozygosity.
Genetic combinations can be maintained generation after generation.

sections.heading: Problems
items: Disease accumulation is a major concern in vegetatively propagated crops.
Sexual recombination may be difficult because flowering or seed set is poor.
Severe inbreeding depression can limit selfing.
Polyploidy and sterility complicate genetic analysis.
Long generation time is a problem in perennial crops.

topics.title: Breeding records and data collection
topics.definition: Accurate records allow breeders to identify, compare, trace and evaluate large numbers of breeding materials.

sections.heading: Need for records
items: Variety development requires evaluation across environments and locations.
Breeders may handle thousands of strains each year.
Complete and accurate records support identification and decision-making.

sections.heading: Major records
items: Accession records.
Project book.
Sowing or planting plan.
Planting list.
Record book of crosses.
Field book.

sections.heading: Maintenance registers
items: Accession register.
Germplasm bank records.
Descriptive blank register.
Crossing programme records.
Single-plant selection register.
Row test and replicated-row test records.
Preliminary and initial evaluation trial records.
Comparative yield and yield evaluation trial records.
Multi-location trial records.
Quality observation notebook.
Segregating-generation notebook.

topics.title: Accession register
topics.definition: An accession register tracks the identity, source, receipt and evaluation history of germplasm or planting material.

sections.heading: Contents
items: Record receipt date.
Record source and accession number.
Assign the number at the receiving unit.
Maintain a short description of planting material.
Record destination for evaluation.
Record evaluation feedback.

sections.heading: Numbering
items: The source describes accession numbers as serial number plus year of entry.
EC denotes exotic collection.
IC denotes indigenous collection.

topics.title: Cross and selection designation
topics.definition: Designation systems provide unique identifiers for crosses, selections and introductions.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Identify breeding material through generations.
Connect a selected line to its original cross or introduction.
Prevent loss of ancestry information during large breeding programmes.

sections.heading: Source convention
items: The source describes codes containing programme or material identifiers and year information.
Selection, cross and introduction series numbers are used to trace material.
Correct designation is essential for pedigree and trial records.

topics.title: Wide or distant hybridization
topics.definition: Wide hybridization crosses individuals from different species or genera to transfer useful variation across reproductive boundaries.

sections.heading: Definitions and history
items: Interspecific hybridization crosses different species within the same genus.
Example: Oryza sativa × O. perennis.
Intergeneric hybridization crosses species belonging to different genera.
Example: wheat × rye.
Wide or distant hybridization includes interspecific and intergeneric crosses.
Thomas Fairchild produced the first cited distant hybrid in 1717: carnation × sweet william.
Raphanobrassica was an amphidiploid radish × cabbage hybrid.
Triticale is cited as an intergeneric hybrid with major potential.

sections.heading: Objectives
items: Transfer disease-resistance genes from wild relatives.
Transfer insect resistance.
Transfer drought resistance and cold tolerance.
Improve quality, such as cotton fibre or tobacco leaf traits.
Improve yield in oats, tobacco, maize and sugarcane.
Transfer CMS, earliness, dwarfness or useful morphological characters.

topics.title: Barriers to wide hybridization and their overcoming
topics.definition: Wide crosses are limited by pre-fertilization, post-fertilization and chromosome-related barriers.

sections.heading: Barriers
items: Poor pollen germination or pollen-stigma incompatibility can prevent fertilization.
Pollen-tube growth may be inhibited in the style.
Embryo development may fail after fertilization.
Hybrid sterility can result from chromosome imbalance or poor chromosome pairing.
Genetic incompatibility may prevent normal hybrid development.

sections.heading: Breeding approaches
items: Use appropriate parents and reciprocal crosses.
Manipulate pollination timing.
Use embryo rescue when hybrid embryos abort.
Double chromosome number where fertility requires chromosome pairing.
Backcross useful hybrids to a cultivated parent to recover agronomic background.
Repeated selection can stabilize useful introgressed characters.

topics.title: Applications of wide hybridization
topics.definition: Wide hybridization broadens the genetic base by moving useful genes from related species or genera into crops.

sections.heading: Applications
items: Disease and insect resistance from wild relatives.
Abiotic stress tolerance such as drought and cold tolerance.
Quality improvement in fibre and leaf products.
Yield improvement.
Transfer of male sterility, earliness and dwarfness.
Creation of new amphidiploids or crop types.

topics.title: Mutation breeding
topics.definition: Mutation breeding uses induced heritable variation to obtain useful changes not readily available through existing variation.

sections.heading: Concept and history
items: Hugo de Vries coined the term mutation in 1900.
Mutation means a sudden heritable change other than ordinary Mendelian segregation and recombination.
1927 marked discovery of X-ray mutagenesis by Muller in Drosophila.
Stadler demonstrated X-ray mutagenesis in barley in 1929.
Auerbach and Robson demonstrated chemical mutagenesis using nitrogen mustard.
After 1953, molecular understanding of DNA expanded mutation studies.

sections.heading: Types by genetic basis
items: Gene mutations alter DNA base sequence.
Changes may involve base substitution, deletion or addition.
Chromosomal mutations alter chromosome structure or number.
Structural changes include deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation.
Numerical changes include polyploidy and aneuploidy.
Cytoplasmic or plasmagene mutations affect genetic material in cytoplasmic organelles.

topics.title: Mutagens and mutation induction
topics.definition: Mutagens are physical or chemical agents used to increase mutation frequency.

sections.heading: Physical mutagens
items: X-rays.
Gamma rays.
Other ionizing radiation may be used according to the material and objective.

sections.heading: Chemical mutagens
items: Nitrogen mustard is cited as an early chemical mutagen.
Chemical mutagens alter DNA or chromosome behavior and can create heritable variation.

sections.heading: Treatment material
items: Seeds, buds, pollen, cuttings and other plant materials can be treated.
Treatment dose must balance mutation frequency with survival and fertility.
The source describes irradiation procedures followed by generation-wise selection.

topics.title: Selection after mutation induction
topics.definition: Mutation breeding requires screening and selection across generations because most induced changes are not immediately fixed or useful.

sections.heading: Generation handling
items: Treated material is advanced to produce segregating mutant generations.
M1 plants are generally treated material and mutation expression is evaluated in later generations.
M2 is important for detecting recessive mutations.
Subsequent generations are used to confirm stability and performance.
Promising mutants are evaluated in replicated trials.

sections.heading: Selection
items: Select for the desired phenotype.
Confirm that the character is heritable and stable.
Compare mutant lines with the parent variety.
Test yield, quality, resistance and adaptation before release.

topics.title: Polyploidy breeding
topics.definition: Polyploid breeding changes chromosome number to create new variation, restore fertility or modify plant size and other traits.

sections.heading: Autopolyploidy
items: Autopolyploidy increases chromosome sets from the same species.
Colchicine is used to induce chromosome doubling.
Polyploids may show larger cells and organs.
Limitations include reduced fertility, meiotic irregularity and difficulty in fixation of desirable types.

sections.heading: Allopolyploidy
items: Allopolyploidy combines chromosome sets from different species.
Chromosome doubling can restore pairing and fertility in a sterile interspecific hybrid.
It can stabilize wide-hybrid combinations.
Limitations include complex inheritance and fertility problems.

topics.title: Breeding for abiotic stress resistance
topics.definition: Abiotic-stress breeding develops crop varieties that tolerate environmental stresses such as temperature, water and salinity.

sections.heading: Temperature stress
items: Cold tolerance is important in rice-growing areas such as Gudalur and Cumbum valley.
Artificial low-temperature and freeze tests are available, but single-plant selection is difficult.
Field testing of segregating lines is considered suitable but can be time-consuming.
High temperature can reduce seed set.
High temperature may break male sterility in male-sterile lines.
Leaf-disc heat tests and desiccation tolerance tests are used.

sections.heading: Water stress
items: About 75% of cultivated area is described as rainfed in the source.
Drought escape means completing the life cycle before severe water deficit.
Drought tolerance can occur with high tissue water potential.
Drought tolerance can also occur with low tissue water potential.
Physiological traits include stomatal aperture, photosynthetic rate and root characteristics.
Proline accumulation in leaves can be used as a drought-screening indicator.
Excess-water tolerance is important in tail-end Cauvery delta areas.
Deep-water paddy with long stems is suited to excess water.

sections.heading: Chemical stress
items: Salinity and alkalinity can be screened using in-vitro techniques.
Rice seedlings may be raised in test tubes containing different salt concentrations.
Similar screening principles can be used for pesticide or herbicide tolerance.

sections.heading: Difficulties
items: Screening requires high skill.
Screening is time-consuming.
Artificial stress conditions can be expensive.
Field conditions may not provide the required stress intensity uniformly.

topics.title: Genetic markers: concept and classes
topics.definition: Genetic markers are heritable biological features associated with loci that can track individuals, chromosomes or genes.

sections.heading: Concept
items: Markers can act as genetic tags near genes controlling traits.
Markers occupy defined genomic positions called loci.
Marker quality is commonly assessed by heterozygosity in the population of interest.
Important properties include abundance, polymorphism, locus specificity and reproducibility.
No single marker is best for every application.

sections.heading: Classes
items: Classical markers include morphological, cytological and biochemical markers.
DNA markers include RFLP, AFLP, RAPD, SSR and SNP systems.
Markers support genetic mapping, germplasm characterization, marker-assisted introgression and variety protection.

sections.heading: History
items: Alfred Sturtevant produced an early genetic map in Drosophila using morphological factors.
Genetic markers progressed from morphological markers to isozyme markers and then DNA markers.

topics.title: Classical morphological and cytological markers
topics.definition: Classical markers use visible traits or chromosome features to identify inherited variation.

sections.heading: Morphological markers
items: Examples include leaf shape, flower colour, pubescence, pod colour, seed shape and fruit shape.
They are easy to observe and inexpensive.
They can be used as indirect selection criteria when linked to target traits.
They are limited in number.
They may be strongly influenced by environment.
Some appear only late in plant development.
The source cites semi-dwarfism selection in rice and wheat as an example.

sections.heading: Cytological markers
items: Cytological markers identify chromosome structure and banding patterns.
Q bands use quinacrine hydrochloride.
G bands use Giemsa stain.
R bands are reversed G bands.
They help classify chromosomes and identify chromosome changes.
They support physical mapping and linkage-group identification.

topics.title: DNA markers and ideal marker characteristics
topics.definition: DNA markers detect heritable DNA-sequence differences and provide genotype-level information largely independent of phenotype.

sections.heading: Characteristics of an ideal marker
items: High polymorphism.
High reproducibility.
Clear inheritance.
Genome-wide or suitable genomic distribution.
High locus specificity.
Easy and reliable assay.
Low cost and high throughput where possible.

sections.heading: Applications
items: Genetic diversity analysis.
Linkage mapping.
Gene tagging.
Germplasm characterization.
Marker-assisted introgression.
Marker-assisted selection.
Variety identification and protection.
Selection of favorable recurrent-parent genome in breeding programmes.

topics.title: Major DNA marker systems
topics.definition: DNA marker systems differ in how polymorphism is detected and in dominance, reproducibility, cost and throughput.

sections.heading: RFLP
items: RFLP detects DNA polymorphism using restriction-fragment differences.
It is based on restriction digestion and hybridization.
It is generally reproducible and codominant but technically demanding.

sections.heading: RAPD
items: RAPD uses short random primers for PCR amplification.
The source states that about 5–50 ng template DNA may be sufficient.
Advantages include speed, simplicity and no requirement for prior sequence information.
Main limitations are low reproducibility and dominant inheritance.
RAPD cannot reliably distinguish homozygous from heterozygous bands.

sections.heading: AFLP
items: AFLP combines restriction digestion with selective PCR amplification.
Main steps are restriction, adapter ligation, preselective amplification, selective amplification and gel analysis.
The source gives typical AFLP fragments of about 80–500 bp.
Advantages include high genomic abundance and many polymorphic bands per reaction.
Limitations include dominant scoring and technical demands.

sections.heading: SSR and SNP
items: SSR markers are based on variation in repeat number at microsatellite loci.
SSRs are highly useful because of polymorphism and locus specificity.
SNP markers detect single-nucleotide differences.
SNPs can support high-throughput genotyping and genomic applications.

topics.title: Marker-assisted selection (MAS)
topics.definition: MAS integrates DNA-marker detection with conventional breeding to select plants carrying desired alleles.

sections.heading: Procedure
items: Select parents in which at least one parent carries the marker allele for the desired trait.
Grow F1 and use markers to confirm hybrids or remove false hybrids.
Screen F2 individuals and retain plants carrying desired marker alleles.
Screen F2:3 rows and select plants with required marker alleles plus desirable phenotypes.
Continue marker screening in F4 and F5.
Bulk best lines around F4:5 or F5:6 using marker and phenotypic information.
Conduct yield, quality, resistance and other performance trials.

sections.heading: Important considerations
items: Phenotypic selection remains useful when the trait can be evaluated reliably.
A marker does not guarantee expression of the target trait.
Marker–QTL association may vary across environments.
Genetic background can affect QTL expression.
QTL × environment, QTL × QTL and QTL × genetic-background interactions should be considered.

sections.heading: When MAS is especially useful
items: Target traits expressed late in plant development.
Recessive target genes.
Traits requiring special or difficult screening conditions.
Traits with strong environmental variability.
Pyramiding several unlinked genes for durable disease or insect resistance.

topics.title: Intellectual property and major forms of protection
topics.definition: Intellectual property protects creations of the mind and can provide recognition or economic rights under law.

sections.heading: Forms
items: IP is intangible and must be expressed in a discernible form to be protectable.
Examples include patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, geographical indications and plant varieties.
Copyright protects literary and artistic works and related rights.
Industrial property includes distinctive signs and technology-related rights.

sections.heading: Distinctive signs
items: Trademarks distinguish goods or services of one enterprise from another.
Geographical indications identify goods associated with a specific geographical origin and its characteristics.

sections.heading: Technology-related protection
items: Patents protect inventions.
Industrial designs protect ornamental or aesthetic aspects of articles.
Trade secrets protect confidential information with commercial value.

topics.title: Patent criteria and plant-variety registration criteria
topics.definition: A patent gives an exclusive right for an invention for a limited period when statutory criteria are satisfied.

sections.heading: Patent criteria
items: Novelty means the invention is not known in prior art.
Non-obviousness means the invention involves an inventive step.
Usefulness means it has industrial application.

sections.heading: Plant variety criteria
items: For PPV&FR registration, varieties must satisfy distinctiveness, uniformity and stability (DUS) criteria.
Distinctiveness means the variety differs from previously known varieties.
Uniformity means essential traits are sufficiently consistent among plants.
Stability means essential characteristics remain after reproduction.

sections.heading: Purpose
items: Patent protection is intended to stimulate innovation and research investment.
Publication of patent information provides technical information while granting limited exclusive rights.

topics.title: Plant variety protection in India
topics.definition: India adopted a sui generis plant-variety protection system through the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001.

sections.heading: Legal framework
items: TRIPS requires WTO members to protect plant varieties through patents or an effective sui generis system under Article 27.3(b).
India adopted a sui generis approach.
The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act came into force in 2001.
The source states that the Act covers almost all plants except microorganisms.

sections.heading: Breeders and researchers
items: Registered breeders receive exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the variety under Section 28(1).
The breeder's rights can pass to a successor, agent or licensee.
Researchers may use protected varieties for research under Section 30.
A protected variety can serve as an initial source for developing other varieties.
Authorization is required when repeated use as a parental line is necessary for commercial production of the new variety.

sections.heading: Protection duration
items: Trees and vines: 18 years from registration in the source table.
Other crops: 15 years from registration.
Extant notified varieties: 15 years from notification under the Seeds Act, 1966.

topics.title: Farmers' rights under plant-variety protection
topics.definition: The source describes farmer-oriented rights intended to recognize conservation, use and contribution of agricultural genetic resources.

sections.heading: Rights listed in the source
items: Farmers may save, use, reuse, exchange and sell farm produce including seed of registered varieties, subject to the Act's provisions.
Farmers can claim compensation if a registered variety fails to perform as represented at registration.
Farmers are exempted from certain registration and proceeding fees described in the source.
A farmer group or community can register a variety evolved, cultivated and conserved by them.
Farmers may seek benefit sharing when their genetic material contributes to a new registered variety.
Compulsory licensing may be sought when a registered variety is unavailable to farmers at a reasonable price.
The source describes protection from innocent infringement where lack of awareness is established.
Farmers and communities may receive recognition or rewards when conserved material contributes genes to registered varieties.

topics.title: Participatory plant breeding
topics.definition: Participatory plant breeding is breeding carried out collaboratively by breeders, farmers and other stakeholders.

sections.heading: Definition and goals
items: PPB involves collaboration among breeders, farmers, marketers, processors, consumers and policy makers.
The approach is especially emphasized for developing-world farming systems with complex and risk-prone conditions.
Goals include increasing production and profitability.
PPB can target the needs of specific user groups or broader user groups.
It builds farmer skills in selection and seed production.

sections.heading: Participation
items: Breeders can direct research toward the needs of specific farmer groups.
Farmers can help breeders assess trade-offs among traits.
On-farm research evaluates varieties under real farming conditions.
Research can be managed by researchers, farmers or both.
Participatory approaches can improve adoption of innovations.

sections.heading: Activities
items: Identify breeding objectives.
Generate genetic variability and provide plants for breeding.
Select within variable populations.
Evaluate experimental varieties through participatory variety selection.
Support variety release.
Popularize new varieties and management information.
Produce seed.

title: Introductory Agrometeorology and Climate Change
description: 45 topics covering Agricultural Meteorology, Weather and Climate, Weather Variables and Elements and more.

topics.title: Agricultural Meteorology
topics.definition: Applied meteorology dealing with crop and animal responses to the physical environment.

sections.heading: Meaning
items: Studies physical atmospheric processes producing weather in relation to agricultural production.
Includes meteorological, climatological and hydrological conditions significant to agriculture.
Focuses on interactions between environmental conditions and agricultural production.

sections.heading: Scope
items: Study climatic resources for effective production.
Quantify favourable weather normals for farm operations.
Develop crop/animal-weather relationships for productivity estimation.
Study weather–crop–pest and disease relationships.
Modify microclimate to increase agricultural productivity.
Delineate agro-ecological zones for efficient resource use and technology transfer.
Prepare crop-weather diagrams and crop-weather calendars.
Develop crop/animal growth simulation models.
Determine and monitor drought for drought management.
Provide value-added weather-based agro-advisories in real time.

topics.title: Weather and Climate
topics.definition: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate describes longer-term average atmospheric conditions.

sections.heading: Weather
items: State of the atmosphere at a specific place and time.
Includes temperature, moisture, wind velocity and barometric pressure.
Usually concerns day-to-day changes over minutes to weeks.

sections.heading: Climate
items: Weather averaged over a long period and large area.
The source uses a 30-year period for climate normals.
Climate system components: atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, land surface and biosphere.

sections.heading: Comparison
items: Weather is studied in meteorology.
Climate is studied in climatology.
Weather uses real-time atmospheric measurements.
Climate uses aggregated weather statistics over long periods.

topics.title: Weather Variables and Elements
topics.definition: The major weather elements used to describe weather and climate are temperature, pressure, wind, humidity and rain.

sections.heading: Major elements
items: Temperature indicates how hot or cold the atmosphere is.
Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere.
Precipitation results from condensation processes and includes rain, snow, hail, sleet, drizzle, fog and mist.
Atmospheric pressure is the weight of air resting on the Earth's surface.
Wind is movement of air masses, especially near the Earth's surface.

sections.heading: Agricultural relevance
items: These elements provide the basis for weather forecasting.
Long-term analysis of the same elements supports climatology.

topics.title: Earth's Atmosphere: Composition
topics.definition: The atmosphere is a thick gaseous envelope surrounding Earth and held by gravitational force.

sections.heading: Gas composition
items: Nitrogen: 78.08% by volume.
Oxygen: 20.95%.
Argon: 0.93%.
Water vapour: 0–4% in the table.
Carbon dioxide: 0.0360% in the table.
Other trace gases include neon, helium, methane, hydrogen, nitrous oxide and ozone.
Nitrogen and oxygen together form about 99% of dry atmospheric volume.

sections.heading: Water vapour
items: Atmospheric vapour may range from zero to about 5% by volume in the text.
More than 90% of total atmospheric vapour occurs up to 5 km.
Water vapour absorbs terrestrial radiation and contributes to atmospheric heating.

sections.heading: Particulate matter
items: Includes dust, salt particles, pollen, smoke and volcanic ash.
Particles remain suspended in the atmosphere.
Selective scattering contributes to blue sky appearance.
Salt particles can act as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud and precipitation formation.

sections.heading: Ozone
items: Ozone is concentrated mainly around 15–55 km in the source discussion.
It absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
The source attributes severe ozone thinning primarily to chlorofluorocarbon emissions.

topics.title: Structure of Earth's Atmosphere
topics.definition: The atmosphere is divided into layers with characteristic temperature and physical properties.

sections.heading: Troposphere
items: Lowest atmospheric layer.
Average height about 12 km in one source description; 9 km at poles and 17 km at equator.
Contains roughly 75–80% of atmospheric mass.
Nearly all water vapour and dust occur here.
Most weather phenomena occur here.
Temperature normally decreases upward at about 6.5°C per km.
Upper boundary is the tropopause.

sections.heading: Stratosphere
items: Extends from roughly 12 km to 50–55 km.
Contains the ozone layer.
Temperature increases with altitude because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
Atmosphere is stable with little weather-producing turbulence.
Upper boundary is the stratopause.

sections.heading: Mesosphere
items: Extends approximately from 50 km to 80–85 km.
Temperature decreases upward.
Most meteors burn up in this layer.
Mesopause is near 80–85 km and is the coldest atmospheric region in the source discussion.

sections.heading: Thermosphere and exosphere
items: Thermosphere begins near 80 km and temperature increases strongly with height.
Lower thermosphere contains the ionosphere.
Auroral phenomena occur in the thermosphere.
Exosphere is the outermost layer and merges into the solar wind.
Exosphere contains very low-density hydrogen and helium and many satellites.

topics.title: Agrometeorological Applications
topics.definition: Applications of atmospheric information for crop planning, productivity prediction and risk management.

sections.heading: Applications
items: Crop-weather calendars support timely farm operations.
Weather-crop relationships support productivity estimation.
Weather information helps manage drought.
Agro-ecological zoning supports resource-efficient production.
Growth simulation models can predict productivity and potential yield.
Weather-based advisories can reduce input costs and improve productivity.

topics.title: Atmospheric Pressure
topics.definition: Pressure exerted by the weight of air in the atmosphere.

sections.heading: Definition and variation
items: Low-pressure areas have less atmospheric mass above them.
High-pressure areas have more atmospheric mass above them.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing elevation.
A one-square-centimetre column of air from sea level to the top of the atmosphere has a mass of about 1.03 kg.
Mean sea-level pressure is about 101.325 kPa = 1013.25 hPa = 1013.25 mbar.
Equivalent mean sea-level pressure is about 29.92 inHg or 760 mmHg.

sections.heading: Pressure and altitude
items: Increasing elevation reduces the mass of overlying air.
Mean sea-level pressure is the adjusted pressure commonly reported in weather reports.

topics.title: Wind and Forces Affecting Wind
topics.definition: Wind is air in motion caused primarily by spatial differences in atmospheric pressure.

sections.heading: Forces
items: Pressure-gradient force controls wind speed.
Pressure gradient is the rate of pressure change over space.
Coriolis force deflects medium- and large-scale air movement due to Earth's rotation.
Coriolis force depends on latitude and wind speed.
Centripetal force acts when wind follows curved paths around pressure centres.
Friction affects wind near the Earth's surface.

topics.title: Types of Wind
topics.definition: Winds are classified according to their scale, persistence and periodic behaviour.

sections.heading: Planetary winds
items: Blow throughout the year between latitude belts in response to pressure differences.
Major prevailing winds include trade winds and westerlies.

sections.heading: Trade winds
items: Blow from subtropical high-pressure belts near 30° toward the equatorial low-pressure belt.
Deflected right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Known as tropical easterlies.
Generally steady in direction and force.

sections.heading: Westerlies
items: Blow from subtropical high-pressure belts toward subpolar low-pressure belts.
Southern Hemisphere westerlies are described as stronger and more constant.
40°–65°S latitudes are associated with Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties.

sections.heading: Periodic winds
items: Direction changes periodically with seasons or daily heating differences.
Examples: monsoons, land/sea breezes, mountain/valley breezes.

sections.heading: Local winds
items: Produced by local temperature and pressure differences.
Types listed: hot, cold, convectional and slope winds.

topics.title: Land and Sea Breezes
topics.definition: Local coastal winds produced by differential heating and cooling of land and water.

sections.heading: Land breeze
items: Occurs mainly at night.
Land cools faster than the sea.
Air flows from relatively higher-pressure land toward lower-pressure water.
Usually weaker than the daytime sea breeze.
Dies as land warms the next morning.

sections.heading: Sea breeze
items: Develops after sunrise as land heats faster than water.
Warm air over land expands and lowers surface pressure.
Air moves from relatively higher-pressure sea toward lower-pressure land.
Strength increases with the land–sea temperature difference.
A strong offshore wind above about 15 km/h can prevent development.

topics.title: Mountain and Valley Breezes
topics.definition: Diurnal mountain winds caused by differential heating and cooling of mountain slopes and valleys.

sections.heading: Valley breeze
items: Occurs during the day.
Heated mountain slopes cause air to move upward from valleys.

sections.heading: Mountain breeze
items: Occurs after sunset.
Cold dense air moves downslope from mountains toward valleys.

topics.title: Cyclones and Anticyclones
topics.definition: Cyclones are low-pressure systems with inward rising flow; anticyclones are high-pressure systems with outward surface flow and subsidence.

sections.heading: Cyclone
items: Large-scale air mass rotating around a strong low-pressure centre.
Northern Hemisphere rotation is counter-clockwise.
Southern Hemisphere rotation is clockwise.
Surface air converges inward and rises near the centre.
Rising air expands and cools, increasing humidity and cloudiness.
Cyclones are generally associated with rain, clouds and unsettled weather.

sections.heading: Tropical cyclone
items: Warm-core system driven by significant convective activity and latent heat release.

Six source-listed requirements: warm sea surface, atmospheric instability, lower/middle tropospheric humidity, sufficient Coriolis force, pre-existing low-level disturbance, and low vertical wind shear.
Called hurricane in the Atlantic/northeastern Pacific.
Called cyclone in the Indian and South Pacific oceans.
Called typhoon in the northwestern Pacific.

sections.heading: Extratropical cyclone
items: Also called mid-latitude or wave cyclone.
Large-scale low-pressure system generally occurring in middle latitudes.
Often develops along strong temperature/dew-point gradients and fronts.
Associated with significant vertical wind shear and jet-stream dynamics.
Usually occurs between about 30° and 60° latitude.
Can produce cloudiness, showers, gales and thunderstorms.
Often develops through frontal waves and later occludes.

sections.heading: Anticyclone
items: High-pressure system.
Northern Hemisphere winds rotate clockwise.
Southern Hemisphere winds rotate counter-clockwise.
Air descends and warms by compression.
Subsidence reduces humidity and cloud formation.
Generally associated with clear skies and light surface winds.

topics.title: Solar Radiation
topics.definition: Radiant energy emitted by the Sun and the prime external energy source for Earth's biosphere.

sections.heading: Sun and energy
items: Solar radiation is the flux of radiant energy from the Sun.
Sun diameter: about 1.39 × 10^6 km.
Mean Sun–Earth distance: about 1.5 × 10^8 km.
Source gives solar surface temperature around 5462 K in one description.
Energy is produced by fusion in which hydrogen is transformed to helium.
The source states about 99% of biosphere energy comes from the Sun.

sections.heading: Insolation
items: Electromagnetic energy radiated into space by the Sun.
Factors affecting insolation: solar constant, atmospheric transparency, duration of daily sunlight and noon solar angle.

topics.title: Heat Transfer Processes
topics.definition: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.

sections.heading: Conduction
items: Heat transfer through matter without bulk movement of the substance.
Heat flows from warmer to cooler parts.
Example: heating along an iron rod.

sections.heading: Convection
items: Heat transfer through actual movement of molecules or fluid masses.
Predominant in many atmospheric weather processes.
Example: boiling water.

sections.heading: Radiation
items: Energy transfer by electromagnetic waves without a material medium.
Solar energy reaches Earth by radiation.
Radiation produces heat when absorbed by a surface.

topics.title: Solar Spectrum and Wavelength Bands
topics.definition: Solar radiation spans a broad electromagnetic spectrum with different wavelengths and biological effects.

sections.heading: Major bands
items: Ultraviolet: about 0.20–0.39 μm.
Visible radiation: about 0.39–0.76 μm.
Infrared: greater than 0.76 μm in the source table.
Visible colours progress from violet through indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red.

sections.heading: Plant significance
items: Visible light is essential for photosynthesis.
Infrared provides thermal energy.
Shorter-than-visible radiation is chemically active and potentially damaging.
Ultraviolet radiation is strongly absorbed by atmospheric ozone.

sections.heading: Wavelength units
items: 1 millimicron = 10^-9 m = 10^-7 cm.

topics.title: Solar Radiation and Crop Plants
topics.definition: Crop production depends on the intensity, quality and duration of solar radiation.

sections.heading: Spectral effects
items: Radiation below visible wavelengths can be detrimental at high exposure.
Infrared has a thermal effect and supplies thermal energy to the plant environment.
Visible light is indispensable to photosynthesis.
Light affects tillering, culm stability, culm length, yield, plant biomass, leaf size and root development.

sections.heading: Critical stages
items: Maize: radiation intensity during the third month is highlighted.
Rice: about 25 days before flowering.
Barley: flowering period.

sections.heading: Specific spectral bands
items: 700–900 nm far-red region influences photoperiodism, germination, flowering and fruit coloration.
720–510 nm is strongly absorbed by chlorophyll and has strong photosynthetic activity.
510–400 nm includes strong chlorophyll/yellow pigment absorption and strong blue-violet photosynthetic effects.
400–315 nm can produce formative and dwarfing effects.
Below 280 nm has lethal/germicidal effects in the source.

topics.title: Radiation Balance, Albedo and Earth Energy Budget
topics.definition: Radiation balance is the difference between incoming and outgoing radiation; albedo is the percentage of incident radiation reflected by a surface.

sections.heading: Radiation properties
items: Absorptivity = absorbed radiant energy / incident radiant energy.
Reflectivity = reflected radiant energy / incident radiant energy.
Albedo is reflectivity expressed as a percentage.
Transmittivity = transmitted radiation / incident radiation.
Emissivity = radiation emitted by a surface / radiation emitted by a blackbody under comparable conditions.
A blackbody completely absorbs incident radiation and has absorptivity and emissivity of unity.

sections.heading: Earth energy budget
items: The atmosphere filters, absorbs, scatters and reflects solar radiation.
Source example: 324 W m^-2 reaching Earth in the upper-atmosphere budget discussion.
236 W m^-2 are re-emitted to space as infrared radiation in the cited budget.
86 W m^-2 are reflected by clouds.
20 W m^-2 are reflected by the ground as short-wave radiation.
Atmospheric absorption and re-radiation contribute to the greenhouse effect.

sections.heading: Albedo values
items: Pure water: 5–20%.
Vegetation: 10–40%.
Clouds: about 55%.
High albedo means more incident solar radiation is reflected.
Albedo depends on incidence angle, surface properties, season and time of day.
Crop-community albedo depends on crop age, ground cover, foliage colour and reflectivity.

topics.title: Outgoing Long-Wave Radiation
topics.definition: Long-wave radiation emitted by the heated Earth and modified by atmospheric absorbers.

sections.heading: Characteristics
items: Average Earth surface temperature is given as about 285 K in the source.
About 99% of emitted terrestrial radiation is in the infrared range of 4–120 μm.
About 90% of outgoing radiation is absorbed by the atmosphere in the source discussion.
Water vapour absorbs in approximately 5.3–7.7 μm and beyond 20 μm.
Ozone absorbs around 9.4–9.8 μm.
CO2 absorbs around 13.1–16.9 μm.
Clouds absorb across broad wavelengths.

sections.heading: Atmospheric window
items: Long-wave radiation escapes relatively freely between about 8.5 and 11 μm.
This region is called the atmospheric window.
The source notes its use in microwave remote sensing and its role in limiting excessive night cooling through counter-radiation.

topics.title: Radiation Laws
topics.definition: Physical relationships connecting wavelength, frequency, energy, emission and temperature.

sections.heading: Wave relation
items: λ = c/ν.
λ = wavelength.
c = velocity of light ≈ 3 × 10^10 cm s^-1.
ν = frequency.

sections.heading: Planck's law
items: E = hν.
h = Planck's constant ≈ 6.62 × 10^-34 J s.
Higher frequency means higher quantum energy.
Shorter wavelength corresponds to higher frequency and energy.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's law
items: a(λ) = e(λ).
A good absorber is a good emitter under similar conditions.

sections.heading: Stefan–Boltzmann law
items: E = σT^4.
T is absolute temperature in kelvin.
σ ≈ 5.673 × 10^-8 W m^-2 K^-4 for the blackbody constant given.

sections.heading: Wien's displacement law
items: λmax = 2897/T μm.
Higher temperature shifts maximum emission toward shorter wavelengths.
For Sun temperature around 5793 K, λmax is about 0.5 μm.
For Earth surface near 287 K, λmax is about 10 μm.

topics.title: Air Temperature and Temperature Factors
topics.definition: Air temperature describes the molecular kinetic state of air and strongly controls atmospheric and crop processes.

sections.heading: Definition and heat transfer
items: Temperature is described as a measure of molecular motion.
Heat is energy associated with molecular motion and transfer due to temperature differences.
Conduction, convection and radiation transfer heat.

sections.heading: Factors affecting air temperature
items: Latitude.
Altitude.
Distribution of land and water.
Ocean currents.
Prevailing winds.
Cloudiness.
Mountain barriers.
Nature of surface and relief.
Convection and turbulence.

sections.heading: Examples
items: Northern India source example: January is the coldest month and June the warmest.
Southern India source example: December is the coldest month and May the warmest.
Land shows larger temperature variations than water.
Ocean currents redistribute heat and create temperature contrasts.

topics.title: Diurnal and Seasonal Temperature Variation
topics.definition: Air temperature changes systematically within a day and across seasons.

sections.heading: Diurnal variation
items: Minimum air temperature generally occurs near sunrise.
Temperature rises after sunrise and reaches a maximum around 13:00–14:00 h.
Temperature then declines toward sunrise.
Difference between daily maximum and minimum is the diurnal range.
Clear days have larger diurnal ranges.
Cloudy conditions reduce daily temperature amplitude.
Daily mean temperature = (daily maximum + daily minimum) / 2.

sections.heading: Seasonal variation
items: Northern Hemisphere winter minimum is stated as January.
Northern Hemisphere summer maximum is stated as July.

sections.heading: Horizontal distribution
items: Isotherms join places with equal temperature.
Temperature generally decreases from equator toward poles.
Land-water distribution modifies latitudinal temperature patterns.
Mountain barriers and local topography alter horizontal temperature distribution.

topics.title: Vertical Temperature Distribution
topics.definition: Atmospheric layers can be distinguished by how temperature changes with altitude.

sections.heading: Troposphere
items: Average height about 14 km in this chapter; about 16 km at equator and 7–8 km at poles.
Seat of weather phenomena.
Temperature decreases upward at about 6.5°C/km.
Contains most atmospheric moisture and aerosols.

sections.heading: Stratosphere
items: Extends roughly from 20 km to 50–55 km in the source chapter.
Called a seat of photochemical reactions.
Temperature increases with height.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and warms the upper stratosphere.
Upper boundary is the stratopause.

sections.heading: Mesosphere and ozonosphere
items: Ozone concentration is highlighted between about 30 and 60 km.
Ozone absorbs UV radiation.
Mesosphere lies approximately 50–80 km.
Mesospheric temperature decreases with height.
Mesopause temperature may reach nearly −95°C in the source.

sections.heading: Thermosphere and exosphere
items: Thermosphere/ionosphere extends from about 80 km to 400 km in the chapter.
Temperature rises again and may reach about 1000°C.
Ionosphere reflects radio waves and supports long-distance radio communication.
Exosphere is the outermost layer, roughly 400–1000 km in this chapter.
Hydrogen and helium predominate in the exosphere.

topics.title: Lapse Rate and Adiabatic Processes
topics.definition: Lapse rate is temperature change with height; adiabatic temperature change occurs without external heat exchange.

sections.heading: Lapse rates
items: Average atmospheric lapse rate is about 6.5°C/km.
Dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 10°C/km.
Moist adiabatic lapse rate is usually below 6°C/km.
Moist air cools more slowly because condensation releases latent heat.

sections.heading: Mountain process
items: Moist air forced upward over mountains expands and cools.
Cooling may cause condensation and precipitation.
Descending air becomes warmer and drier after losing moisture.
Descending air warms at the dry adiabatic rate in the source explanation.

sections.heading: Adiabatic change
items: No outside heat is involved.
Rising air expands and cools.
Sinking air compresses and warms.

topics.title: Temperature Inversion
topics.definition: A temperature inversion occurs when temperature increases with altitude over a layer instead of decreasing normally.

sections.heading: Causes
items: Ground air can cool faster than overlying air during clear cooling nights.
A warm layer may pass over a lower cold layer.
Cold air can drain downslope and be replaced by warmer air.

sections.heading: Significance
items: Influences cloud formation and precipitation.
Can cause fog near the ground.
Reduces visibility and can affect air navigation.
Affects diurnal temperature behaviour and conversion of incoming solar radiation to heat.

topics.title: Heat Units and Growing Degree Days
topics.definition: Heat units quantify accumulated warmth above a crop-specific threshold during growth.

sections.heading: GDD concept
items: Heat unit represents departure of mean daily temperature above a minimum threshold.
Base temperatures in the source commonly range from 4.5–12.5°C.
6.0°C is stated as a commonly used value.

sections.heading: Formula
items: GDD = Σ[(Tmax + Tmin)/2 − Tb].
Tmax = daily maximum air temperature.
Tmin = daily minimum air temperature.
Tb = crop base or threshold temperature.

sections.heading: Uses
items: Guide agricultural operations and planting land use.
Forecast crop harvest dates, yield and quality.
Estimate labour requirements.
Support introduction of crops and varieties into new areas.
Predict likelihood of successful crop growth.

topics.title: Heat and Cold Injuries in Crops
topics.definition: Extreme temperatures cause physiological and physical injuries to crop plants.

sections.heading: Heat injury
items: Thermal death point is given as about 50–60°C, varying with species.
Aquatic and shade-loving plants may be killed at around 40°C.
High temperature causes desiccation.
It disrupts photosynthesis and respiration.
High temperature increases respiration and rapidly depletes stored food.

sections.heading: Cold injury
items: Chilling injury affects warm-climate plants exposed to low temperatures.
Sugarcane, sorghum and maize may show chlorotic bands when night temperature falls below 20°C in the source example.
Freezing injury forms ice crystals in plant tissues and dehydrates cells.
Examples include frost damage in potato and tea.
Suffocation can occur under thick ice/snow due to restricted oxygen entry.
Heaving occurs when ice crystals expand soil and mechanically lift plants.

sections.heading: Specific injury
items: Stem griddle is bark/stem injury associated with high daytime and low nighttime temperatures.
Young cotton seedlings in sandy soil may be affected when soil temperature exceeds 60°C.

topics.title: Role of Temperature in Crop Production
topics.definition: Temperature controls crop distribution, development, physiological processes and productivity.

sections.heading: Crop effects
items: Influences crop and vegetation distribution.
Affects leaf production, expansion and flowering.
Changes gas and liquid diffusion rates.
Affects solubility of substances.
Biochemical reaction rates increase strongly with temperature; the source states reactions may double or more per 10°C rise.
Affects enzyme stability and system equilibrium.
Most higher plants grow between about 0–60°C; crop plants are more restricted, around 10–40°C.
Maximum dry matter production is stated around 20–30°C.
High temperature plus high humidity favours some pests and diseases.
High night temperature increases respiration and metabolism.

sections.heading: Cardinal temperatures
items: Crops have minimum, optimum and maximum temperatures.
Wheat and barley: minimum 0–5°C; optimum 25–31°C; maximum 31–37°C.
Sorghum: minimum 15–18°C; optimum 31–36°C; maximum 40–42°C.

sections.heading: Thermoperiodism
items: Response of living organisms to regular temperature changes between day and night or seasons.

topics.title: Soil Temperature
topics.definition: Soil temperature influences seed, root and microbial processes and is controlled by meteorological and soil factors.

sections.heading: Importance
items: Governs uptake of water and nutrients.
Controls soil microbial activity; source optimum range is 18–30°C.
Influences seed germination and root development.
Influences mineralization of organic nitrogen.
Low soil temperature favours greater persistence of organic matter.
Affects mineral weathering and soil reactions.
Influences soil structure and exchangeable ions.

sections.heading: Meteorological factors
items: Solar radiation directly affects soil temperature.
Wind/convection transfers heat to the soil.
Evaporation cools soil.
Condensation and freezing can release heat.
Precipitation may warm or cool soil depending on its temperature.

sections.heading: Soil factors
items: Slope/aspect affect received insolation.
Sandy soils warm faster than clay soils.
Light soils generally show larger temperature ranges.
Tillage and soil mulch modify heat flow and moisture.
Organic matter lowers heat capacity and thermal conductivity while increasing water-holding capacity.
Dark soils absorb more radiation than light soils.
Moisture increases heat capacity and conductivity and cools the surface through evaporation.

sections.heading: Daily and seasonal variation
items: At 5 cm depth, daily change can exceed 10°C.
At 20 cm the daily change is smaller.
At about 80 cm, diurnal changes are practically nil.
Heat penetrates downward with a time lag.
Seasonal variations penetrate deeper than diurnal variations.
Plant canopy reduces seasonal soil-temperature variation.

topics.title: Atmospheric Humidity
topics.definition: Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in air.

sections.heading: Meaning and sources
items: Humidity is a highly variable climatic factor.
Source gives atmospheric water vapour as roughly 0–4% by volume, averaging around 2%.
Measured with a hygrometer.
Water vapour enters the atmosphere through evaporation, plant transpiration and animal respiration.

sections.heading: Importance
items: Supports precipitation formation.
Absorbs incoming and terrestrial radiation and influences Earth's heat budget.
Stores latent energy important in storms and cyclones.
Influences sensible temperature and human cooling.

topics.title: Absolute Humidity
topics.definition: Weight of actual water vapour present per unit volume of air.

sections.heading: Definition
items: Usually expressed as grams of water vapour per cubic metre of air.
Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.
At 10°C, one cubic metre of air can hold about 11.4 g water vapour in the source example.
At 21°C, the same volume can hold about 22.2 g.

sections.heading: Limitation
items: Not a fully reliable index because temperature and pressure change air volume and therefore absolute humidity.

topics.title: Relative Humidity and Saturation
topics.definition: Relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour content to the moisture-holding capacity of air at a given temperature, expressed as a percentage.

sections.heading: Relative humidity
items: Adding moisture by evaporation increases relative humidity.
Cooling air decreases its moisture-holding capacity and increases relative humidity.
Saturated air has relative humidity of 100%.
Air containing half of its moisture-holding capacity has relative humidity of 50%.
Relative humidity strongly influences evaporation.

sections.heading: Dew point
items: Temperature at which a given air sample becomes saturated without changing its moisture content.
Further cooling below the dew point promotes condensation.

topics.title: Specific Humidity and Mixing Ratio
topics.definition: Specific humidity relates water-vapour mass to total moist-air mass; mixing ratio relates water-vapour mass to dry-air mass.

sections.heading: Specific humidity
items: Weight of water vapour per unit weight of air.
Usually expressed in grams per kilogram.
Less affected by changes in pressure or temperature than absolute humidity.

sections.heading: Mixing ratio
items: Mass of water vapour divided by mass of dry air.
Expressed as grams of water vapour per kilogram of dry air.

topics.title: Saturation and Vapour Pressure
topics.definition: Saturation occurs when evaporation and condensation reach dynamic equilibrium at a given temperature.

sections.heading: Saturation
items: Saturation does not mean evaporation stops.
In a closed water system, evaporation initially exceeds condensation.
At equilibrium, evaporation rate equals condensation rate and the air is saturated.
Higher temperature permits more water to remain in the vapour phase.

sections.heading: Vapour pressure
items: Saturation vapour pressure increases with air temperature.
Below 0°C, saturation curves differ over liquid water and ice.
Supercooled liquid water can persist below 0°C in clouds.

sections.heading: Vapour pressure deficit
items: VPD = saturated vapour pressure (SVP) − actual vapour pressure (AVP).
VPD is useful in crop-growth and atmospheric-moisture studies.

topics.title: Condensation
topics.definition: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid or solid form when atmospheric conditions exceed moisture-holding capacity.

sections.heading: Requirements
items: Cooling moist air can reduce moisture-holding capacity below actual vapour content.
Condensation generally begins when air temperature reaches or falls below the dew point.
Relative humidity near 100% means the air is near saturation.
Dust, smoke, pollen and ocean salt can act as hygroscopic condensation nuclei.

sections.heading: Ways condensation can occur
items: Air temperature can fall to the dew point at approximately constant volume.
Air volume can increase without addition of heat.
Combined temperature and volume changes can reduce moisture-holding capacity.
Evaporation can add moisture to the air.

sections.heading: Products
items: Condensation may produce dew, frost, fog, mist and clouds.
Direct vapour-to-solid deposition is described as sublimation in the source.

topics.title: Adiabatic and Non-Adiabatic Cooling
topics.definition: Cooling processes that produce condensation are classified into adiabatic and non-adiabatic changes.

sections.heading: Adiabatic cooling
items: Rising air expands and cools without external heat loss.
Vertical air displacement is a major cause of adiabatic temperature change.
Katabatic flow is cold, dense air moving downslope.

sections.heading: Non-adiabatic cooling
items: Includes cooling by radiation, conduction or mixing with colder air.
Radiational cooling can produce fog or clouds when nuclei are present.
Contact cooling can produce dew, frost or fog.
Effects are mainly confined to a thin atmospheric layer.
Source states non-adiabatic cooling generally produces dew, fog or frost rather than substantial precipitation.

topics.title: Dew, Frost, Fog, Mist, Haze and Smog
topics.definition: These are near-surface atmospheric moisture or particulate phenomena formed under different temperature, humidity and condensation conditions.

sections.heading: Dew
items: Water droplets deposited on cool solid surfaces such as leaves, grass and stones.
Ideal conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, cold and long nights.
Dew point must be above freezing.

sections.heading: White frost
items: Forms on cold surfaces when condensation occurs at or below 0°C.
Moisture deposits as minute ice crystals rather than liquid droplets.
Formation conditions resemble dew except temperature is at or below freezing.

sections.heading: Fog
items: Cloud with base at or very near the ground.
Visibility is less than 1 km in the source.
Radiation fog forms from radiational cooling and is common in winter.
Advection fog forms when warm air moves over a cold surface; it is thick and persistent.
Frontal or precipitation fog forms near converging warm and cold air masses.

sections.heading: Mist
items: Contains more moisture per nucleus than fog in the source description.
Droplets are less coalesced, so mist is less dense and dissipates faster.
Visibility is more than 1 km but less than 2 km.

sections.heading: Haze and smog
items: Haze occurs when dust, smoke and dry particles reduce sky clarity without condensation.
Sources include farming in dry weather, traffic, industry and wildfires.
Smog = smoke + fog.
Source links smog to coal burning, vehicle emissions and industrial fumes.

topics.title: Importance and Variation of Humidity for Crops
topics.definition: Atmospheric humidity interacts with temperature, rainfall and wind to influence crop water relations, pests, diseases and yield.

sections.heading: Crop effects
items: Helps determine which crops can be grown in a region.
Affects internal plant water potential.
Influences transpiration and potential evapotranspiration.
Determines crop water requirement.
High humidity can reduce irrigation requirement by reducing evapotranspiration losses.
High humidity can prolong crop survival under moisture stress.
Very high or very low relative humidity is generally unfavorable for high yields in the source.
High humidity favours some fungi, bacteria and pests.
Examples include potato blight and thrips/jassid damage.
High humidity during grain filling can reduce yield.
Very high relative humidity is described as beneficial to maize, sorghum and sugarcane but harmful to sunflower and tobacco.
Moderate relative humidity above 40% is described as generally safe for most crops.

sections.heading: Variation
items: Absolute humidity is highest near the equator and lowest near the poles.
Absolute humidity is minimum around sunrise and maximum around 14:00–15:00 in the source.
Relative humidity is generally maximum near sunrise and minimum around 14:00–15:00.
The source gives relative humidity around 80% at the equator and around 85% at the poles, with about 70% near horse latitudes.

topics.title: Climatic Normal
topics.definition: A climatic normal is the average value of a weather element over 30 years.

sections.heading: Meaning and use
items: The period may be represented by weekly, monthly or annual averages.
Crop distribution, production and productivity depend on climatic normals.
Crop selection based on optimum climatic requirements can improve production potential.

topics.title: Weather Forecasting
topics.definition: Prediction of weather from the next few hours to seasonal periods.

sections.heading: Importance for agriculture
items: Weather has major social and economic impacts.
The source states weather aberrations alone can explain up to 50% variation in crop production.
Rainfall is especially important for crop production and regional economy.
Forecasts support moisture conservation during weak monsoon conditions.
Forecasts support flood-relief planning during strong monsoon conditions.
Timely pest and disease warnings can reduce recurring crop losses.
Forecasts help plan water use.
Reliable forecasts can support sustainability and reduce damage from adverse weather.

sections.heading: Forecast types
items: Nowcast: next few hours.
Short-range: about 24 hours, with outlook for another 24 hours.
Medium-range: about 3–7/10 days.
Long-range: beyond 7 days up to a season.
Seasonal climate forecast supports farm decisions, especially rainfall-related decisions.

topics.title: Forecast Services, Users and Accuracy
topics.definition: Forecast services differ in lead time, predicted elements, methods and agricultural users.

sections.heading: Service table
items: Nowcasting: IMD; thunderstorms, dust storms, cold/heat waves; lead time 1–2 hours; source accuracy 90–98%.
Short range: IMD; cloud spread, rainfall, temperature and cyclone warnings; lead time about 1 day; source accuracy 80–90%.
Medium range: IMD; rainfall, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed/direction and cloud cover; 3–10 days; source accuracy 70–75%.
Long range: IMD; seasonal rainfall; 30–40 days in the source table; source accuracy about 60%.

sections.heading: Methods
items: Synoptic method uses surface and upper-air observations from multiple locations and prepares charts of atmospheric status.
Statistical methods include multiple regression and ARIMA.
Numerical weather prediction integrates equations representing Coriolis, frictional, pressure-gradient and gravitational forces.
NWP model results depend strongly on accurate initial conditions.

sections.heading: Farmer use
items: Forecasters should understand crops grown in each agroclimatic zone.
Forecast warnings should match crop growth stages.
Farmers need to understand and interpret weather bulletins.

topics.title: Climate Change and Global Warming
topics.definition: Climate change is a significant long-term change in expected regional or global weather patterns; accelerated change is linked in the source to anthropogenic activities and greenhouse gases.

sections.heading: Climate change
items: Can occur over decades, centuries or much longer periods.
The source emphasizes faster recent change associated with industrialization, urbanization, deforestation, agriculture and land-use change.
Scenarios include higher temperature, changed precipitation and higher atmospheric CO2.
The greenhouse effect is described as a natural process that helps maintain a warm Earth surface.

sections.heading: Agricultural pathways
items: Higher CO2 can directly affect crop and weed growth.
CO2-driven climate changes can alter temperature, rainfall and sunshine.
Sea-level rise can inundate farmland and increase salinity of coastal groundwater.
Crop production is weather-dependent, so climate changes can affect productivity.
Elevated CO2 and temperature affect respiration, photosynthesis, growth, reproduction and water use.

sections.heading: GWP values
items: Source gives Global Warming Potential values of CO2 = 1, CH4 = 25 and N2O = 310 for the cited comparison.

topics.title: Climate Variability
topics.definition: Climate variability refers to temporal changes in weather phenomena associated with atmospheric circulation and natural or human-related drivers.

sections.heading: Meaning and impacts
items: Occurs from year to year and across regions.
Recurring drought and desertification threaten land-dependent livelihoods.
Weather-related disasters include droughts, floods, ice storms, dust storms, landslides, lightning-associated storms and forest fires.

sections.heading: External causes
items: Solar output changes.
Earth orbital eccentricity varies from nearly circular to more elliptical.
Precession causes wobble of Earth's axis.
Earth's axial tilt is given as varying between 21.8° and 24.4°.

sections.heading: Internal and anthropogenic causes
items: Changes in atmospheric greenhouse-gas composition.
Land-surface changes including afforestation and deforestation.
Southern Oscillation/El Niño–La Niña dynamics involving western tropical Pacific sea-surface temperature.
Anthropogenic greenhouse gases and aerosols.

topics.title: El Niño, La Niña and Climate Variability
topics.definition: El Niño and La Niña are natural short-term climate fluctuations associated with tropical Pacific Ocean conditions and the Southern Oscillation.

sections.heading: ENSO effects
items: El Niño is associated with tropical Pacific warming.
La Niña is associated with tropical Pacific cooling.
Strong events can produce year-to-year changes in temperature and rainfall in many regions.
The source links strong events with extreme weather such as flooding and drought.
These short-term fluctuations are described as smaller than the long-term 20th-century warming trend.

sections.heading: Related drivers
items: Southern Oscillation Index is described through normalized pressure differences between Tahiti and Darwin.
Natural variability can also arise from volcanic aerosols and changes in Earth's orbit.

topics.title: Effects of Climate Change on Agriculture
topics.definition: Climate change affects crop production through changes in temperature, rainfall, atmospheric CO2 and related biological processes.

sections.heading: Major effects
items: Higher greenhouse-gas concentrations are expected to increase Earth's temperature.
Changes in weather can alter crop production and productivity.
Elevated CO2 and temperature affect photosynthesis, respiration, growth, reproduction and water use.
CO2 effects can differ with latitude and environmental context.

sections.heading: Evidence in model simulations
items: The source describes simulations using only natural factors as showing negligible warming or slight cooling over the 20th century.
Including greenhouse-gas emissions and other human activities produced temperature changes closer to observations in the source discussion.

topics.title: Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation in Agriculture
topics.definition: Agricultural adaptation combines weather services, resilient crops, improved water and nutrient management, and risk-reduction practices.

sections.heading: Adaptation measures
items: Provide value-added weather services to help farmers manage current climate risks.
Shift planting dates when appropriate.
Choose varieties with different growth durations.
Modify crop rotations.
Establish early-warning systems for pest and disease outbreaks.
Use integrated pest management under changing climatic conditions.
Use participatory and formal breeding for heat-, drought- and salinity-tolerant varieties.
Develop short-duration varieties that mature before peak heat.
Select genotypes with higher per-day yield potential to offset heat-related shortening of growth periods.

sections.heading: Drought prevention
items: Use on-farm reservoirs in medium lands.
Grow pulses and oilseeds instead of rice in uplands where suitable.
Use ridge-and-furrow systems in cotton.
Use intercrops instead of pure crops in uplands.
Use land grading and leveling.
Stabilize bunds with stone and grasses.
Use graded line bunds and contour trenches for runoff collection.
Use conservation furrows, mulching and more FYM.

sections.heading: Efficient water and fertilizer use
items: Use frequent but shallow irrigation where appropriate.
Use drip and sprinkler irrigation for high-value crops.
Irrigate at critical crop stages.
Use optimum fertilizer doses and split nitrogen/potassium applications.
Use deep fertilizer placement.
Use neem, karanja and other nitrification inhibitors.
Use lime in acid soils.
Use micronutrients such as zinc where needed.

title: Livestock & Poultry Management
description: 10 topics covering Role of Livestock in National Economy, Reproduction in Farm Animals and Poultry, Housing Principles and Space Requirements for Livestock and Poultry and more.

topics.title: Role of Livestock in National Economy
topics.definition: Animal husbandry is an integral component of Indian agriculture supporting the livelihood of more than two-thirds of the rural population, providing nutrient-rich food products, draught power, organic manure, fuel, and acting as living capital and insurance against crop failure.

sections.heading: Importance in Rural Economy
items: Integral part of agricultural production: India accounts for ~57.3% of the world's buffalo population, 14.7% of cattle, and 20.4% of small ruminants.
Employment generation: Engages ~20.5 million workers in animal farming; agriculture overall engages ~57% of total working population and 73% of rural labour force.
Women empowerment: Over three-fourths of labour demand in livestock production is met by women, reaching ~90% in Punjab and Haryana.

Nutritional security: Contributes significantly to milk and egg availability; per capita milk availability stands at 283 g/day (vs. ICMR recommendation of 300 g/day) and egg availability at 55 eggs/year.
Income and power generation: Generates around 16% of farmer income, provides draught/draft power for ploughing, threshing, water harvesting, and transportation.
Soil fertility and by-products: Supplies dung, urine, and organic manure; provides feedstock for gobar gas plants; yields slaughterhouse by-products and medicinal inputs (serum, vaccines).

sections.heading: Production of Major Livestock Products (2011-12)
items: Milk: 127.9 million tonnes (annual growth rate ~5%).
Eggs: 66.45 billion numbers.
Wool: 44.73 million kg.
Meat: 5.5 million tonnes (growth rate ~13%).
Fish: 86.66 lakh tonnes (33.71 lakh tonnes marine, 52.95 lakh tonnes inland).

sections.heading: Major Challenges in Animal Husbandry
items: Low animal productivity: Indian cattle average annual milk yield is 1,172 kg (~50% of global average).
Feed and fodder deficit: Deficit of 11% dry fodder, 35% green fodder, and 28% concentrate feed; only 5% of cropped area grows fodder.
Breeding and AI constraints: Poor conception rates and limited AI infrastructure; crossbred population remains low (16.6% in cattle, 21.5% in pigs, 5.2% in sheep).
Disease outbreaks: Recurrent losses due to FMD, BQ, PPR, and avian influenza.

Inadequate infrastructure and financial support: Insufficient public expenditure (~12% of agri-budget), low formal credit share (<4%), inadequate registered slaughterhouses, and only 6% livestock insurance coverage.

topics.title: Reproduction in Farm Animals and Poultry
topics.definition: The physiological processes, anatomical structures, and management practices involved in gametogenesis, mating, fertilization, gestation, and artificial insemination across domestic livestock and avian species.

sections.heading: Male Reproductive System (Mammals)
items: Testes: Paired ovoid organs located in scrotum, site of spermatogenesis and testosterone synthesis.
Epididymis: Coiled tube for sperm maturation, storage, and transport.
