It is Omni-directional and is therefore useful for places where wind changes direction frequently.
15.1.2.2 Darrieus Rotor VAWT: The most common type of VAWT is the Darrieus wind turbine.
The design of these types of turbines looks like an eggbeater.
Generally, an external power source is required to start the rotation.
The starting torque is very low.
In the newer design, three or more blades are used which results in a higher solidity for the rotor.
Solidity is measured by blade area over the rotor area.
New Darrieus type turbines are not held up by guy wires, but have an external structure connected to the top bearing ().
Savonius rotor for wind turbine

topics.title: Applications by turbine size and grid connection
topics.definition: Applications by turbine size and grid connection.

sections.heading: Source-derived points
items: 15.2 Applications There are perhaps four distinct categories of wind power which should be discussed.
These are:
• Small, non-grid connected
• Small, grid connected
• Large, non-grid connected
• Large, grid connected By small, we mean a size appropriate for an individual to own, up to a few tens of kilowatts.
Large refers to utility scale.
15.2.1 Small, Non-Grid Connected If one wants electricity in a location not serviced by a utility, one of the options is a wind turbine, with batteries to level out supply and demand.
This might be a vacation home, a remote antenna and transmitter site, or a Third-World village.
The costs will be high, on the order of $0.50/kWh, but if the total energy usage is small, this might be acceptable.
The alternatives, photovoltaics, microhydro, and diesel generators, are not cheap either, so a careful economic study needs to be done for each situation.
15.2.2 Small, Grid Connected The small, grid connected turbine is usually not economically feasible.
The cost of windgenerated electricity is less because the utility is used for storage rather than a battery bank, but is still not competitive.

In order for the small, grid connected turbine to have any hope of High Mechanical Efficiency Centrifugally Stable Darrieus Turbine financial breakeven, the turbine owner needs to get something close to the retail price for the wind-generated electricity.
One way this is done is for the owner to have an arrangement with the utility called net metering.
With this system, the meter runs backward when the turbine is generating more than the owner is consuming at the moment.
The owner pays a monthly charge for the wires to his home, but it is conceivable that the utility will sometimes write a check to the owner at the end of the month, rather than the other way around.
The utilities do not like this arrangement.
They want to buy at wholesale and sell at retail.
They feel it is unfair to be used as a storage system without remuneration.
For most of the twentieth century, utilities simply refused to connect the grid to wind turbines.
The utility had the right to generate electricity in a given service territory, and they would not tolerate competition.
Then a law was passed that utilities had to hook up wind turbines and pay them the avoided cost for energy.
Unless the state mandated net metering, the utility typically required the installation of a second meter, one measuring energy consumption by the home and the other energy production by the turbine.
The owner would pay the regular retail rate, and the utility would pay their estimate of avoided cost, usually the fuel cost of some base load generator.
The owner might pay $0.08 to $0.15 per kWh, and receive $0.02 per kWh for the wind-generated electricity.
This was far from enough to economically justify a wind turbine, and had the effect of killing the small wind turbine business.
15.2.3 Large, Non-Grid Connected These machines would be installed on islands or in native villages in the far north where it is virtually impossible to connect to a large grid.
Such places are typically supplied by diesel generators, and have a substantial cost just for the imported fuel.
One or more wind turbines would be installed in parallel with the diesel generators, and act as fuel savers when the wind was blowing.
This concept has been studied carefully and appears to be quite feasible technically.
One would expect the market to develop after a few turbines have been shown to work for an extended period in hostile environments.

It would be helpful if the diesel maintenance companies would also carry a line of wind turbines so the people in remote locations would not need to teach another group of maintenance people about the realities of life at places far away from the nearest hardware store.
15.2.4 Large, Grid Connected We might ask if the utilities should be forced to buy wind-generated electricity from these small machines at a premium price which reflects their environmental value.
Many have argued this over the years.
A better question might be whether the small or the large turbines will result in a lower net cost to society.

Given that we want the environmental benefits of wind generation, should we get the electricity from the wind with many thousands of individually owned small turbines, or should we use a much smaller number of utility-scale machines?
If we could make the argument that a dollar spent on wind turbines is a dollar not spent on hospitals, schools, and the like, then it follows that wind turbines should be as efficient as possible.

Economies of scale and costs of operation and maintenance are such that the small, grid connected turbine will always need to receive substantially more per kilowatt hour than the utility-scale turbines in order to break even.
There is obviously a niche market for turbines that are not connected to the grid, but small, grid connected turbines will probably not develop a thriving market.
Most of the action will be from the utility-scale machines.
Sizes of these turbines have been increasing rapidly.
Turbines with ratings near 1 MW are now common, with prototypes of 2 MW and more being tested.
This is still small compared to the needs of a utility, so clusters of turbines are placed together to form wind power plants with total ratings of 10 to 100 MW.

title: Soil and Water Conservation Engineering
description: 122 topics covering Soil and Water Conservation, Soil Erosion, Problems Arising due to Soil Erosion and more.

topics.title: Soil and Water Conservation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: Soil conservation is the control of soil erosion in order to maintain agricultural productivity.

sections.heading: Causes of Soil Erosion
sections.text: Soil erosion is often the effect of many natural causes, such as water and wind. There are also human factors which increase the rate of soil erosion such as construction, cultivation and other activities.

sections.heading: Why Soil Conservation?
sections.text: Conservation is not just the responsibility of soil and plant scientists, hydrologists, wildlife managers, landowners, and the forest or mine owner alone. All citizens should be made aware about the importance of natural resources as our lives depend on that and everyone should be involved in the process of caring of these resources properly and using them intelligently.

topics.title: Soil Erosion
topics.definition: The loosening of the soil from its place and its transportation from one place to another, resulting in the detachment, transportation, and deposition of soil particles.

sections.heading: What is Soil Erosion?
sections.text: Soil erosion is the process of detachment, transportation, and deposition of soil particles. It occurs when wind or water dislodges soil particles from their place and transports them to another location.

sections.heading: Phases of Soil Erosion
items: Detachment: The dislodging of the soil particle from the soil mass by erosive agents.
Transportation: The entrainment and movement of detached soil particles (sediment) from their original location.

sections.heading: Global Sediment Load
rows: Highest suspended sediment discharge due to high monsoon rainfall

topics.title: Problems Arising due to Soil Erosion
topics.definition: The resulting imbalance in the ecosystem is revealed through various undesirable effects, such as degradation of soil surfaces, frequent occurrence of intense floods etc.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text: over exploitation in many parts of the world, including some parts of India

sections.heading: Effects
items: degradation of soil surfaces
frequent occurrence of intense floods

topics.title: Importance of Soil Conservation
topics.definition: Soil conservation is crucial in India due to the large area subjected to soil degradation, which threatens the country's food security.

sections.heading: Causes of Soil Degradation
sections.text: India loses about 150 M-ha to water or wind erosion, and an additional 4 M-ha through ravines and gullies. This accounts for 53.3% of the country's total geographical area.

sections.heading: Effects of Soil Degradation
sections.text: Soil degradation threatens India's food security, with a projected population of two billion by 2100 and stagnant food grain production at 211 million tons for the last five years.

sections.heading: Strategies for Soil Conservation
items: Maintain vegetation cover in vulnerable areas to prevent erosion.
Use partial harvesting forests and seasonally dry or wet areas for pasture instead of arable land.
Implement crop rotation to prevent soil exhaustion.
Use contour ploughing in vulnerable areas.
Carefully manage irrigation to reduce soil salinity development.
Manage livestock grazing to prevent overgrazing.
Restrict construction and urbanization to lower agricultural potential areas.
Secure pledges to restore land to its former condition before granting permission for extractive industries.

topics.title: Causes of Soil Degradation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: Soil degradation may result from natural causes and human-induced causes.

sections.heading: Natural Causes
sections.text: Topographic and climatic factors such as steep slopes, frequent floods and tornadoes, storms and high-velocity wind, high-intensity rains, leaching in humid regions, and drought in dry regions are among the natural causes.

sections.heading: Anthropogenic Causes
sections.text: Deforestation and overexploitation of vegetation, shifting cultivation, soil desurfacing, overgrazing, indiscriminate use of agrochemicals and lack of soil conservation practices, and overextraction of ground water are some anthropogenic causes of soil degradation.

sections.heading: Main Causes of Human-Induced Soil Degradation
items: deforestation
overgrazing
mismanagement of agricultural land
overexploitation
bio-industrial activities

topics.title: Deforestation
topics.definition: The conversion of a forest into a non-forest use such as farmland, ranches, pasture, industrial complexes, and urban areas.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.text: Deforestation is expanding and accelerating into the remaining areas of undisturbed forest, and the quality of the remaining forests is declining. Deforestation processes include industrial logging, clear felling, indiscriminate cutting, forest fires, shifting cultivation, and encroachment.

sections.heading: Environmental Impacts
sections.text: The effects of deforestation are loss of forest, loss of biodiversity, climate change, and natural disasters such as cyclones, flood and drought, disruption of water cycle, decline in water quality, soil erosion, and sedimentation.

sections.heading: Consequences for Soil
sections.text: Cutting trees in large tracts results in the climate getting drier in that area. Forest clearance exposes the bare soil to the scorching effect of the sun and the beating action of the rains. Significant amount of top soil is lost by erosion.

sections.heading: Consequences for Climate
sections.text: Deforestation increases the carbon dioxide emission into the atmosphere. Tropical forests account for about 20 % of total global carbon dioxide (CO) emissions

topics.title: Shifting Cultivation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: Shifting cultivation or slash-and-burn agriculture is an ancient farming system usually practiced by the indigenous people in the hilly areas of the humid tropics.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Shifting Cultivation
sections.text: In this system, a patch of forest, usually on gentle slopes or on summits of hills, is cleared, vegetation is slashed and burned, holes are dug in soil with elementary tools, and seeds of assorted crops are sown before monsoon. Seeds germinate and grow rainfed, and the crops are harvested after 6–8 months. Then the land is left fallow. Farmers clear a new patch of forest for cultivation in the next season.

sections.heading: Effects on Soil and Water
sections.text: The effect of burning is, however, temporary. Rains following burning remove bases rapidly by erosion and leaching. Growing evidence suggests that shifting cultivation in its distorted form leads to an adverse effect on soil and water.

sections.heading: Changes in Rotation Period
items: Overpopulation
Settlement of plain landers to hills
Scarcity of available land for cropping

topics.title: Overgrazing
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: Overgrazing is a major cause of soil degradation worldwide.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.text: Livestock are the main source of income in many arid and semiarid countries. Domestic stocks are widely diverse and consist of camels, donkeys, horses, cows, sheep, and goat.

sections.heading: Consequences of Overgrazing
sections.text: The forage and overgrazing of livestock cause a chain of degradation, critically reducing vegetation cover and soil fertility, as well as increasing erosion.

sections.heading: Mechanisms of Erosion
items: Domestic animals rapidly clear vegetation, placing stress on a land that already has a low vegetation cover.
They also move in large groups and have sharp hooves that easily break up the soil, leaving it susceptible to erosion.

sections.heading: Impact on Soil Fertility
sections.text: Erosion decreases fertile organic content of the soil. The lack of organic matter can lead to desertification through reduced nutrient availability for plant growth.

topics.title: Soil Desurfacing
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Soil desurfacing refers to the removal of a layer of surface soil for many different purposes, including construction of road and railroads and making of bricks.

sections.heading: Importance of Surface Soil
sections.text: The surface soil is the most fertile part of the soil; it contains the highest organic matter and nutrients and possesses the most suitable physical and chemical conditions for plant growth.

sections.heading: Effects of Soil Desurfacing
items: decreases organic matter
decreases nutrients
reduces available water
exposed subsoil is more compact
significantly reduces soil quality and crop yields

topics.title: Monocropping
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: The practice of growing a single crop year after year on the same land, in the absence of rotation through other crops.

sections.heading: Effects on Soil Fertility
sections.text: The roots of the crop draw the same kind and proportion of nutrients from the soil for a long period of time. The nutrient status of the soil becomes imbalanced after a prolonged period of cropping.

sections.heading: Impact on Ecosystems
sections.text: Particular types of insects and pests proliferate. Farmers become increasingly dependent on pesticides.

topics.title: Mismanagement of Irrigation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Sustainability and Environment
topics.definition: Irrigation in arid lands can further enhance desertification through salinization and alkalinization.

sections.heading: Causes of Mismanagement of Irrigation
sections.text: It is not possible for farming to occur without artificial irrigation in arid lands where there is a deficiency of moisture. However, irrigation in arid lands can further enhance desertification through salinization and alkalinization.

sections.heading: Effects of Mismanagement of Irrigation
sections.text: Salinization occurs when irrigation water evaporates quickly, leaving natural salts at the surface of the soil. Over a long time, excessive quantities of salts accumulate at or near the soil surface, making it increasingly difficult for plants to extract water from the soil.

sections.heading: Importance of Leaching Requirement
sections.text: Irrigation water must consider the leaching requirement (extra water to leach the salts) of the soil.

topics.title: Use of Heavy Farm Machineries
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Heavy farm machineries are used in mechanized agriculture by developed countries.

sections.heading: Impact on Soil Degradation
sections.text: The impact of heavy farm machineries on soil degradation is discussed in more detail in connection with soil compaction.

topics.title: Soil Erosion
topics.definition: Soil erosion is the detachment and transportation of soil material from one place to another through the action of wind, water in motion or by the beating action of rain drops.

sections.heading: Factors Influencing Soil Erosion
items: Energy group: potential ability of rainfall, runoff and wind to cause erosion (termed erosivity)
Resistance group: erodibility of the soil, depending on its mechanical and chemical properties
Protection group: plant cover, intercepting rainfall and reducing velocity of runoff and wind

sections.heading: Rate of Soil Loss
sections.text: The rate of soil loss is normally expressed in units of mass or volume per unit area per unit of time. Under natural conditions, annual rates are of the order of 0.0045 t ha for areas of moderate relief and 0.45 t ha for steep relief.

sections.heading: Impacts of Soil Erosion
sections.text: Excessive or enhanced soil erosion due to poor land management can result in both on-site and off-site impacts that are detrimental to a whole range of receptors. Where soil erosion occurs, the soil resource can be severely depleted if the rate of erosion exceeds the rate of natural soil formation.

topics.title: Types of Soil Degradation
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Soil degradation encompasses five main types, including water erosion, wind erosion, chemical deterioration, physical deterioration, and biological activity degradation.

sections.heading: Types of Soil Degradation
sections.text: There are five main types of soil degradation, including water erosion, wind erosion, chemical deterioration, physical deterioration, and degradation of biological activity.

topics.title: Agents of Soil Erosion
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Soil erosion is the removal of soil from the land's surface by natural forces such as water, wind, or ice.

sections.heading: Agents of Soil Erosion
sections.text: Water erosion is the removal of soil from the land's surface by running water, including runoff from melted snow and ice. Sheet erosion occurs when thin layers of soil are removed from sloping land due to overland flows. Rill and gully erosion occur when water removes soil from small channels or streams.

sections.heading: Types of Wind Erosion
items: Saltation: Soil particles are carried away by wind in the form of small leaps.
Suspension: Smallest soil particles are thrown into the air and transported by wind to long distances.
Surface creep: Heavier soil particles are pushed or spread along the surface by wind.

sections.heading: Gully Erosion
rows: Gully erosion is an advanced stage of sheet erosion.
The rate of gully erosion depends on various factors such as runoff producing characteristics, drainage area, soil characteristics, and alignment.

topics.title: Landslides or Slip Erosion
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The hydraulic pressure caused by heavy rains increases the weight of the rocks at cliffs, which come under the gravitational force and finally slip or fall off.

sections.heading: Landslides
sections.text: Sometimes entire hillock may slide down. In this type of erosion, water and gravity act together.

sections.heading: Stream Bank Erosion
items: The rivers during floods splash their water against the banks and thus cuts through them.
Particularly at curves, water strikes with great speed and the bank caves in alongside.

topics.title: Water Erosion: Forms of Water Erosion
topics.definition: Soil detachment, transport, and deposition are the three main processes of water erosion.

sections.heading: Forms of Water Erosion
sections.text: Water erosion occurs through three main processes: soil detachment, transport, and deposition.

sections.heading: Soil Detachment
items: Soil detachment occurs after the soil adsorbs raindrops and pores are filled with water.
Raindrops loosen up and break down aggregates.
Weak aggregates are broken apart first.
Detached fine particles move easily with surface runoff.
When dry, detached soil particles form crusts of low permeability.

sections.heading: Transport
items: Detached soil particles are transported in runoff.
Smaller particles (e.g., clay) are more readily removed than larger (e.g., sand) particles.
The systematic removal of fine particles leaves coarser particles behind.
The selective removal modifies the textural and structural properties of the original soil.
Eroded soils often have coarse-textured surface with exposed subsoil horizons.

sections.heading: Deposition
items: Transported particles deposit in low landscape positions.
Most of the eroded soil material is deposited at the downslope end of the fields.
Placing the deposited material back to its origin can be costly.
Runoff sediment transported off-site can reach downstream water bodies and cause pollution.
Runoff sediment is deposited in deltas along streams.
The texture of eroded material is different.

topics.title: Water Erosion Processes
topics.definition: The three main processes of water erosion are detachment, transport, and deposition.

sections.heading: Detachment
sections.text: Soil detachment occurs after the soil adsorbs raindrops and pores are filled with water. Raindrops loosen up and break down aggregates. Weak aggregates are broken apart first. Detached fine particles move easily with surface runoff. When dry, detached soil particles form crusts of low permeability.

sections.heading: Transport
sections.text: Detached soil particles are transported in runoff. Smaller particles (e.g., clay) are more readily removed than larger (e.g., sand) particles. The systematic removal of fine particles leaves coarser particles behind. The selective removal modifies the textural and structural properties of the original soil.

sections.heading: Deposition
sections.text: Transported particles deposit in low landscape positions. Most of the eroded soil material is deposited at the downslope end of the fields. Placing the deposited material back to its origin can be costly. Runoff sediment transported off-site can reach downstream water bodies and cause pollution.

topics.title: Sheet Erosion
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
topics.definition: Sheet erosion is the removal of a thin layer of soil from the whole slope, primarily by raindrop impact and shallow surface flow.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.text: Soil particles are detached primarily by raindrops and secondarily by frost, hooves of farm animals, tillage, and mechanical action of farm machines. Detached particles are transported by runoff water as overland flow.

sections.heading: Types of Sheet Erosion
items: Raindrop erosion
Laminar erosion
Rillet erosion
Layer erosion

sections.heading: Characteristics and Processes
rows: Intensity of accumulation of runoff water depends on the height of the water stream, the coarseness of the surface, vegetation, or crop distribution.

topics.title: Rill Erosion
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
topics.definition: Rill erosion occurs when rainfall exceeds the rate of infiltration, causing water to accumulate on the surface and move along sloping lands, concentrating in tiny channels called rills.

sections.heading: Causes and Effects
sections.text: Rill erosion is caused by large amounts of material released and transported for variable distances in concentrated areas. It can lead to high soil loss, but the small channels do not usually interfere with tillage implements.

sections.heading: Formation and Characteristics
sections.text: Rills are less than 30 cm deep and are formed by the cutting action of flowing water detaching soil particles. The amount of soil loss may be high, but the small channels do not usually interfere with tillage implements.

sections.heading: Factors Influencing Rill Erosion
items: Precipitation intensity and frequency
Soil permeability and resistance
Land slope and surface roughness
Tillage lines, rows of crops, and exposed roots

sections.heading: Types of Rill Erosion
rows: Ridge formation with sharply cut rillets and gullies
Material of varying resistance, vertical openings

topics.title: Gully Erosion
topics.definition: The main feature of gully erosion is the volume and velocity of water at the lowest level.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Gullies
sections.text: Gullies may grow into gorges and canyons in high altitudes and very steep slopes. Gullies may be flat, narrow, broad, and round.

sections.heading: Types of Gully Forms
items: Flat forms occur mostly on shallow soil or in connection with a specific lithic structure of the slope.
Narrow, acute forms are created with a narrow V-section, the breadth of the gully usually being equal to its depth or smaller.
Broad gullies have a wide bottom and are U shaped.

sections.heading: Active Gullies
sections.text: Active gullies maintain steep or even perpendicular sides. It happens frequently that recent forms replace older forms so that their origin and age cannot be assessed from superficial observation.

topics.title: Riverbank/Stream Bank Erosion
topics.definition: The process of erosion that occurs along the banks of rivers and streams, characterized by the formation of gullies, canyons, and other landforms.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Gully Erosion
sections.text: Gullies may grow into gorges and canyons in high altitudes and very steep slopes. Gullies may be flat, narrow, broad, and round.

sections.heading: Types of Gullies
items: Flat forms occur mostly on shallow soil or in connection with a specific lithic structure of the slope.
Narrow, acute forms are created with a narrow V-section, the breadth of the gully usually being equal to its depth or smaller.
Broad gullies have a wide bottom and are U shaped.

sections.heading: Factors Influencing Gully Erosion
sections.text: The main feature of gully erosion is the volume and velocity of water at the lowest level. The energy of flowing water increases its cutting and smashing power and often results in bank erosion.

topics.title: Gully Erosion
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
topics.definition: A channel or miniature valley cut by concentrated runoff through which water commonly flows only during and immediately after heavy rains.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Gully Erosion
sections.text: Any concentration of surface runoff is a potential source of gully erosion. A gully is too large to be filled by normal tillage practices.

sections.heading: Types of Gullies
items: Dendritic
Branching
Linear

sections.heading: Distinction between Ravine, Gully and Rills
sections.text: A gully is too large to be filled by normal tillage practices. A ravine is a deep narrow gorge.

topics.title: Development of Gullies
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The main processes in the development of gullies are waterfall erosion and channel erosion.

sections.heading: Process of Development
sections.text: Gullies usually start with channel erosion. When an overfall develops at the head of the gully, the gully continues to develop by waterfall erosion.

sections.heading: Types of Erosion
items: Waterfall erosion extends the gully head
Channel erosion enlarges the depth and width of gullies

topics.title: Principles of Gully Control
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Minimizing surface runoff is essential in gully control.

sections.heading: Factors Affecting Gully Erosion
sections.text: The rate of gully erosion depends primarily on the runoff producing characteristics of the watershed, the watershed area, soil characteristics, size-shape and slope of gully etc.

sections.heading: Causes of Watershed Deterioration
items: Misuse of land (man made changes)
Short intensive rainstorms
Prolonged rains of moderate intensity
Rapid snow melts

sections.heading: Methods for Gully Control
items: Improvement of gully catchments to reduce and regulate the runoff rates (peak flows)
Diversion of surface water above the gully area
Stabilization of gullies by structural measures and accompanying re-vegetation

topics.title: Gully Control Measures
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Preventing the formation of gully is much easier than controlling it once it has formed.

sections.heading: Planning for Gully Control
sections.text: One of the major steps in a gully control programme is to plan the control of runoff from the drainage area. The various methods employed for controlling runoff may be considered in the following order:

topics.title: Retention of Runoff on the Drainage Area
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Retention of runoff on the drainage area can be achieved through good crop management and applicable conservation practices.

sections.heading: Methods for Reducing Runoff
sections.text: crop management and applicable conservation practices such as contouring, strip cropping, bunding, terracing etc. Where contour bunds are used, runoff is greatly reduced. On cultivated areas, small and medium sized gullies can also be reclaimed by placing a series of earthfills across the gully.

topics.title: Diversion of Runoff Around the Gullied Area: The most effective
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: control of gullies is by complete elimination of runoff from the gullied area.

sections.heading: Methods for Diverting Runoff
sections.text: Terraces and diversion ditches are generally used for diverting runoff from its natural outlet.

sections.heading: Use of Terraces
sections.text: Terraces are very effective in the control of small gullies on cultivated fields or even medium size shallow gullies.

sections.heading: Alternative Methods for Diversion Ditches
sections.text: If the slope above a gully is too steep for terracing, or if the drainage area is pasture or woodland, diversion ditches may be used to keep the runoff out of the gully.

sections.heading: Conveyance of Runoff through the Gully
sections.text: If it is not possible to either retain or divert the runoff, then runoff must be conveyed through the gully itself.

topics.title: Sod Flumes
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A sod flume is a type of structure used to control overfall in gullies, providing a protected surface for runoff to flow into the gully.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.text: The design of sod flume serves the purpose of preventing further waterfall erosion by providing a protected surface over which the runoff may flow into the gully. Slope varies with the soil type, size of watershed, height of overfall and type of sod used.

sections.heading: Design Parameters
items: Slope: varies with soil type, watershed size, overfall height, and sod type.
Maximum depth of flow: 30 cm.

sections.heading: Design Guidelines
sections.text: The flume should be wide enough to maintain a non-erosive velocity. A slope of 4:1 is considered the steepest for its design.

topics.title: Temporary Gully Control Structures (TGCS)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: TGCS have a life span of 3 to 8 years and they are pretty effective where the amount of runoff is not too large.

sections.heading: Types of TGCS
items: Woven wire check dams
Brush dams
Loose rock dams
Plan or slab dams
Log check dams
Boulder check dams

sections.heading: Purpose and Function
sections.text: These are made of locally available materials. Basic purposes they serve are to retain more water as well as soil for proper plant growth and prevent channel erosion until sufficient vegetation is established on the upstream side of the gully.

topics.title: Design Criteria for Temporary Check Dams
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The overall height of a temporary check dam should not exceed 75 cm, with an effective height of about 30 cm being sufficient.

sections.heading: Design Considerations

topics.title: Soil Loss Estimation by Universal Loss Soil Equation Introduction
topics.definition: The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) is a widely accepted method to predict average annual soil loss caused by sheet and rill erosion.

sections.heading: Limitations of the USLE
sections.text: While it can estimate long-term annual soil loss and guide conservationists on proper cropping, management, and conservation practices, it cannot be applied to a specific year or a specific storm.

topics.title: The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)
topics.definition: The most widely used empirical model worldwide for estimating soil loss, developed in the USA.

sections.heading: Limitations of the USLE
sections.text: The USLE makes simplified assumptions in the processes of soil erosion and has limited consideration of complex factors.

sections.heading: Advantages of the USLE
sections.text: The USLE is simple, easy to use, and does not require numerous input parameters or extensive data sets for prediction.

sections.heading: Equation Components
items: R: rainfall and runoff erosivity index
K: erodibility factor
LS: topographic factor
C: cover and management factor
P: support practice factor

sections.heading: Equation Formula
sections.text: A = R*K*LS*C*P, where A is average annual soil loss (Mg ha)

topics.definition: The EI is computed as the product of total storm energy times the intensity of the rain.

sections.heading: Computing the EI
sections.text: The USLE uses the annual EI which is computed by adding the EI values from individual storms that occurred during the year.

sections.heading: Relationship to Soil Loss
sections.text: According to Wischmeier and Smith (1978), the EI corresponds closely to the amount of soil loss from a field.

sections.heading: Limitations of the USLE-Computed EI
sections.text: The USLE-computed EI is only valid for rain intensities ≤ 63.5mm h.

sections.heading: Modifications for Tropical Regions

sections.heading: History and Development

topics.title: Limitations of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE)
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The USLE model applies only to sheet erosion since it is based on rain as a source of energy, making it unsuitable for linear or mass erosion.

sections.heading: Applicability Limitations
sections.text: The USLE model has been tested and verified in plain and hilly countries with 1-20% slopes, but excludes young mountains with steeper than 40% slopes.

sections.heading: Regional Limitations
items: only applicable to the American Great Plains
not suitable for mountainous regions

sections.heading: Temporal Limitations
sections.text: The model applies only for average data over 20 years and is not valid for individual storms.

sections.heading: Methodological Limitations
sections.text: The USLE neglects certain interactions between factors to distinguish the individual effect of each factor, such as slope combined with plant cover or soil type along with slope.

sections.heading: Omission of Sediment Deposition
sections.text: The USLE does not calculate sediment deposition.

topics.title: Soil Loss Measurement Techniques
topics.definition: Data on soil erosion and its controlling factors can be collected in the field or, for simulated conditions, in the laboratory.

sections.heading: Advantages of Field Measurements
sections.text: For realistic data on soil loss, field measurements are the most reliable, but because conditions vary in both time and space, it is often difficult to determine the chief causes of erosion or to understand the processes at work.

sections.heading: Limitations of Field Measurements
sections.text: Because conditions vary in both time and space, it is often difficult to determine the chief causes of erosion or to understand the processes at work.

sections.heading: Advantages of Laboratory Experiments
sections.text: Experiments designed to lead to explanation are best undertaken in the laboratory, where the effects of many factors can be controlled.

sections.heading: Need for Field Verification
sections.text: Because of the artificiality of laboratory experiments, however, some confirmation of their results in the field is desirable.

topics.title: Experimental Design
topics.definition: The process of planning, conducting, and analyzing experiments to assess the influence of one or more factors on a specific outcome.

sections.heading: Designing Experiments
sections.text: Experiments are usually carried out to assess the influence of one or more factors on the rate of erosion. In a simple experiment to study the effect of slope steepness, it is assumed that all other factors likely to influence erosion are held constant.

sections.heading: Factors to Consider
items: range of steepnesses
specific steepnesses within the range
levels for factors being held constant

sections.heading: Experimental Error and Variability
sections.text: Measurements are subject to error. Since no single measurement of soil loss can be considered as the absolutely correct value, it is virtually impossible to quantify errors.However; they can be assessed in respect of variability.

sections.heading: Experimental Design Considerations
sections.text: A decision is also needed on what levels to set for the factors being held constant, e.g. whether slope length should be 5 or 50m, or the rainfall intensity 20 or 200mmh-1.

sections.heading: Data Collection and Analysis
sections.text: A problem faced in many experiments is how much data to collect. For instance, if the objective of a study is to measure total soil loss over a period of time, this can be achieved by collecting in bulk all the soil washed or blown from an area.

sections.heading: Best Practices for Experimental Design
sections.text: Experiments should have clearly conceived objectives, define what needs to be measured and at what level of accuracy, and be set up in such a way that they can be easily repeated by others.

topics.title: Field Measurements and Experiments
topics.definition: Field measurements may be classified into two groups: those designed to determine soil loss from relatively small sample areas or erosion plots, often as part of an experiment, and those designed to assess erosion over a larger area, such as a drainage basin.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.text: Field measurements may be classified into two groups:

sections.heading: Types of Field Measurements
items: determine soil loss from small sample areas or erosion plots
assess erosion over larger areas

topics.title: Erosion Plots: Bounded Plots
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Bounded plots are physically isolated pieces of land used to study erosion, with both runoff and soil loss monitored.

sections.heading: Design and Construction
sections.text: Plots are made of stable materials like sheet metal, wood, or other non-rotting materials. Edges extend 150–200mm above the soil surface and are embedded in the soil to prevent shifting.

sections.heading: Layout and Data Collection
sections.text: A collecting trough or gutter channels sediment and runoff into tanks, with an overflow system for large plots. However, this setup has several sources of error, including silting and inadequate covering against rainfall.

sections.heading: Considerations and Limitations
items: Collecting tanks overflowing during extreme events
Tanks floating out of saturated ground
Runoff entering the top of the plots
Damage from termites, spiders, and baboons

topics.title: Gerlach Troughs
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech | Business and Agribusiness | Sustainability and Environment | Communication and Extension
topics.definition: An alternative method of measuring sediment loss and runoff using simple metal gutters, closed at the sides and fitted with a movable lid.

sections.heading: Design and Layout
sections.text: Two or three gutters are placed side-by-side across the slope and groups of gutters are installed at different slope lengths, arranged in plan to ensure a clear run to each gutter from en echelon the slope crest.

sections.heading: Calculating Soil Loss
items: Soil loss per unit width is normal.
If an areal assessment is required, assume a catchment area equal to the width of the gutter times the length of the slope.

sections.heading: Advantages and Limitations
sections.text: Gerlach troughs can be employed for sample measurements of soil loss at a large number of selected sites over a large area due to their cheapness and simplicity. However, on curved slopes, the catchment area must be surveyed in the field.

topics.title: Changes in Ground Level
topics.definition: The simplest way of measuring changes in ground level over time is to use an erosion pin, a 250–300 mm long nail driven through a washer into the soil.

sections.heading: Installation and Measurement
sections.text: A large number of pins, usually installed on a grid system, is needed to obtain representative data over a large area. A disadvantage of erosion pins is that they can be easily disturbed by livestock and wildlife or stolen by the local population.

sections.heading: Alternative Approach
sections.text: An alternative approach is to establish a network of metal pegs, set unobtrusively in concrete at ground level so that their position remains stable over time. The method, pioneered by Hudson (1964) on rangeland in Zimbabwe, is known as the erosion bridge.

sections.heading: Erosion Bridge Method
sections.text: A portable aluminium girder is placed across any two adjacent pegs from which vertical readings of the depth to the soil surface can be taken at regular intervals. Between readings the girder is removed.

topics.title: Splash Erosion Measurements
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Erosion measurements in the field using splash boards, small funnels or bottles to collect splashed material.

sections.heading: Methods of measuring splash erosion
sections.text: Erosion plots, Gerlach troughs, erosion pins and erosion bridges provide information on erosion by rainsplash, overland flow and rills combined. Attempts to assess the relative contributions of each are based on separate measurements of splash erosion and rill erosion with the balance being attributed to overland flow.

sections.heading: Field methods
items: Splash boards
Small funnels or bottles

sections.heading: Alternative approach
sections.text: The field splash cup method, where a block of soil is isolated by enclosing it in a central cylinder and the material splashed out is collected in a surrounding catching tray.

topics.title: Rill Erosion Measurement
topics.definition: The simplest method of assessing rill erosion is to establish a series of transects, 20–100 m long, across the slope and positioned one above the other.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Establish a series of transects, 20–100 m long, across the slope and positioned one above the other.

sections.heading: Limitations

depends on identifying rill edges

topics.title: Gully Erosion Measurement
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Rates of gully erosion are calculated from differences in elevation between DEMs of different dates.

sections.heading: Measurement Techniques
sections.text: Erosion from relatively small gullies can be assessed using the same profiling technique as described above for rills. For larger gullies, sequential surveys using aerial photography are more suitable.

sections.heading: Aerial Photography Surveys
items: More recent surveys of gullies use large-scale (1 : 10,000) aerial photography to construct high resolution digital elevation models (DEMs). Digitally generated DEMs can match the accuracy of traditional analytical photogrammetric techniques and are much faster to produce.

topics.title: Catchments Sediment Yield
topics.definition: The sediment yield of a catchment is obtained from measurements of the quantity of sediment leaving a catchment along the river over time.

sections.heading: Measurement Methods
sections.text: Recording stations are established at the exit point for the automatic measurement of discharge, using weirs and depth recorders, and suspended sediment concentrations in the river water. Water samples are taken at set times with specially designed integrated sediment samplers, or the sediment concentration is monitored continuously by recording the turbidity of the water.

sections.heading: Limitations of Measurement Methods
sections.text: Bucket samples are not recommended because they contain only the surface water and cannot provide information on the sediment being transported throughout the depth and width of the river channel. With measurements made at set times, there is a need to extrapolate the data to cover the period between samples.

sections.heading: Sediment Discharge Rating Curve
sections.text: The standard approach is to establish a sediment discharge rating curve in which the sediment concentration (C) is related to the water discharge () by the equation C =aQ(6.2).

sections.heading: Accuracy and Sampling Frequency
sections.text: The accuracy of this method is highly dependent on the frequency of sampling. The likelihood of underestimation increased as the sampling frequency decreased, since, with longer sampling intervals, the record is likely to include fewer flood events.

sections.heading: Turbidity Meter Limitations
sections.text: The turbidity meter does not give a true record because the measurements are subject to errors associated with the influence of the particle size of the sediment load, the magnitude of the sediment concentration, the presence of organic matter and the need to keep the sensors clear of algae.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Despite these problems, the method is currently the best available to provide estimates of suspended sediment yield, especially if high frequency data are needed. It should be recognized, however that, because of the need for regular calibration and maintenance, such data come at greater cost compared to using rating curves.

topics.title: Reservoir Surveys
topics.definition: A method used to measure the amount of sediment accumulated in a reservoir, which can indicate erosion rates in the catchment upstream.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: Reservoir surveys involve measuring the depth of the reservoir using manual soundings or echo-sounders, and creating a contour map of the bottom. The volume of sediment is then calculated and compared to the initial volume to determine erosion rates.

sections.heading: Calculations
items: Volume below lowest contour: product of area of lowest contour and mean depth from bottom

sections.heading: Data Analysis
sections.text: The volume is converted into mass, divided by the catchment area to give an erosion value in t ha, which is then adjusted for sediment representation and time since reservoir construction.

sections.heading: Caesium-137 Tracer
sections.text: Caesium-137 is the most commonly used tracer in soil erosion measurement. It was produced in the fall-out of atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons from the 1950s to 1970s.

sections.text: Laboratory experiments are used to study soil erosion and deposition, but they have limitations due to scale-equivalence issues.

topics.title: Runoff Simulation
topics.definition: A setup used in experimental geomorphology to simulate runoff, often using a flume with adjustable slope and controlled discharge.

sections.heading: Setup and Design
sections.text: The Experimental Geomorphology Laboratory at the University of Leuven uses an aluminium and plexiglass flume to simulate runoff. The flume is 4m long and 0.4m wide, with a controlled discharge from a cylinder with ten openings.

sections.heading: Adjusting Slope and Discharge
sections.text: The slope of the flume can be adjusted to different steepnesses, and rainfall simulators positioned over the top. The discharge is controlled by a tap, with water pumped from a container at the upper end.

sections.heading: Reducing Edge Effects
sections.text: To reduce edge effects, sediment can be collected from a narrow strip down the centre of the plot instead of collecting for the whole plot width. This helps to eliminate the problem of difficult-to-eliminate edge effects.

sections.heading: Simulating Rill Erosion
sections.text: The short length of the flume makes it difficult to simulate rill erosion, but the supply of runoff at the top of the slope can be adjusted to simulate different slope lengths.

sections.heading: Adding Sediment
sections.text: Sediment can also be added to the runoff upslope of the test soil to further simulate real-world conditions.

topics.title: Wind Tunnels
topics.definition: A laboratory facility used to study wind erosion, where air is supplied by a fan through a honeycomb shield into a convergence zone, test section, and divergence zone.

sections.heading: Design of Wind Tunnels
sections.text: Wind tunnels are shaped so that air enters through a honeycomb shield, serving as a flow straightener, into a convergence zone, where flow is constricted, passes through the test section and leaves through a divergence zone.

sections.heading: Types of Wind Tunnels
items: Open-circuit tunnels
Closed-circuit tunnels

sections.heading: Characteristics of Closed-Circuit Tunnels
rows: Easier due to less upstream contact with boundary walls

topics.title: Principles of Erosion Control
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Soil erosion takes place both due to natural causes and anthropogenic factors, with adverse effects including loss of valuable top soil, sedimentation in rivers and irrigation canals, and structural damages.

sections.heading: Erosion Control Measures
sections.text: Soil erosion control measures are adopted to reduce or minimize the intensity of the adverse effects. Catchment Area Treatment (CAT) is adopted to reduce soil loss from catchments due to runoff flow, after ascertaining erosion severity on sub-watershed basis.

sections.heading: Catchment Area Treatment (CAT)
sections.text: CAT comprises mechanical (engineering) and vegetative (afforestation) measures. Mechanical and vegetative practices on agricultural lands are employed on the milder slopes for conservation of soil, by farming across the slope of the land.

sections.heading: Principles Underlying Erosion Control
sections.text: The basic principle underlying this approach is to cause reduction in the effect of the runoff velocity and, thereby reduce soil erosion. On steeper slopes, mechanical measures (such as terracing) and other structures are constructed to reduce the effect of the slope on runoff velocity.

sections.heading: Types of Vegetative and Mechanical Practices
items: Mechanical measures (such as terracing)
Vegetative practices

topics.title: Strip Cropping
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The practice of growing strips of crops having poor potential for erosion control, alternated with strips of crops having good potential for erosion control.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.text: Close growing crops act as barriers to runoff flow and reduce the runoff velocity generated from the strips of intertilled crops, and eventually reduce soil erosion.

topics.title: Buffer Strip Cropping
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Buffer strip cropping is practiced where uniform strips of crops are laid out for smooth operation of farm machinery, while farming on a contour strip cropping layout.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Buffer strip cropping is practiced where uniform strips of crops are laid out for smooth operation of farm machinery, while farming on a contour strip cropping layout.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.text: Buffer strips of legumes, grasses and similar other crops are laid out between the contour strips as correction strips, as illustrated in Fig. 7.4.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.text: Buffer strips provide very good protection and effective control of soil erosion from strips of intertilled crops.

topics.title: Minimum Tillage
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The operation in which tillage and sowing are combined in one operation.

sections.heading: Benefits of Minimum Tillage
sections.text: Such operations create a coarse soil surface and fine lumps of soil between rows. The loose and porous texture of the soil allows a good infiltration capacity. The surface runoff by this operation is reduced by about 35% and soil erosion by about 40%.

topics.title: Strip Tillage
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A cultivation operation where narrow strips of soil are loosened, leaving the land between uncultivated.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text: This operation is an improvement over the no tillage system. In this type of cultivation, narrow strips of approximately 0.2 m width and 0.1 m depth are generally laid out following the contour, and the land between the strips left uncultivated.

items: Fig. 7.7 shows strip tillage done by tractor drawn implement.
Fig. 7.8 shows strip tillage done by animal drawn implement.

rows: Stubbles are not present in the constructed narrow strips.
This helps in sowing operations and facilitates better plant growth.

topics.title: Mulching
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Mulches are used to minimize rain splash, reduce evaporation, control weeds, reduce temperature of soil in hot climates, and allow temperature conducive to microbial activity.

sections.heading: Types of Mulches
sections.text: Stubbles, trash, other type of vegetation and polythene are some of the most common types of mulches used.

sections.heading: Benefits of Mulching
items: minimize rain splash
reduce evaporation
control weeds
reduce temperature of soil in hot climates
allow temperature conducive to microbial activity

topics.title: Contour Farming
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The practice of cultivation along contours, carried out approximately on contours.

sections.heading: Benefits of Contour Farming
sections.text: Contour farming reduces soil erosion by about 30%, increases moisture content by about 40%, and reduces surface runoff by about 13%.

sections.heading: Implementation of Contour Farming
items: Laying out contour guide lines first
Carrying out tillage operations simultaneously

sections.heading: Effectiveness of Contour Farming
sections.text: Furrow cultivation on contours has been found to be the most effective soil conservation measure.

topics.title: Strip Cropping
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The practice of growing alternating strips of crops with poor potential for erosion control and those with good potential, to reduce soil erosion.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.text: Close growing crops act as barriers to runoff flow and reduce the runoff velocity generated from the strips of intertilled crops, and eventually reduce soil erosion.

topics.title: Buffer Strip Cropping
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Buffer strip cropping is practiced where uniform strips of crops are laid out for smooth operation of farm machinery, while farming on a contour strip cropping layout.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Buffer strip cropping is practiced where uniform strips of crops are laid out for smooth operation of farm machinery, while farming on a contour strip cropping layout.

sections.heading: Layout
items: Uniform strips of crops
Contour strip cropping layout

topics.title: Bunds (Contour Bunds, Graded Bunds) and their Design
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: A bund is an engineering measure of soil conservation used to create obstruction across the path of surface runoff to reduce water velocity.

sections.heading: Design of Bunds
sections.text: Bunds are simply embankment like structures, constructed across the land slope.

sections.heading: Types of Bunds
items: Erosion control bunds
Moisture conservation bunds

topics.title: Contour Bunds
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Contour bunds are a type of bund used to prevent soil erosion, recommended for areas with low annual rainfall, permeable soils, and gentle land slopes.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Uses
sections.text: The choice of bund type depends on land slope, rainfall, soil type, and the purpose of the bund. Contour bunds are suitable for areas with low annual rainfall (< 600 mm), agricultural fields with permeable soils, and gentle land slopes.

sections.heading: Comparison with Graded Bunds
items: Used in areas with high rainfall and relatively impervious soil for safe disposal of excess runoff.
Not suitable for black cotton soils due to severe erosion problems.

sections.heading: Performance in Different Soil Conditions
sections.text: Bunds can stand well in shallow, medium, and medium deep soils. However, they fail in deep black soil due to cracks that allow water to flow through, causing breaches and severe damage to fields.

topics.title: Contour Bunds
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Contour bunds are laid out in areas with less rainfall and permeable soils to prevent soil erosion and conserve rainwater.

sections.heading: Main Functions
items: It reduces the length of slope which in turn reduces the soil erosion.
The water is impounded for some time and gets recharged into the soil which helps in crop cultivation.

sections.heading: Limitations
items: The contour bunds are suitable for those areas, which receive the annual rainfall less than 600 mm
It is not suitable for clayey soils
Contour bunding is not suitable on the land slopes greater than 6%

topics.title: Graded Bunds
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Graded bunds are laid out in areas where the land is susceptible to water erosion, the soil is less permeable and the area has water logging problems.

sections.heading: Design and Construction
sections.text: A graded bund system is designed to dispose of excess runoff safely from agricultural fields. A graded bund is laid out with a longitudinal slope gradient leading to outlet.

sections.heading: Types of Graded Bunds
items: uniformly-graded bunds
variable-graded bunds

sections.heading: Variable-Graded Bunds
sections.text: The variable-graded bunds are required where bunds need longer lengths, owing to which the cumulative runoff increases towards the outlets. In these types of bunds, variations in the grade are provided at different sections of the bund to keep the runoff velocity within the desired limits so as not to cause any soil erosion.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Due to crossing of farm implements, the bunds are disturbed and some soil is lost. Proper maintenance is required at regular interval.

topics.title: Type of Bund
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The type of bund (contour or graded bund) to be constructed depends upon the rainfall and soil condition.

sections.heading: Construction Considerations
sections.text: Contour bunds are preferred for construction in areas receiving annual rainfall less than 600 mm and where soil moisture is a limiting factor for crop production. Graded bunds are recommended in heavy and medium rainfall areas.

topics.title: Spacing of the Bunds
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The spacing of bunds should meet specific criteria to ensure optimal water management.

sections.heading: Principles for Spacing of Bunds
sections.text: The seepage zone below the upper bund should meet the saturation zone of the lower bund; the bunds should check the water at a point where the water attains erosive velocity; and the bund should not cause inconvenience to agricultural operations.

sections.heading: Formula for Determining Spacing
sections.text: The formula used to determine spacing is: V.I. = vertical interval between consecutive bunds, S = land slope (percent), and a and b are constants depending on soil and rainfall characteristics.

sections.heading: Modified Formula for Heavy Rainfall
sections.text: For areas of heavy rainfall: V.I. = vertical interval in cm, S = land slope in percent

sections.heading: Modified Formula for Low Rainfall
sections.text: For areas with low rainfall: V.I. = vertical interval in cm, S = land slope in percent

sections.heading: Relationship Between Horizontal and Vertical Spacing
items: H.I. = V.I. / S
where H.I. indicates the horizontal distance of the bund and V.I. is the vertical interval

topics.title: Length of Bund
topics.definition: The length of a bund, which is the width of the area between two ditches or waterways.

sections.heading: Side Slopes
sections.text: The side slopes of a bund are typically 1.5 to 1, 2 to 1, or 2.5 to 1.

topics.title: Area Lost Due to Bunding
topics.definition: The area lost due to main contour bund is calculated by multiplying the length of contour bund per hectare with its base width.

sections.heading: Calculating Area Lost Due to Main Contour Bund
sections.text: It is calculated by multiplying the length of contour bund per hectare with its base width. i.e A= 10000/HI * b = 100S/VI * b

sections.text: The above equation can also be written in the following form to compute the area lost in percentage due to bunding: A(%) = 1.3*S*b/VI

topics.title: Construction of Bunds
topics.definition: The construction of bunds should start from the ridge and continue down the valley to ensure protection during rain.

sections.heading: General Construction Guidelines
sections.text: Construction of bunds should start from the ridge and continue down the valley. This will ensure protection of the bunds if rains occur during construction. The base width area of the bund should be cleared of vegetation and the soil in this area should also be slightly distributed so that good binding can be achieved when the bund is formed over it.

sections.heading: Burrow Pits
items: The burrow pits for the soil are generally located on the upstream side of the bund.
The burrow pits should have a uniform depth of 30 cm and the width can be varied as per necessity.
The burrow pits should be continuous and no breaks are to be left.

sections.heading: Construction Process
sections.text: When the soil is dug, the clods should not be put on the bund at a time. The earth should be put in layers of 15 cm and consolidated by trampling. The templates of the specified dimensions are used for checking the bund section.

sections.heading: Final Shaping and Ramming
sections.text: The bund section should be finally shaped, trimmed and slightly rammed on the top and the sides.

sections.heading: Terraces
rows: An earth-embankment constructed across the slope to control runoff and minimize soil erosion.
A terrace acts as an intercept to land slope, and divides the sloping land surface into strips.

sections.heading: Types of Terraces
items: Broad-base terraces are adapted where the main purpose is either to remove or retain water on sloping land suitable for cultivation.
Bench terraces are mainly used to reduce the land slope.

topics.title: Design of Bench Terraces
topics.definition: The design of bench terraces involves determining the type, spacing, width, and cross-section of the terraces based on rainfall, soil conditions, and slope.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.text: The design of bench terraces consists of determining the type, spacing, width, and cross-section of the terraces based on rainfall, soil conditions, and slope.

sections.heading: Terrace Spacing
items: dependent upon the depth of the cut
equal to double the depth of cut

sections.heading: Factors Limiting Depth of Cut
sections.text: The factors that limit the depth of cut are the soil depth in the area and the slope.

topics.title: Cross Section of Bench Terraces
topics.definition: The design of the terrace cross section consists of deciding on the batter slope, dimensions of the shoulder bund, inward slope of the terrace, and drainage channel.

sections.heading: Design Considerations for Terrace Cross Sections
sections.text: The design of the terrace cross section consists of deciding (1) the batter slope, (2) dimensions of the shoulder bund, (3) inward slope of the terrace and the dimensions of the drainage channel in case of terraces sloping inward, and (4) outward slope in case of terraces sloping outward.

sections.heading: Batter Slope
sections.text: The batter slope is mainly for the stability of the fill or the embankment. The flatter the batter slope, the larger the area lost due to bench terracing.

sections.heading: Drainage Channel
items: provided at the inner edge of the terrace to dispose of the runoff

topics.title: Alignment of Bench Terraces
topics.definition: Alignment of bench terraces should start from the ridge and progress towards the valley.

sections.heading: Designing the Alignment
sections.text: The average land slope of the area to be terraced should be determined by taking levels and then the specifications of the terrace should be worked out. Contour lines may be marked with the help of a leveling instrument.

sections.heading: Marking Terrace Widths
sections.text: Taking a contour line as the centre line, the terrace width may be marked on the ground.

sections.heading: Examining and Adjusting Alignment
sections.text: The alignment may now be examined and suitable adjustments should be made wherever necessary taking into considerations the local conditions like depressions, sharp turns, field boundaries etc. that exist at the site.

sections.heading: Constructing Bench Terraces
items: Construction of the bench terraces may be started from the highest terrace and proceeded downwards.
By this method, the top soil and the subsoil get mixed up and the top soil may not be available for the terrace surface.

sections.heading: Managing Runoff
sections.text: In bench terraced areas, suitable outlets should be provided to dispose of the runoff safely. In most of the cases one of the sides of the hill slope where vegetation is well established can be used as the outlet.

sections.heading: Alternative Outlets
sections.text: Where such outlets are not available or feasible, waterways are to be formed to dispose of the runoff.

topics.title: Bench Terraces Maintenance
topics.definition: New terraces should be carefully maintained, especially during the first two years.

sections.heading: Planting Risers
sections.text: After cutting a terrace, its riser should be shaped and planted with grass as soon as possible. Sod-forming or rhizome-type grasses are better than those of the tall or bunch-type.

sections.heading: Additional Protection Methods
items: Stones can protect and support risers when available.
Hydro-seeding is an additional protection method.
A piece of rock, a brick, or a cement block may be needed to check water flow on steeper channels.

sections.heading: Outlet Drainage
sections.text: The outlet for drainage-type terraces is the point where the run-off leaves the terrace and goes into the waterway. Its gradient is usually steep and should be protected by sods of earth.

sections.heading: Water Flow Checks
items: A piece of rock, a brick, or a cement block may be needed to check water flow on steeper channels.
Similar checks are required for level bench terraces where the water falls from the higher terraces onto those below.

sections.heading: Shoulder Bunds
sections.text: The shoulder bund should be planted with permanent vegetation and ploughing of the toe of bund should be avoided.

sections.heading: Batter Slope Protection
sections.text: The batter slope of the terraces should be stabilized and protected by establishing deep rooted and soil binding spreading type of grasses.

topics.title: Benches
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The toe drains should be always open and properly graded; water must not be allowed to accumulate in any part of the terrace.

sections.heading: Maintenance
sections.text: Obstacles such as continuous mounds or beds must be removed at regular intervals to allow water to pass to the toe drain. Grasses and weeds should be removed from the benches. Correct gradients should be maintained and reshaped immediately after crops are harvested. Ploughing must be carried out with care so as not to destroy the toe drains and the grade.

sections.heading: Design
sections.text: The toe drains should be always open and properly graded; water must not be allowed to accumulate in any part of the terrace. All runoff should be allowed to collect at the toe drains for safe disposal to the protected waterway.

topics.title: Risers
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Grasses should be grown well on the risers.

sections.heading: General Care
sections.text: Weeds and vines which threaten the survival of the grasses should be cut down or uprooted. Grasses should not be allowed to grow too high. Any small break or fall from the riser must be repaired immediately.

sections.heading: Livestock Management
sections.text: Cattle should not be allowed to trample on the risers or graze the grasses.

sections.heading: Water Management
sections.text: Runoff should not be allowed to flow over the risers on reverse-sloped terraces.

topics.title: Soil Productivity
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Soil productivity should be maintained by means of proper crop rotation and the use of fertilizers.

sections.heading: Improving Soil Structure
sections.text: Deep ploughing, ripping or sub-soiling is needed to improve the structure of the soils on the cut part of the bench terraces.

sections.heading: Increasing Soil Fertility
sections.text: Green manuring, compost or sludge is needed in the initial period in order to increase soil fertility.

topics.title: Grassed Water Ways and Their Design
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: Grassed waterways are natural or manmade constructed channels established for the transport of concentrated flow at safe velocities from the catchment using adequate erosion resistant vegetation which cover the channels.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.text: These channels are used for the safe disposal of excess runoff from the crop lands to some safe outlet, namely rivers, reservoirs, streams etc. without causing soil erosion.

sections.heading: Use of Grassed Waterways
items: Terraced and bunded crop lands
Diversion channels
Spillways
Contour furrows

sections.heading: Outlet Construction
sections.text: The grassed waterways outlets are constructed prior to the construction of terraces, bunds etc. because grasses take time to get established on the channel bed.

topics.title: Support Practice Factor (P)
topics.definition: The support practice factor is a measure of the amount of support provided by a crop or plant to other crops growing nearby.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text: The support practice factor is a measure of the amount of support provided by a crop or plant to other crops growing nearby.

topics.title: Purpose of Grassed Waterways
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Business and Agribusiness
topics.definition: Grassed waterways are used as outlets to prevent rill and gully formation, while also improving soil aeration and water quality.

sections.heading: Benefits of Grassed Waterways
sections.text: These waterways can reduce sedimentation of nearby water bodies and pollutants in runoff. The vegetation improves the soil aeration and water quality (impacting the aquatic habitat) due to its nutrient removal through plant uptake and sorption by soil.

sections.heading: Wildlife Habitat
sections.text: The waterways can also provide a wildlife habitat.

topics.title: Design of Grassed Waterways
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The designs of grassed waterways are similar to the design of irrigation channels and are designed based on their functional requirements.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.text: Generally, these waterways are designed for carrying the maximum runoff for a 10- year recurrence interval period. The rational formula is invariably used to determine the peak runoff rate. Waterways can be shorter in length or sometimes, can be even very long.

sections.heading: Design Criteria
items: For shorter lengths, the estimated flow at the waterways outlets forms the design criterion.
For longer lengths, a variable capacity waterway is designed to account for the changing drainage areas.

topics.title: Size of Waterway
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The size of the waterway depends upon the expected runoff.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
sections.text: A 10 year recurrence interval is used to calculate the maximum expected runoff to the waterway. As the catchment area of the waterway increases towards the outlet, the expected runoff is calculated for different reaches of the waterway and used for design purposes.

sections.heading: Cross-Sectional Area Calculation
sections.text: The cross-sectional area is calculated using the formula: a = Q/V (9.1) where, = cross-sectional area of the channel, Q = expected maximum runoff, and = velocity of flow.

topics.title: Shape of Water Way
topics.category: Technical and Production Science | Digital Literacy and AgTech
topics.definition: The shape of the waterway depends upon the field conditions and type of the construction equipment used.

sections.heading: Common Shapes Adopted
sections.text: The three common shapes adopted are trapezoidal, triangular, and parabolic shapes.

sections.heading: Preferred Shape for Farm Machinery
items: parabolic shape
trapezoidal shape with very flat side slopes

topics.definition: The velocity of flow in a grassed waterway is dependent on the condition of the vegetation and the soil erodibility.

sections.heading: Design Dimensions for Trapezoidal Cross-section Fig. 9.2. Parabolic Cross-section
sections.text: The velocity of flow through the grassed waterway depends upon the ability of the vegetation in the channel to resist erosion.

sections.heading: Recommended velocities of flow based on the type of vegetation
items: 1.0 m/sec
2.5 m/sec

sections.heading: Types of Soil
sections.text: Permissible velocities are given for various types of soils.

topics.title: Design of Cross-Section
topics.definition: The design of a cross-section in agriculture refers to the selection of soil types that can withstand high velocities.
